This module defines the explicit smooth positive-density LSI convention \(2\alpha H\le J\) and guards real-valued conversions by finite divergence and Fisher information.

steps.title: tiltedMeasure
steps.body: For a real relative density \(r\), define \(\rho_r(dx)=r(x)\nu(dx)\) using withDensity (ENNReal.ofReal ∘ r). Positivity and normalization are later hypotheses, rather than part of this raw measure definition. A normalized positive \(r\) is the density of the current law relative to the target.

steps.title: relativeFisher
steps.body: Define \(I_\nu(r)=\int\|\nabla\log r\|^2d\rho_r\) as an extended nonnegative integral. The explicit density is differentiated pointwise, avoiding differentiation of an arbitrary almost-everywhere Radon–Nikodym representative. Later real-valued estimates prove finiteness before taking toReal.

steps.title: IsLogSobolev
steps.body: The target is a probability and satisfies \(2\alpha\operatorname{KL}(\rho_r\mid\nu)\le I_\nu(r)\) for every strictly positive \(C^1\) normalized relative density. The factor \(2\alpha\) fixes the convention used throughout the proof. This test class and its normalization are explicit; the definition contains no algorithm or entropy-decay claim.

steps.title: Why finite KL and Fisher information are separate obligations
steps.body: Apply the extended LSI to the supplied positive \(C^1\) probability density. Both KL and Fisher are assumed finite, so ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal preserves the inequality. Nonnegativity of \(2\alpha\) identifies the real value of its embedding, giving \(2\alpha H_\nu(r)\le I_\nu(r)_{\mathbb R}\).

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyFlow.lean.title: Relative entropy along an identified density path
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyFlow.lean.summary: Density entropy is the real conversion of the actual KL divergence of the tilted measure. With finite-entropy guards, LSI and a supplied dissipation inequality give exponential entropy decay along this path.

steps.title: Define actual density entropy with its finiteness guard
steps.body: Define the real entropy of a specified relative density as \(H_ u(r)=\operatorname{KL}(r u\mid u)_{\mathbb R}\). It uses the same tiltedMeasure and actual Mathlib KL as the LSI definition. Applications must separately establish finite KL before using it as an ordinary entropy value.

steps.title: Apply the finite real LSI at every time
steps.body: At each interpolation time, positivity, \(C^1\) regularity, normalization, and finite KL/Fisher allow IsLogSobolev.entropy_le_fisher to give \(2\alpha H(t)\le I(t)\). Combine this with the explicit right-dissipation identity and entropy continuity in entropy_decay_of_dissipation. The conclusion is decay at rate \(2\alpha\) for that admissible density path; identifying an actual evolution with the path remains an application obligation.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ULALaw.lean.title: Actual Gaussian ULA laws and their frozen-drift interpolation
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ULALaw.lean.summary: Define the frozen-drift law \(\rho_{k,t}=\operatorname{Law}(X_k-t\nabla U(X_k)+\sqrt{2t}Z)\), with independent standard Gaussian \(Z\), and \(\rho_{k+1}=\rho_{k,h}\). The endpoint and probability identities connect the entropy argument to the actual algorithm.

steps.title: ulaEntropy
steps.body: Set \(H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\rho_k\mid\nu)_{\mathbb R}\). The definition uses the actual extended KL of the ULA law, followed by toReal. Separate theorems prove finite KL wherever this is used as ordinary real entropy; the definition alone would not exclude infinity.

steps.title: ulaEntropy zero
steps.body: Substitute the definitional identity \(\rho_0=\mu\) into the entropy definition. This gives \(H_0=\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid\nu)_{\mathbb R}\), the initial term appearing in the final exponential bound.

steps.title: interpolationLaw
steps.body: Define \(\rho_t=(T_t)_*(\mu\otimes\gamma)\), where \(T_t(x,z)=x-t\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\). The product encodes independence. This is an alias of the actual ulaLawStep; its frozen-drift Gaussian interpolation interpretation applies to \(t\ge0\).

steps.title: ulaLaws
steps.body: Iterate the actual independent-Gaussian transition at fixed step \(h\): \(\rho_k=P_h^k\mu\). The definition is on measures, while the separate chain-law theorems identify independent iid implementations with these same laws.

steps.title: interpolationLaw endpoint
steps.body: At elapsed time \(h\), the interpolation from \(\rho_k\) is \(P_h\rho_k\). The preceding successor identity therefore proves \(\rho_{k,h}=\rho_{k+1}\). This is the law equality used to turn a continuous interpolation bound into the discrete entropy step.

steps.title: ulaLaws isProbability
steps.body: Induct from the initial probability \(\mu\). At the successor rewrite the iterate as one interpolation step at time \(h\), then apply probability preservation. Every algorithm law is therefore a probability before applying KL and LSI identities.

steps.title: interpolationLaw zero
steps.body: At \(t=0\), both the drift increment and Gaussian increment vanish, so the update map is first-coordinate projection. Integrating out the standard Gaussian probability returns \(\mu\). This endpoint identity needs no potential regularity.

steps.title: ulaLaws zero
steps.body: The zeroth iterate of a function is the identity, hence \(\rho_0=\mu\). Lean uses definitional equality, which makes the initial-entropy rewrite exact rather than an asymptotic endpoint argument.

steps.title: ulaLaws succ
steps.body: The successor-iterate identity gives \(\rho_{k+1}=P_h(\rho_k)\). Lean invokes Function.iterate_succ_apply', whose order matches applying one more transition to the current law.

steps.title: interpolationLaw isProbability
steps.body: Lipschitzness makes the gradient continuous and the joint update measurable. The product \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) is a probability, and its pushforward has the same total mass. Evaluating the mapped measure on the whole space proves normalization of \(\rho_t\).

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianDrift.lea.title: Gaussian displacement and frozen-gradient error energy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianDrift.lea.summary: For \(Y_t=X-t\nabla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\), independent Gaussian noise makes the cross term vanish, giving \(\mathbb E\|Y_t-X\|^2=t^2\mathbb E\|\nabla U(X)\|^2+2td\). Gradient Lipschitzness bounds the corresponding frozen-gradient error by \(L^2\) times this moment.

steps.title: integral norm sq stdGaussian
steps.body: Choose a finite orthonormal basis and use \(\|Z\|^2=\sum_i\langle e_i,Z\rangle^2\). Each standard Gaussian coordinate has second moment one, proved using its dual variance formula and zero mean. Gaussian \(L^2\) membership justifies integrating the finite sum, giving \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2=d\), also when \(d=0\).

steps.title: integral norm sq affine stdGaussian
steps.body:
Expand \(\|ag(X)+bZ\|^2=a^2\|g(X)\|^2+2ab\langle g(X),Z\rangle+b^2\|Z\|^2\). The \(L^2\) hypothesis on \(g\) and Gaussian \(L^2\) membership prove all three terms integrable on the independent product.

The product bilinear-integral theorem factors the cross expectation as \(\langle\mathbb Eg(X),\mathbb EZ\rangle=0\). The product marginals identify the first energy, and integral_norm_sq_stdGaussian identifies the noise energy. Hence the integral is \(a^2\mathbb E\|g\|^2+b^2d\).

steps.title: malaProposal sub initial
steps.body: Subtract \(x\) from \(T_t(x,z)=x-t\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\). Additive cancellation leaves \(-t\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\). This algebraic identity shows why a state second moment is unnecessary when only displacement energy is estimated.

steps.title: frozen displacement second moment
steps.body: Apply the affine Gaussian energy formula with \(a=-t\), \(b=\sqrt{2t}\), and \(g=\nabla U\). For \(t\ge0\), \(b^2=2t\), yielding \(\mathbb E\|T_t-X\|^2=t^2\mathbb E\|\nabla U(X)\|^2+2td\). Independence and centering have already discharged the cross term.

steps.title: frozen gradient error energy
steps.body:
Lipschitzness gives \(\|\nabla U(T_t)-\nabla U(X)\|^2\le L^2\|T_t-X\|^2\) pointwise. Convert integrability of the squared gradient to \(L^2\) membership, so the displacement has an integrable squared norm.

Continuity of the proposal and gradient proves measurability of the squared discrepancy. Domination by the integrable displacement energy proves its integrability; integral_mono and the exact displacement moment then give \(L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). This is a joint-law estimate; a state-space conditional drift is constructed separately.

steps.title: frozen displacement memLp
steps.body: Pull the square-integrable initial gradient to the first product coordinate and the square-integrable Gaussian identity to the second. Their scalar multiples and sum lie in \(L^2\). The displacement identity rewrites this sum as \(T_t(X,Z)-X\).

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/KLOfDensity.lean.title: Identify density entropy and Fisher integrals
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/KLOfDensity.lean.summary: For a strictly positive relative density, with the stated differentiability and integrability, the actual likelihood ratio equals \(\log r\). This identifies the formal KL divergence with \(\int r\log r\,d\nu\), proves its finiteness and identifies the real Fisher value with its score-energy integral.

steps.title: llr tiltedMeasure ae eq log
steps.body: The with-density measure is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu\), and its Radon–Nikodym derivative equals ofReal r \(\nu\)-almost everywhere. Absolute continuity transfers that equality to \(\rho_r\)-almost everywhere. Taking the real logarithm gives the actual log-likelihood ratio \(\log r\).

steps.title: klDiv tiltedMeasure ne top
steps.body: Absolute continuity follows from the with-density construction. Integrability of \(r\log r\) gives integrability of \(\log r\) under \(\rho_r\), and the log-likelihood identity identifies that with the KL integrand. The standard finite-KL criterion therefore proves \(\operatorname{KL}(\rho_r\mid\nu)<\infty\).

steps.title: densityEntropy eq integral
steps.body: For normalized \( u\) and \( ho_r\), the finite-KL integral formula has mass correction \( u(E)- ho_r(E)=0\). Replace the log-likelihood ratio by \(\log r\), then change density to obtain \(H_ u(r)=\int r\log r\,d u\). The integrability premise is used before invoking that formula.

steps.title: relativeFisher toReal eq integral
steps.body: Nonnegativity and integrability identify the real value of the extended Fisher integral with the ordinary integral under \( ho_r\). The weighted-measure formula then rewrites it as \(I_ u(r)_{\mathbb R}=\int r\| abla\log r\|^2d u\). Both representations refer to the same supplied density.

steps.title: integral tiltedMeasure
steps.body: For measurable \(r\ge0\), the Bochner with-density formula gives \(\int g\,d\rho_r=\int r(x)g(x)d\nu\). The embedded density is finite pointwise and has real value \(r\), so the theorem's extended-to-real scalar action simplifies to ordinary multiplication.

steps.title: integrable log tiltedMeasure iff
steps.body: Apply the with-density integrability criterion to \(g=\log r\). Since the density is measurable, finite, and nonnegative, it yields \(\log r\in L^1(\rho_r)\iff r\log r\in L^1(\nu)\). This is the exact entropy-integrability bridge used before converting KL to real values.

steps.title: relativeFisher ne top
steps.body: The squared score is nonnegative. Its ordinary integrability implies finiteness of its extended nonnegative integral, by the hasFiniteIntegral_iff_ofReal criterion. That extended integral is exactly relativeFisher.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDerivative.title: Differentiate the entropy integrand under domination
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDerivative.summary: The scalar identity \((r\log r)\prime=r\prime(\log r+1)\), for \(r>0\), lifts to an integral derivative under the explicitly supplied common local integrable bound. Domination is a premise, not a consequence of Gaussian convolution in this module.

steps.title: hasDerivAt mul log
steps.body: If \(r(t)>0\), the product and logarithm chain rules give \((r\log r)'=\dot r\log r+r\dot r/r\). Positivity supplies \(r(t)\ne0\), so cancellation gives \(\dot r(\log r+1)\). Lean proves that cancellation explicitly before simplifying the derivative expression.

steps.title: hasDerivAt integral mul log of dominated
steps.body:
For almost every spatial point, apply hasDerivAt_mul_log throughout a common time neighborhood. Its derivative is bounded in norm by the supplied integrable spatial envelope, uniformly over that neighborhood.

The dominated differentiation theorem uses this bound, integrability of \(r_t\log r_t\), and measurability of both integrands. It concludes both integrability of \(\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\) and \(\frac d{dt}\int r_t\log r_t d\nu=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)d\nu\). The derivative of the integral is a conclusion, not a hypothesis.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Regularity.lean.title: Local regularity needed for actual entropy calculus
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Regularity.lean.summary: A LocalEntropyRegularity package supplies positive densities, time derivatives, and local integrable domination. Its consequences prove finite KL, continuity, derivatives and a production inequality for the identified density entropy; existence of these packages is retained as a premise.

steps.title: LocalEntropyRegularity
steps.body: At a fixed time \(t\), store a common time neighborhood, an integrable spatial envelope for \(\dot r_u(\log r_u+1)\), local pointwise positivity/differentiability, and measurability/integrability of the entropy integrands. These are sufficient data for dominated differentiation. The structure contains no derivative of the entropy integral and no entropy-production estimate.

steps.title: LocalEntropyRegularity.hasDerivAt entropy
steps.body: Pass the stored neighborhood, envelope, and pointwise derivative fields to hasDerivAt_integral_mul_log_of_dominated. It concludes both integrability of the differentiated integrand and the derivative formula for \(\int r_t\log r_t d\nu\). This is the calculus theorem supplied by the local data, not a field assumed in them.

steps.title: Test an admissible forced weak equation
steps.body: Use local dominated differentiation to compute \(H'(t)=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)d\nu\). The forced weak equation, weighted Fisher integrability, and drift-energy integrability then permit the entropy test and integrated Young inequality. The result is \(H'(t)\le-3I(t)/4+E(t)\), with \(E(t)=\int r_t\|e_t\|^2d\nu\). No numerical bound on \(E(t)\) is assumed in this declaration.

steps.title: klDiv finite of localRegularity
steps.body: The local regularity data include integrability of \(r_t\log r_t\). Positivity and \(C^1\) regularity give a measurable nonnegative density. Apply klDiv_tiltedMeasure_ne_top to obtain finite actual KL before interpreting its toReal value as entropy.

steps.title: densityEntropy continuousOn of regular
steps.body: At every point of the closed interval, dominated differentiation makes the ordinary entropy integral differentiable and hence continuous. Normalization and the finite-entropy density formula identify that integral with actual KL entropy at every interval point. ContinuousOn.congr transfers continuity to \(t\mapsto\operatorname{KL}(\rho_t\mid\nu)_{\mathbb R}\).

steps.title: densityEntropy hasDerivWithinAt of regular
steps.body:
The ordinary entropy integral has the derivative computed by local regularity. Its equality with actual KL is known only for normalized densities in \([0,T]\), so the proof works with right derivatives at \(t\in[0,T)\).

In a sufficiently small right neighborhood, \(u\ge t\ge0\) and \(u<T\), so the density formula identifies both functions there and at \(t\). congr_of_eventuallyEq transfers the derivative to actual KL. This avoids requiring path normalization outside the interpolation interval.

steps.title: Express the production bound using relative Fisher information
steps.body: Convert squared-score integrability under \(\rho_t\) into weighted Fisher integrability under \(\nu\) by the with-density criterion. Apply the regular weak-equation derivative estimate, and identify its weighted integral with relativeFisher's real value. Pair that estimate with the actual-KL right derivative from the preceding theorem to get \(H'(t)\le-3I(t)/4+E(t)\) for the identified density law.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ScoreCalculus.lea.title: Relative scores turn the weak equation into entropy production
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ScoreCalculus.lea.summary: The chain rule \(\nabla\log r=\nabla r/r\) converts the entropy test \(\log r+1\) into the relative score. The weak identity supplied for this test then gives Fisher dissipation, with an extra score/error pairing when drift forcing is present.

steps.title: gradient log of pos
steps.body: The logarithm chain rule gives \(D\log r(x)=r(x)^{-1}Dr(x)\) when \(r(x)>0\). The real Hilbert-space gradient is the Riesz representative of the derivative; linearity of that identification gives \(\nabla\log r(x)=r(x)^{-1}\nabla r(x)\).

steps.title: gradient log add one of pos
steps.body: Adding a constant to a scalar function leaves its Fréchet derivative unchanged. Apply the gradient's derivative-based definition to obtain \(\nabla(\log r+1)=\nabla\log r\). The explicit differentiability/positivity arguments align the statement with the entropy-test calculus.

steps.title: inner gradient entropy test
steps.body: Rearrange the positive-density score identity to \( abla r=r abla\log r\). Pair this with \( abla(\log r+1)= abla\log r\) and use \(\langle s,s angle=\|s\|^2\). The Dirichlet integrand is therefore \(\langle abla r, abla(\log r+1) angle=r\| abla\log r\|^2\).

steps.title: entropy production of weak identity
steps.body: The strictly positive \(C^1\) density makes \(\psi=\log r+1\) a \(C^1\) test. The entropy derivative integrability is supplied, and the pointwise gradient identity converts its Dirichlet integrability to the supplied weighted Fisher integrability. Substitute this admissible test into the explicit weak equation to obtain \(\int\dot r(\log r+1)d u=-\int r\| abla\log r\|^2d u\).

steps.title: Test the weak equation with a noncompact function
steps.body: Use the same \(C^1\) entropy test in the forced weak equation. Rewrite the Dirichlet term by inner_gradient_entropy_test and the forcing gradient by gradient_log_add_one_of_pos. The three explicit integrability conditions justify the substitution, giving entropy production \(-I+\int r\langle e,\nabla\log r\rangle d\nu\). Admissibility of this noncompact test remains part of the weak-equation premise.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDecay.lean.title: Integrate a forced entropy-dissipation inequality
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDecay.lean.summary: An integrating factor solves \(H\prime\le-aH+b\) as \(H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+(b/a)(1-e^{-at})\), under the displayed positive-rate, continuity and one-sided derivative assumptions. The entropy wrapper supplies the appropriate rate from LSI and dissipation.

steps.title: A scalar affine comparison from right derivatives
steps.body: For continuous \(H\) with right derivative bounded by \(-aH+b\), \(a>0\), compare it to the exact scalar ODE solution. The one-sided Grönwall theorem accepts the right derivative through its right-slope liminf inequality. Simplifying its explicit solution gives \(H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+(b/a)(1-e^{-at})\). Neither \(H\) nor \(b\) needs to be nonnegative.

steps.title: Scalar LSI and dissipation give rate 2α
steps.body: The supplied dissipation identity is \(H'=-I\), and the scalar LSI premise is \(2\alpha H\le I\). Therefore \(H'\le-2\alpha H\). Apply the affine comparison theorem with \(a=2\alpha\) and \(b=0\), obtaining \(H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\). This scalar theorem does not itself establish the dissipation identity for a law-valued evolution.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DriftError.lean.title: Spend one quarter of Fisher information on drift error
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DriftError.lean.summary: Young’s inequality \(\langle a,b\rangle\le\frac14\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2\) bounds the error pairing in entropy production. Weighted energy integrability yields an actual integral inequality \(H\prime\le-\frac34J+\mathcal E\).

steps.title: inner le quarter norm sq add norm sq
steps.body: Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\langle e,s\rangle\le\|e\|\|s\|\). Expand the nonnegative square \((\|e\|-\|s\|/2)^2\ge0\) to get \(\|e\|\|s\|\le\|e\|^2+\|s\|^2/4\). This is the Young coefficient that preserves three quarters of Fisher information.

steps.title: integrable weighted inner of energy
steps.body: Multiply the absolute Young bound by the nonnegative weight \(r\). It dominates \(|r\langle e,s\rangle|\) by \(r\|s\|^2/4+r\|e\|^2\). Both energy functions are integrable, so the assumed measurability and Integrable.mono' prove integrability of the cross term.

steps.title: entropy production le of forced weak identity
steps.body: First derive cross-term integrability from the two finite energies and its measurability. The forced weak identity tested by \(\log r+1\) gives production \(-I+\int r\langle e,s\rangle\). Insert the integrated Young bound to obtain \(-\frac34I+\int r\|e\|^2\). The entropy differential inequality is therefore proved from the stated spatial weak identity.

steps.title: abs inner le quarter norm sq add norm sq
steps.body: Use the absolute Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(|\langle e,s\rangle|\le\|e\|\|s\|\), followed by the same square expansion. The absolute-value version controls integrability of the signed cross term before its integral is estimated.

steps.title: integral weighted inner le quarter fisher add energy
steps.body: Multiply the pointwise Young inequality by \(r\ge0\), then integrate. The supplied integrability permits splitting the upper integral and pulling out \(1/4\). Thus \(\int r\langle e,s\rangle\le\frac14\int r\|s\|^2+\int r\|e\|^2\). No probability normalization of the weight is needed.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/OneStep.lean.title: The conditional one-step KL contraction with bias 6
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/OneStep.lean.summary: Assume the displayed LSI, gradient-moment and interpolation differential bounds. For \(0

steps.title: Absorb a small initial-entropy forcing into the exponential gap
steps.body: For \(0\le x\le1/4\), the tangent bound for the exponential gives \(e^{-3x/2}\ge1/2\). Multiply \(e^{x/2}\ge1+x/2\) by \(e^{-3x/2}\); then \(e^{-x}\ge e^{-3x/2}+(x/2)e^{-3x/2}\ge e^{-3x/2}+x/4\). This quantitative rate gap absorbs the initial-entropy forcing.

steps.title: Uniform forcing, affine comparison and the coefficient 6
steps.body:
Combine \(2\alpha H\le I\) and \(H'\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\). The gradient bound \(G_0\le(4L^2/\alpha)H(0)+2dL\) and \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\) give a uniform inequality \(H'\le-(3\alpha/2)H+b\), with \(b=(\alpha/4)H(0)+(5/2)hdL^2\). The proof establishes \(hL\le1/4\), \(\alpha h\le1/4\), and the coefficient bound \(h^2L^2(4L^2/\alpha)\le\alpha/4\) before this substitution.

Apply affine_decay_of_deriv_right_le and bound its forcing integral by \(bh\), using \(1-e^{-ah}\le ah\). The exponential-gap lemma absorbs \((\alpha h/4)H(0)\), changing the decay factor from \(e^{-3\alpha h/2}\) to \(e^{-\alpha h}\). Nonnegativity of \(H(0)\) justifies multiplying that scalar bound. Finally enlarge the remaining nonnegative \((5/2)h^2dL^2\) term to \(6h^2dL^2\), obtaining the stated one-step estimate.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DiscreteEntropy.l.title: Iterate entropy contraction and obtain the bias constant 8
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DiscreteEntropy.l.summary: Starting from \(H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2dL^2\), induction retains the exact geometric sum. The small-step denominator estimate \(1-e^{-\alpha h}\ge\frac34\alpha h\) gives \(H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+8hdL^2/\alpha\).

steps.title: Keep the exact geometric sum before simplifying it
steps.body: Set \(q=e^{-\alpha h}\in(0,1)\), \(b=6h^2dL^2\). The affine recurrence theorem sums \(H_{k+1}\le qH_k+b\) into \(H_k\le q^kH_0+b(1-q^k)/(1-q)\). Rewrite \(q^k=e^{-\alpha hk}\) using the exponential natural-multiple identity. No sign assumption on \(H_0\) is needed.

steps.title: three quarters mul le one sub exp neg
steps.body: The tangent bound \(e^x\ge1+x\), multiplied by \(e^{-x}\), gives \(1-e^{-x}\ge x/(1+x)\). For \(0\le x\le1/4\), elementary positive-denominator algebra shows \(x/(1+x)\ge3x/4\). This lower bound controls the geometric-series denominator in the bias floor.

steps.title: discrete entropy recurrence bound
steps.body: The nonnegative forcing gives \(H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+6h^2dL^2/(1-e^{-\alpha h})\). For \(\alpha h\le1/4\), the denominator is at least \(3\alpha h/4>0\). Divide and cancel to obtain the bias floor \(8hdL^2/\alpha\). Lean proves positivity of the denominator before multiplying across it.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/RegularizedTheore.title: Derive entropy calculus from regular interpolation hypotheses
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/RegularizedTheore.summary:
This wrapper replaces a supplied entropy derivative estimate with explicit regular density data, a forced weak identity and an error-energy bound. It then invokes the conditional ULA entropy endpoint. Constructing those regular interpolation data remains a displayed premise.

The full actual Gaussian ULA endpoint in UnconditionalTheorem.lean derives all necessary analytic estimates from smoothness, LSI, and finite initial KL. This module retains a reusable interface for explicitly specified interpolation data.

steps.title: Construct the entropy-calculus hypotheses and invoke the actual-law theorem
steps.body:
First use the density/law identity to prove probability normalization along each interpolation. Local regularity proves finite actual KL, score integrability proves finite Fisher, and densityEntropy_continuousOn_of_regular gives continuity of actual entropy.

Define the candidate derivative \(H'_k(t)=\int\dot r_{k,t}(\log r_{k,t}+1)d\pi_U\). The regular weak-equation theorem proves that this is the actual right derivative and that it is bounded by \(-3I/4+E\). Insert the supplied drift-energy bound \(E\le t^2L^2G_k+2tdL^2\), then invoke ula_kl_bound_of_interpolation.

The final estimate is therefore derived without assuming an entropy derivative, a production inequality, or a discrete recurrence. This wrapper still explicitly requires the regular density construction, its admissible weak equation, its drift-energy estimate, and the entropy-to-gradient moment bound; the wrapper does not itself construct them from LSI.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationData.title: A reusable regular-interpolation interface
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationData.summary:
The RegularInterpolationData structure bundles density paths identifying the actual ULA interpolation, regularity, weak-equation and error controls. Its methods derive path probability, finite KL, the one-step recurrence and the iterated entropy bound. Existence of this package is not asserted by its definition.

The full actual Gaussian ULA endpoint in UnconditionalTheorem.lean derives all necessary analytic estimates from smoothness, LSI, and finite initial KL. This module retains a reusable interface for explicitly specified interpolation data.

steps.title: Specify the actual laws, density regularity and energy data
steps.body: Package the relative densities \(r_{k,t}\), their time derivatives, and drift fields together with the exact law identity, positivity, spatial regularity, local entropy domination, finite score/error energies, admissible weak equation, drift-energy bound, and gradient-moment bound. These remain explicit mathematical inputs. No entropy derivative, entropy recurrence, or convergence estimate is a structure field.

steps.title: RegularInterpolationData.path probability
steps.body: The data's law field identifies the tilted density with the actual interpolation from \(\rho_k\). Probability preservation proves that interpolation is normalized. Rewrite by the law identity to obtain normalization of each density along the supplied path.

steps.title: RegularInterpolationData.kl finite
steps.body: Use local entropy regularity to prove finite KL for each relative density, then apply the time-zero law identification in ula_kl_finite_of_interpolation. The target probability instance is explicit; in the final theorem it is supplied by the LSI hypothesis.

steps.title: RegularInterpolationData.one step
steps.body: Define \(H'_k(t)\) by the differentiated entropy integral. The regular weak-equation theorem proves its right-derivative identity and Fisher/drift production bound. Data fields supply probability, KL/Fisher finiteness, continuity, numerical error-energy and gradient bounds. Feed these proved ingredients to ula_kl_one_step_of_interpolation to derive the recurrence rather than assuming it in the data.

steps.title: RegularInterpolationData.kl bound
steps.body: Unpack every analytic field into ula_kl_bound_of_regular_interpolation, retaining LSI, potential smoothness, and the step regime as separate arguments. Its already proved differentiation, one-step estimate, and geometric iteration give the full displayed KL bound for the actual ULA laws represented by the data.

UnadjustedLangevin/Gibbs.lean.title: Gibbs normalization and second moments
UnadjustedLangevin/Gibbs.lean.summary: On a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, differentiability and \(m\)-strong convexity with \(m>0\) imply that \(\pi(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\) is a probability measure with finite second moment. This establishes existence of the target measure used throughout the coupling proof.

steps.title: gibbsWeight
steps.body: The unnormalized density is \(w_U(x)=e^{-U(x)}\), embedded in \([0,\infty]\) with ENNReal.ofReal. This choice lets the partition integral retain the value infinity; positivity of the exponential ensures that embedding does not discard any part of the density.

steps.title: gibbsPartition
steps.body: The partition function is \(Z_U=\int e^{-U(x)}\,dx\), formed as a nonnegative extended integral. At this definition no finiteness assumption is made. Later normalization uses separate proofs of \(0<Z_U\) and \(Z_U<\infty\), which are needed to justify cancellation with its inverse.

steps.title: gibbsMeasure
steps.body: Define \(\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\) using volume.withDensity. The inverse is the extended nonnegative inverse. The definition therefore exists for every potential, while the later probability theorem proves that it has total mass one under the stated strong convexity assumptions.

steps.title: integrable exp neg mul norm sq
steps.body: For \(a>0\), \(e^{-a\|x\|^2}\) is Lebesgue integrable in finite dimension. The Lean proof specializes GaussianFourier.integrable_cexp_neg_mul_sq_norm_add to real positive precision \(a\) and zero linear term, then takes the real part. The complex Gaussian integrand is the real embedding of the desired exponential, so the final simplification identifies the functions exactly. This also includes dimension zero.

steps.title: strongConvex quadratic lower bound
steps.body: Apply the strong supporting-plane inequality at zero: \(U(x)\ge U(0)+\langle\nabla U(0),x\rangle+\frac m2\|x\|^2\). Cauchy–Schwarz and \(ab\le a^2/m+(m/4)b^2\), valid for \(m>0\), absorb the linear term. The result is \(U(x)\ge U(0)-\|\nabla U(0)\|^2/m+(m/4)\|x\|^2\). Lean isolates this scalar square inequality before its final arithmetic rearrangement.

steps.title: integrable exp neg of strongConvex
steps.body: Exponentiating the quadratic lower bound gives \(e^{-U(x)}\le e^{-U(0)+\|\nabla U(0)\|^2/m}e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\). The right side is an integrable Gaussian multiple. Differentiability supplies continuity and measurability of the left side, so Integrable.mono' transfers integrability from that explicit dominating function.

steps.title: integrable norm sq mul exp neg mul norm sq
steps.body: For \(a>0\), split the Gaussian decay into two equal factors. The scalar function \(s\mapsto s e^{-(a/2)s}\) is bounded on \([0,\infty)\), so \(\|x\|^2e^{-a\|x\|^2}\le C_a e^{-(a/2)\|x\|^2}\). The remaining Gaussian is integrable; the proof checks measurability and nonnegativity before applying domination.

steps.title: integrable norm sq mul exp neg of strongConvex
steps.body: Multiply the previous Gibbs Gaussian domination by \(\|x\|^2\). Its right side has the form \(C\|x\|^2e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\), whose integrability was proved separately. The pointwise inequality uses \(\|x\|^2\ge0\), so multiplying it preserves order; this is the second-moment input for the normalized measure.

steps.title: gibbsPartition pos
steps.body: The continuous function \(e^{-U}\) is strictly positive everywhere. Its extended integral cannot vanish: a zero integral of a nonnegative measurable function would force it to vanish almost everywhere, contradicting positivity on a nonzero-volume open set. This proves \(0<Z_U\) without requiring an upper bound on \(Z_U\).

steps.title: gibbsPartition ne top
steps.body: Strong convexity with \(m>0\) has already given ordinary integrability of \(e^{-U}\). For a nonnegative integrable function its extended integral is finite. Unfolding gibbsPartition identifies that integral exactly with \(Z_U\), giving the guard needed for inverse cancellation.

steps.title: gibbsPartition eq ofReal integral
steps.body: Nonnegativity and integrability identify the extended integral with the embedded real integral: \(Z_U=\operatorname{ofReal}(\int e^{-U}\,dx)\). The proof uses the genuine integral/lintegral comparison theorem, so it cannot identify an infinite partition with the default real value of an undefined integral.

steps.title: integral exp neg pos
steps.body: Combine \(0<Z_U\) with \(Z_U=\operatorname{ofReal}(\int e^{-U}\,dx)\). Positivity of ofReal is equivalent to positivity of its real argument, proving that the ordinary normalizing constant is strictly positive and allowing real division by it later.

steps.title: isProbabilityMeasure gibbsMeasure
steps.body: The mass of a density measure is its extended density integral. Pull the constant \(Z_U^{-1}\) out to get \(\pi_U(H)=Z_U^{-1}Z_U\). The proofs that \(Z_U\ne0\) and \(Z_U\ne\infty\) justify this product being one. This theorem constructs the IsProbabilityMeasure instance rather than assuming normalization.

steps.title: integrable norm sq gibbsMeasure
steps.body: Changing measure converts integrability under \(\pi_U\) to integrability of \(Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\|x\|^2\) under volume. The weighted second moment is already integrable, and the real normalizing factor is a finite scalar. The with-density theorem supplies the almost-everywhere measurability and finiteness guards for this conversion.

steps.title: memLp id gibbsMeasure
steps.body: For the identity random variable, membership in \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\) is equivalent to integrability of \(\|x\|^2\). The identity is measurable, and the preceding weighted-moment theorem supplies the integral. Lean uses the \(p=2\) characterization of MemLp, retaining the actual function before passing to any quotient class.

steps.title: memLp sub const gibbsMeasure
steps.body: Since \(\pi_U\) is a probability, the constant map \(x\mapsto z\) belongs to \(L^2\). Subtract it from the identity, already in \(L^2(\pi_U)\), to obtain \(x\mapsto x-z\in L^2(\pi_U)\). This is a moment assertion for every chosen center, without requiring that the center minimize the potential.

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsConcentration.le.title: Concentration around a minimizer without differentiability
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsConcentration.le.summary: For a continuous \(q\)-strongly convex potential \(F\), \(q>0\), and an explicitly supplied minimizer \(z\), this module proves the equilibrium radius \(\int\|x-z\|^2d\pi_F\le2d/q\). The proof uses dilation and convexity, so it also applies to the nonsmooth potentials used by proximal algorithms.

steps.title: strongConvex mode quadratic bound
steps.body: Use strong convexity at the midpoint of \(z\) and \(x\), then use minimality \(F(z)\le F((z+x)/2)\). Rearranging yields \(F(x)\ge F(z)+(q/4)\|x-z\|^2\). This argument uses values of \(F\), not a derivative or a first-order optimality assertion at the minimizer.

steps.title: integrable exp neg of continuous strongConvex mode
steps.body: For \(q>0\), the midpoint bound gives \(e^{-F(x)}\le e^{-F(z)}e^{-(q/4)\|x-z\|^2}\). Translation invariance reduces integrability of the majorant to the centered Gaussian integral. Continuity makes the density measurable, so domination proves integrability without differentiability of \(F\).

steps.title: integrable sq dist mul exp neg of continuous strongConvex mode
steps.body: Multiply the translated Gaussian bound by \(\|x-z\|^2\). Translation preserves Lebesgue measure, and a quadratic times a decaying Gaussian is integrable. Lean transports that integrability through \(x\mapsto x-z\) and then applies the nonnegative domination theorem to the desired weighted moment.

steps.title: Contract toward the mode
steps.body: For \(0<r<1\), compare \(F(z+r(x-z))\) with \(F(x)\) using strong convexity and \(F(z)\le F(x)\). Exponentiating and using \(e^u\ge1+u\) produces a linear correction in \(\|x-z\|^2\). The dilation \(x\mapsto z+r(x-z)\) multiplies volume by \(r^d\), hence \(Z+(q/2)r(1-r)M\le r^{-d}Z\), with \(M=\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}dx\).

steps.title: integral sq dist mul exp neg le of continuous strongConvex mode
steps.body: Subtract \(Z\) from the dilation inequality and divide by \(1-r>0\). As \(r\uparrow1\), \((r^{-d}-1)/(1-r)\to d\), while \((q/2)rM\to(q/2)M\). The order-closed limit theorem yields \(M\le(2d/q)Z\). Lean proves the one-sided derivative limit of the scalar power before passing the inequality to the limit.

steps.title: integrable sq dist gibbs of continuous strongConvex mode
steps.body: The density-measure integrability criterion changes the desired \(\pi_F\)-integral into a constant multiple of \(\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}dx\). Its finiteness follows from the continuous, strongly convex mode estimate. No score moment or smoothness assumption is introduced during normalization.

steps.title: integral sq dist gibbs le of continuous strongConvex mode
steps.body: First prove \(Z>0\), \(Z<\infty\), and integrability of the weighted distance. Then write \(\int\|x-z\|^2d\pi_F=M/Z\) and apply \(M\le(2d/q)Z\). Cancellation is justified by positivity of \(Z\); the result is \(\mathbb E_{\pi_F}\|X-z\|^2\le2d/q\), including \(d=0\).

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsScore.lean.title: Subgaussian Gibbs score and its sharp second moment
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsScore.lean.summary: Differentiability, an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and finite Gibbs normalization suffice for \(\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\pi\le Ld\). Strong convexity is used only by the final wrapper to derive normalization.

steps.title: gibbsWeight mul exp score le
steps.body: The descent lemma gives \(U(x+v)\le U(x)+\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle+(L/2)\|v\|^2\). Negate and exponentiate, then rearrange to \(e^{-U(x)}e^{-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}e^{-U(x+v)}\). Lean first establishes the real inequality and then embeds it in the extended nonnegative numbers.

steps.title: gibbs score lmgf le
steps.body: Integrate the pointwise exponential-score bound. Translation invariance gives \(\int e^{-U(x+v)}dx=Z_U\); normalization cancels this factor, leaving \(\mathbb E_{\pi_U}e^{-\langle\nabla U,v\rangle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\). Finiteness of \(Z_U\) is explicit because extended inverse cancellation needs it.

steps.title: gibbs score subgaussian
steps.body: Apply the preceding bound with the vector \(-tv\), for every real \(t\). The exponent becomes \(t\langle\nabla U,v\rangle\) and the right side is \(e^{t^2L\|v\|^2/2}\). This is exactly HasSubgaussianMGF with variance proxy \(L\|v\|^2\); the proof also establishes exponential integrability required by that structure.

steps.title: sq le exp add exp neg sub two
steps.body: The series \(\cosh a=\sum_{n\ge0}a^{2n}/(2n)!\) has nonnegative terms, so retaining its first two terms gives \(\cosh a\ge1+a^2/2\). Substitute \(2\cosh a=e^a+e^{-a}\) and rearrange to \(a^2\le e^a+e^{-a}-2\). Lean uses Real.hasSum_cosh with sum_le_hasSum, explicitly proving nonnegativity of every discarded even-power term.

steps.title: integral sq le of subgaussian
steps.body: Integrate \(t^2X^2\le e^{tX}+e^{-tX}-2\), giving \(t^2\mathbb EX^2\le2(e^{ct^2/2}-1)\). Subgaussianity provides the exponential integrability and hence the square integrability needed here. Divide by \(t^2\) for \(t\ne0\), and let \(t\to0\) to obtain \(\mathbb EX^2\le c\). Lean computes the scalar limit before applying closedness of order.

steps.title: integral norm sq gradient gibbs le
steps.body: Choose an orthonormal basis \((e_i)_{i=1}^d\) and use Parseval: \(\| abla U(x)\|^2=\sum_i\langle abla U(x),e_i angle^2\). Each coordinate is subgaussian with proxy \(L\), hence has second moment at most \(L\). Finite-sum integrability permits integration term by term, yielding \(\mathbb E_{\pi_U}\| abla U\|^2\le Ld\).

steps.title: memLp gradient gibbsMeasure
steps.body: The coordinate subgaussian bounds prove integrability of every squared gradient coordinate. Summing over the finite orthonormal basis proves integrability of \(\|\nabla U\|^2\). Lipschitz continuity provides strong measurability, and the MemLp square criterion packages those facts as \(\nabla U\in L^2(\pi_U)\).

steps.title: integral norm sq gradient gibbs le of strongConvex
steps.body: Strong convexity with \(m>0\) supplies the finite-partition premise of the score theorem. Substitute that proof into the first-order smoothness result to obtain \(\mathbb E_{\pi_U}\|\nabla U\|^2\le Ld\). The strong convexity constant is used for normalization here; it does not appear in the sharp score bound.

UnadjustedLangevin/StationaryMoments.lea.title: Transfer the Gibbs score estimate to an L² reference
UnadjustedLangevin/StationaryMoments.lea.summary: A reference variable \(Y\) whose law is \(\pi\) inherits \(\|\nabla U(Y)\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld}\). The assertion that its law is Gibbs is a displayed premise here.

steps.title: lpDrift norm le of gibbs law
steps.body: The representative of lpDrift equals \( abla U(Y)\) almost everywhere. Change variables using \(P\circ Y^{-1}=\pi_U\), so its squared \(L^2(P)\) norm is \(\int\| abla U\|^2d\pi_U\le Ld\). Nonnegativity of the norm and of \(Ld\) then gives \(\| abla U(Y)\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\). The law identity, rather than independence, is the input to this transfer.

steps.title: lpDrift norm le of strongConvex gibbs law
steps.body: Use strong convexity to prove \(Z_U<\infty\), and apply the previous law-transfer theorem with that proof. The conclusion is the same \(\sqrt{Ld}\) bound for the lifted drift of any \(L^2\) variable with Gibbs law. There is no separate assumed drift-moment bound hidden in this specialization.

UnadjustedLangevin/Generator.lean.title: The Langevin generator annihilates Gibbs averages
UnadjustedLangevin/Generator.lean.summary: For compactly supported \(C^2\) test functions, \(\mathcal L\varphi=\Delta\varphi-\langle\nabla U,\nabla\varphi\rangle\) has zero Gibbs mean. These identities establish infinitesimal invariance; they alone do not assert stationarity of a stochastic process.

steps.title: directionalGenerator
steps.body: For a fixed direction \(v\), define \(L_v\varphi(x)=D(D\varphi(\cdot)[v])(x)[v]-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle D\varphi(x)[v]\). The first term is a directional second derivative of the test; the second is the directional gradient drift. No Hessian of \(U\) is part of this definition.

steps.title: langevinGenerator
steps.body: Choose the standard orthonormal basis and set \(L\varphi=\sum_iL_{e_i}\varphi\). The finite sum makes the construction meaningful in dimension zero and gives a direct path to directional integration by parts. A subsequent identity proves that this is the usual basis-independent \(\Delta\varphi-\langle\nabla U,\nabla\varphi\rangle\).

steps.title: integral gibbs eq weighted
steps.body: Unfold the normalized density and use the integral change-of-density theorem: \(\int f\,d\pi_U=(Z_U^{-1})_{\mathbb R}\int e^{-U(x)}f(x)dx\). Continuity of \(U\) makes the density measurable. The factor is written (gibbsPartition U)⁻¹.toReal because the partition was defined in extended nonnegative scalars.

steps.title: integrable gibbs of continuous hasCompactSupport
steps.body: A continuous compactly supported \(f\) gives a continuous compactly supported product \(e^{-U}f\), hence a Lebesgue-integrable function. The with-density integrability criterion and multiplication by the real normalization factor transfer this fact to \(\pi_U\). This explicitly supplies the integrability needed by subsequent linearity arguments.

steps.title: fderiv exp neg apply
steps.body: Apply the chain rule to \(x\mapsto e^{-U(x)}\): \(D(e^{-U})(x)[v]=-e^{-U(x)}DU(x)[v]\). The real Hilbert gradient identity rewrites \(DU(x)[v]\) as \(\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\). Only differentiability of \(U\) is used.

steps.title: integral weighted directionalGenerator eq zero
steps.body: Differentiate \(e^{-U(x)}D\varphi(x)[v]\) in direction \(v\). The product rule gives exactly \(e^{-U(x)}L_v\varphi(x)\). Since derivatives of a compactly supported \(C^2\) test remain compactly supported, this weighted first derivative is integrable and has zero integral by integration by parts. The proof establishes continuity and compact support before invoking that theorem.

steps.title: integral directionalGenerator gibbs eq zero
steps.body: Apply the weighted-to-Gibbs integral formula to \(L_v\varphi\). Its weighted Lebesgue integral is zero, so multiplication by the normalization factor still gives zero. This is infinitesimal invariance for a single direction and does not yet identify the law of a time-evolving process.

steps.title: continuous directionalGenerator
steps.body: The \(C^2\) hypothesis makes the first and second derivatives of \(\varphi\) continuous. The gradient of \(U\) is continuous by its Lipschitz hypothesis. Evaluating continuous linear maps in the fixed direction \(v\), multiplying the scalar factors, and subtracting therefore gives continuity of \(L_v\varphi\).

steps.title: hasCompactSupport directionalGenerator
steps.body: Outside the compact support of \(\varphi\), the test is locally zero, so its first and second derivatives vanish there. Both terms of \(L_v\varphi\) therefore vanish. The support inclusion puts the support of the generator inside the same compact set; no support property of \(U\) is required.

steps.title: integrable directionalGenerator gibbsMeasure
steps.body: Combine continuity of \(L_v\varphi\) with preservation of compact support. The established compact-support Gibbs integrability theorem then gives absolute integrability. This permits ordinary integral algebra, even though the ambient generator is not bounded uniformly for arbitrary tests.

steps.title: integrable langevinGenerator gibbsMeasure
steps.body: The full generator is the finite sum of its directional pieces. Each piece is integrable under \(\pi_U\), so the finite-sum integrability theorem applies. Finiteness of the basis is the reason no exchange of an infinite series and integral is required.

steps.title: integral weighted langevinGenerator eq zero
steps.body: Expand the finite basis sum defining \(L\varphi\) and distribute the Gibbs weight over it. Compact support supplies integrability of every summand, allowing \(\int\sum_i e^{-U}L_{e_i}\varphi=\sum_i\int e^{-U}L_{e_i}\varphi\). Every directional integral vanishes, hence so does their sum.

steps.title: integral langevinGenerator gibbs eq zero
steps.body: Normalization changes \(\int L\varphi\,d\pi_U\) into the real inverse partition times its weighted Lebesgue integral. The latter was proved to be zero. This establishes the full Gibbs infinitesimal invariance identity for compactly supported \(C^2\) tests.

steps.title: langevinGenerator eq laplacian sub inner
steps.body: The sum of the directional second derivatives over an orthonormal basis is the Laplacian. For the drift sum, \(D\varphi(x)[e_i]=\langle abla\varphi(x),e_i angle\); Parseval turns the sum of products with \(\langle abla U(x),e_i angle\) into \(\langle abla U(x), abla\varphi(x) angle\). The proof rewrites the basis definition into this conventional formula pointwise.

steps.title: integral laplacian sub gradient gibbs eq zero
steps.body: Replace the conventional expression \(\Delta\varphi-\langle\nabla U,\nabla\varphi\rangle\) by the equal basis-defined generator inside the integral. The established zero-generator integral then closes the result. The rewrite makes the displayed mathematical identity refer to the same function that the preceding Lean proof integrated.

UnadjustedLangevin/GeneratorDirichlet.le.title: Gibbs Dirichlet form, symmetry and dissipation
UnadjustedLangevin/GeneratorDirichlet.le.summary: For compactly supported \(C^2\) tests \(\varphi,\psi\), the generator obeys \(\int\varphi\mathcal L\psi\,d\pi=-\int\langle\nabla\varphi,\nabla\psi\rangle d\pi\). This provides the symmetric Dirichlet form at the test-function level.

steps.title: fderiv exp neg mul apply
steps.body: Differentiate the product \(e^{-U}\varphi\): \(D(e^{-U}\varphi)(x)[v]=e^{-U(x)}(D\varphi(x)[v]-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\varphi(x))\). Lean combines the product rule with the already proved derivative of the Gibbs weight, then collects the common exponential factor algebraically.

steps.title: integral weighted directional dirichlet
steps.body: Integrate by parts the derivative of \(e^{-U}\varphi\) against \(D\psi[v]\). The weighted product rule separates a \(D\varphi[v]D\psi[v]\) term from the drift term, giving \(\int e^{-U}\varphi L_v\psi=-\int e^{-U}D\varphi[v]D\psi[v]\). Compact support and \(C^2\) regularity justify every derivative and integral involved.

steps.title: integral directionalGenerator dirichlet gibbs
steps.body: Convert both sides of the weighted directional identity to Gibbs integrals. The same real normalization factor multiplies both integrals, producing \(\int\varphi L_v\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int D\varphi[v]D\psi[v]d\pi_U\). This is a change of measure, with no new integration-by-parts step.

steps.title: integrable gradient inner gibbsMeasure
steps.body: The gradients are continuous; the gradient of the compactly supported test \(\varphi\) vanishes outside its compact support. Thus \(x\mapsto\langle\nabla\varphi(x),\nabla\psi(x)\rangle\) is continuous with compact support. The general compact-test Gibbs integrability theorem applies even though \(\psi\) itself need not have compact support in this statement.

steps.title: integrable test mul langevinGenerator gibbsMeasure
steps.body: The generator of the \(C^2\) test \(\psi\) is continuous under the Lipschitz-gradient assumption on \(U\). Multiplication by the continuous compactly supported \(\varphi\) makes the product compactly supported, hence Gibbs integrable. This is the exact product needed on the left side of the Dirichlet identity.

steps.title: integral langevinGenerator dirichlet gibbs
steps.body: Sum the directional Dirichlet identities over the orthonormal basis. Finite-sum integrability allows the integral to pass through the sum, and Parseval identifies \(\sum_iD\varphi[e_i]D\psi[e_i]=\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle\). Therefore \(\int\varphi L\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle d\pi_U\).

steps.title: integral langevinGenerator symmetric gibbs
steps.body: Apply the Dirichlet identity in both orders \((\varphi,\psi)\) and \((\psi,\varphi)\). Symmetry of the real inner product makes the resulting energy integrands equal pointwise. Hence \(\int\varphi L\psi\,d\pi_U=\int\psi L\varphi\,d\pi_U\).

steps.title: integral langevinGenerator self gibbs
steps.body: Specialize the bilinear identity to \(\psi=\varphi\), then rewrite \(\langle abla\varphi, abla\varphi angle=\| abla\varphi\|^2\). This identifies the quadratic generator form exactly: \(\int\varphi L\varphi\,d\pi_U=-\int\| abla\varphi\|^2d\pi_U\).

steps.title: integral langevinGenerator dissipative gibbs
steps.body: The self-pairing identity expresses the generator quadratic form as minus an integral of a nonnegative square. The integral is nonnegative, so its negative is at most zero. The proof uses the actual integrable energy established earlier, giving dissipativity on compactly supported \(C^2\) tests.

UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinIntegral.lean.title: Existence of the additive Langevin integral equation
UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinIntegral.lean.summary: In a complete real normed space, a globally Lipschitz drift and a continuous additive path \(B\), \(B(0)=0\), determine a continuous solution of \(Y_t-x=-\int_0^tg(Y_s)ds+B_t\) on every finite nonnegative horizon. The construction is deterministic and later applies with the Banach space \(L^2(P)\).

steps.title: Solve on a short interval
steps.body:
Remove the additive input by writing \(Y(t)=Z(t)+B(t)\). The new unknown satisfies \(Z(t)=x+\int_0^t f(s,Z(s))ds\), with \(f(s,z)=-g(z+B(s))\). This time-dependent drift is \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(z\) and continuous in time even though \(B\) need not be differentiable.

Bound \(\|B(t)\|\le C'\) on the compact interval and set \(G=\|g(x)\|+LC'\), radius \(a=2hG\), and drift bound \(M=G+La\). The condition \(Lh\le1/2\) proves \(Mh\le a\), giving the ball-invariance condition in IsPicardLindelof. The proof checks these bounds and invokes ODE.FunSpace.exists_isFixedPt_next.

The chosen fixed point gives a continuous \(Z\) with its integral identity. Add back \(B\), use \(B(0)=0\), and rewrite the negative drift integral to obtain \(Y(t)-x=-\int_0^tg(Y(s))ds+B(t)\). The solution is represented as a real-time function, with the required identity asserted on \([0,h]\).

steps.title: splice langevin integral
steps.body: Use \(Y(t)\) up to time \(a\), and \(Z(t-a)\) afterward. The equality \(Z(0)=Y(a)\) makes the pasted path continuous at the join. Split \(\int_0^t=\int_0^a+\int_a^t\), translate the second integral, and add the two supplied equations; the terms \(B(a)\) cancel, giving the same equation on \([0,a+b]\).

steps.title: exists langevin integral
steps.body: Choose a positive segment length small enough that \(L\delta\le1/2\). Construct the first Picard segment, then repeatedly solve with initial state at the previous endpoint and shifted input \(B(a+s)-B(a)\). The splicing lemma combines finitely many segments covering the prescribed horizon. The local contraction restriction determines the construction mesh and imposes no restriction on the final horizon.

steps.title: exists lp langevin integral small
steps.body: Apply the Banach-space Picard theorem to \(H=L^2(P;K)\), \(g(X)=\operatorname{lpDrift}(\nabla U)(X)\). The lifted drift has the same Lipschitz constant as \(\nabla U\). Completeness of \(L^2\) and continuity of the supplied \(L^2\)-noise path are the exact fixed-point hypotheses.

steps.title: exists lp langevin integral
steps.body: Use the finite-horizon Banach-space existence theorem with the lifted gradient drift. The conclusion is continuity in the \(L^2\) norm and an equality of \(L^2\) classes at every time in the horizon. The Bochner time integral therefore lives in the same Hilbert space; no pathwise differentiability of the random noise is asserted.

UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinUniqueness.le.title: Stability and uniqueness for additive-noise solutions
UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinUniqueness.le.summary: Two solutions driven by the same continuous additive noise satisfy \(\|Y_t-Z_t\|\le e^{Lt}\|x-y\|\) on the prescribed interval. Equality of initial values gives uniqueness. Only global Lipschitzness is used here; the sharper contractive estimate uses strong convexity elsewhere.

steps.title: langevin integral stability
steps.body: Subtract the two integral equations so that their common additive input cancels. The integral norm inequality and Lipschitz drift give \(u(t)\le\|x-y\|+L\int_0^t u(s)ds\), where \(u(t)=\|Y(t)-Z(t)\|\) is continuous. Grönwall's inequality yields \(u(t)\le\|x-y\|e^{Lt}\). All time integrals are justified by continuity on the compact horizon.

steps.title: langevin integral unique
steps.body: Set the two initial states equal in the stability estimate. The right side becomes \(0e^{Lt}=0\), forcing \(\|Y(t)-Z(t)\|=0\) for each \(t\in[0,h]\). Norm-zero equivalence gives equality of the vectors, packaged in Lean as EqOn on the interval.

steps.title: lp langevin integral stability
steps.body: Specialize Banach-space stability to the actual lifted gradient on \(L^2(P;K)\). Its Lipschitz theorem supplies the required constant, so \(\|Y(t)-Z(t)\|_2\le e^{Lt}\|Y(0)-Z(0)\|_2\). This compares solutions with a common \(L^2\)-noise input and possibly different initial random variables.

steps.title: lp langevin integral unique
steps.body: Apply the same-input uniqueness theorem in \(L^2(P;K)\). Equality here is equality of \(L^2\) classes for each time, hence almost-everywhere equality of representatives at each fixed time. The conclusion does not by itself select one exceptional null set valid simultaneously at every real time.

UnadjustedLangevin/EulerLimit.lean.title: Euler approximations converge to the integral solution
UnadjustedLangevin/EulerLimit.lean.summary: This module proves a deterministic convergence theorem for additive Euler discretization. With mesh \(h=T/n\), its terminal value converges to the continuous integral solution, including when the state space itself is \(L^2(P)\).

steps.title: additiveEulerChain
steps.body: Define \(X_0=x\) and \(X_{k+1}=X_k-hg(X_k)+B((k+1)h)-B(kh)\). The additive input is one fixed function evaluated at mesh endpoints; consequently the numerical chain and the integral solution can be compared with exactly matching noise increments.

steps.title: additiveEulerChain zero
steps.body: Evaluating the recursive definition at index zero gives \(X_0=x\). Lean proves this by definitional equality; no continuity of the input or positivity of the mesh is required for this initialization identity.

steps.title: additiveEulerChain succ
steps.body: Unfold the successor clause once to expose \(X_{k+1}=X_k-hg(X_k)+\Delta B_k\). This definitional identity is the equation used when subtracting the exact solution's increment and deriving the error recurrence.

steps.title: langevin integral increment
steps.body: Subtract the integral equations at \(b\) and \(a\). Continuity of \(g\circ Y\) makes it interval integrable, so interval-integral additivity gives \(\int_0^b-\int_0^a=\int_a^b\). Thus \(Y(b)-Y(a)=-\int_a^b g(Y(s))ds+B(b)-B(a)\), including oriented intervals when \(b<a\).

steps.title: finite euler recurrence bound
steps.body: From \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), \(e_0=0\), \(q\ge1\), and \(b\ge0\), induction proves \(e_n\le nbq^n\). In the successor step bound \(q\cdot kbq^k+b\) by \((k+1)bq^{k+1}\), using \(q^{k+1}\ge1\). This coarse bound avoids dividing by \(q-1\), so it also covers \(q=1\).

steps.title: explicitEuler norm sub le
steps.body: Write the difference as \((x-y)-h(g(x)-g(y))\). The triangle inequality and Lipschitzness give \(\|\cdot\|\le\|x-y\|+hL\|x-y\|=(1+Lh)\|x-y\|\). The hypothesis \(h\ge0\) removes the absolute value in the scalar norm.

steps.title: additiveEulerChain error le of drift modulus
steps.body: At one step the common noise cancels. The Euler map contributes \((1+Lh)e_k\), and the exact integral remainder contributes at most \(h\varepsilon\), because the drift changes by at most \(\varepsilon\) within one mesh interval. Apply the finite recurrence bound and \((1+Lh)^n\le e^{Lnh}\), then use \(nh=T\) to obtain \(e_n\le T\varepsilon e^{LT}\).

steps.title: additiveEulerChain tendsto
steps.body: The continuous drift path \(g\circ Y\) is uniformly continuous on \([0,T]\). Given any positive error tolerance, choose a drift modulus \(\varepsilon\) making \(T\varepsilon e^{LT}\) small, then take the mesh \(T/(n+1)\) below its continuity radius. The previous error bound gives endpoint convergence. The case \(T=0\) is separated so no division by the horizon is needed.

steps.title: lp langevin integral euler tendsto
steps.body: Apply the deterministic matching-input Euler convergence theorem in \(L^2(P;H)\), using the Lipschitz lifted gradient. The numerical endpoint converges in the \(L^2\) norm to the constructed solution at \(T\). This is the topology later used to pass smooth bounded tests and identify laws.

UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardTaylor.lea.title: A uniform cubic remainder for smooth test functions
UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardTaylor.lea.summary: Second-order expansions of smooth compactly supported tests have a remainder bounded by a constant times \(\|v\|^3\). These analytic estimates support weak forward-equation calculations.

steps.title: secondOrderExpansion
steps.body: Define \(T_2\varphi(x;v)=\varphi(x)+D\varphi(x)[v]+\frac12D^2\varphi(x)[v,v]\). The iterated Fréchet derivative is a continuous bilinear map, evaluated twice at the same displacement. This separates the deterministic polynomial from the Gaussian expectation calculations performed later.

steps.title: secondOrderExpansion remainder le
steps.body: Restrict \(\varphi\) to the segment \(t\mapsto x+tv\). Its third scalar derivative is \(D^3\varphi(x+tv)[v,v,v]\), bounded by \(C\|v\|^3\). Taylor's theorem with the factorial remainder gives \(|\varphi(x+v)-T_2\varphi(x;v)|\le(C/6)\|v\|^3\). Lean identifies the first three coefficients with the iterated Fréchet derivatives.

steps.title: compactSmooth secondOrderExpansion remainder
steps.body: Smoothness makes \(D^3\varphi\) continuous, and compact support of \(\varphi\) implies compact support of its derivatives. Hence its operator norm is globally bounded by some nonnegative constant. Apply the previous Taylor theorem and absorb the factor \(1/6\) into that constant to obtain a uniform cubic remainder bound.

UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardAdapted.le.title: Solutions depend measurably on their initial state and past noise
UnadjustedLangevin/WeakForwardAdapted.le.summary: The integral solution remains in any complete invariant subspace containing the initial state and noise. Applying this principle to the subspace of random variables measurable with respect to a smaller sigma algebra proves the needed adaptedness statement.

steps.title: An invariant-subspace principle
steps.body: Solve the same integral equation inside the complete submodule \(S\), using drift invariance, \(x\in S\), and \(B(t)\in S\). Include this solution back into the ambient space; continuous linearity of the inclusion commutes with the Bochner integral. Ambient uniqueness identifies it with \(Y\), so every \(Y(t)\) lies in \(S\).

steps.title: lpDrift aestronglyMeasurable
steps.body: A Lipschitz map is continuous, so composing it with an almost-everywhere strongly measurable \(X\) preserves that measurability for the specified sub-sigma-algebra. The representative of the lifted drift agrees almost everywhere with this composition. Transport across that equality proves the result independently of the representative selected for the \(L^2\) class.

steps.title: lp langevin integral aestronglyMeasurable
steps.body: The \(L^2\) variables measurable for a sub-sigma-algebra form a complete closed submodule. The preceding composition theorem makes that submodule invariant under the lifted drift. Apply submodule preservation using measurability of the initialization and every noise value up to \(T\); the integral solution then belongs to the same submodule at each time.

steps.title: lpLangevinPast
steps.body: Define the past sigma-algebra as the join of the sigma-algebra generated by the initial variable and those generated by \(B(t)\), \(0\le t\le T\). Lean uses MeasurableSpace.comap and suprema to construct this information explicitly from the chosen measurable representatives.

steps.title: lpLangevinPast le
steps.body: Every generator of the past is measurable in the ambient sigma-algebra. The universal property of a supremum of sigma-algebras therefore gives \(\mathcal F_T\le\mathcal F\). This inclusion is required to use the closed \(L^2\) subspace of variables measurable from the past.

steps.title: lpLangevinPast initial
steps.body: The sigma-algebra generated by the initial variable is one summand of the defining join for \(\mathcal F_T\). Its inclusion makes the initial variable measurable for \(\mathcal F_T\), and the measurable representative of an \(L^2\) variable supplies the almost-everywhere strong-measurability formulation used by the submodule theorem.

steps.title: lpLangevinPast noise
steps.body: For \(t\in[0,T]\), the sigma-algebra generated by \(B(t)\) is included in the indexed join defining the past. Measurability of the representative with respect to its generated sigma-algebra then extends along this inclusion, giving \(B(t)\)'s measurability from \(\mathcal F_T\).

steps.title: lp langevin integral naturalPast
steps.body: Apply the sub-sigma-algebra solution theorem to the explicitly generated \(\mathcal F_T\). The three preceding declarations discharge its ambient inclusion, initialization, and noise-measurability premises. Thus every solution value up to \(T\) is measurable from initialization and past noise, with no adaptedness assumption added to the solution.

UnadjustedLangevin/FokkerPlanck.lean.title: A weak forward-equation interface and a conditional stationarity route
UnadjustedLangevin/FokkerPlanck.lean.summary: The weak Fokker–Planck equation is formulated by integrating \(\mathcal L\varphi\) against time-dependent probability measures. The final theorem in this module assumes uniqueness of this weak equation explicitly; the main ULA development proves stationarity by the separate Metropolis approximation route.

steps.title: IsWeakFokkerPlanckSolution
steps.body: A curve \(\rho_t\) is in this weak solution class when it is probability valued, has the stated moment and integrability properties, and satisfies the integrated generator equation against every compactly supported \(C^2\) test. The structure fields keep the analytic conditions visible, preventing a formal real integral from substituting for an unproved integrable quantity.

steps.title: constant gibbs isWeakFokkerPlanckSolution
steps.body: Use the proved Gibbs normalization and second moment for the probability and moment fields. Compact-support generator integrability supplies the test-integral fields. Finally \(\int L\varphi\,d\pi_U=0\) makes the time integral vanish, while the constant curve has zero change in \(\int\varphi\,d\rho_t\). These verify each field of the weak equation for the stationary candidate.

steps.title: WeakFokkerPlanckUnique
steps.body: This proposition quantifies over two curves in the stated weak solution class with the same initial measure and requires their equality throughout \([0,T]\). It is a named analytic uniqueness obligation. Defining the proposition does not prove it, and no axiom or automatic instance makes it available.

steps.title: gibbs stationary of weakFokkerPlanckUniqueness
steps.body: Compare the supplied weak solution \(\rho\) with the constant Gibbs weak solution constructed above. Their time-zero measures agree by hypothesis. The explicit hunique premise therefore identifies them at every time. Applying this conditional bridge to a stochastic process still requires its law curve to satisfy the weak equation and requires this uniqueness premise.

UnadjustedLangevin/TestMeasure.lean.title: Compactly supported smooth tests determine a finite measure
UnadjustedLangevin/TestMeasure.lean.summary: On a finite-dimensional real normed space, finite measures agreeing on all compactly supported smooth tests are equal. Agreement on compactly supported \(C^2\) tests is sufficient as well.

steps.title: measure eq of integral contDiff eq
steps.body:
Let \(\xi=\mu+ u\), so both finite measures are absolutely continuous with respect to \(\xi\). Write their Radon–Nikodym densities as \(f=d\mu/d\xi\) and \(g=d u/d\xi\). Equality of the given smooth compact test integrals becomes \(\int\varphi f\,d\xi=\int\varphi g\,d\xi\).

The smooth-test uniqueness theorem ae_eq_of_integral_contDiff_smul_eq proves \(f=g\) almost everywhere, using their locally integrable real values. Both derivatives are finite almost everywhere because the measures are finite, so equality of real values lifts back to equality of the extended densities. Reconstructing each measure as ξ.withDensity of its Radon–Nikodym derivative gives \(\mu= u\).

steps.title: measure eq of integral contDiff two eq
steps.body: Every smooth test is \(C^2\), so the assumed equality on compactly supported \(C^2\) functions applies to the smooth test class used by the preceding measure-determination theorem. Supply that restricted equality and obtain equality of the finite Borel measures. No density or absolute continuity is needed.

UnadjustedLangevin/LpCharacteristic.lean.title: Characteristic functions are continuous in L²
UnadjustedLangevin/LpCharacteristic.lean.summary: At each fixed frequency, the characteristic function of the law of a real \(L^2\) variable depends continuously on that variable. Consequently centered Gaussian laws are closed under \(L^2\) convergence, with variance given by the squared norm.

steps.title: centeredCharacteristic
steps.body: Set \(c_t(x)=e^{itx}-1\), represented by the unit-radius circle map centered at \(-1\). Subtracting one makes \(c_t(0)=0\), which is the condition needed by the Lipschitz composition construction on \(L^2\).

steps.title: centeredCharacteristic lipschitz
steps.body: Multiplication by \(t\) is \(|t|\)-Lipschitz, and the unit circle parametrization is \(1\)-Lipschitz. Composing gives \(|c_t(x)-c_t(y)|\le|t||x-y|\). The proof identifies the nonnegative Lipschitz constants before applying the composition theorem.

steps.title: centeredCharacteristic zero
steps.body: At zero the exponential is one, hence \(c_t(0)=e^0-1=0\). Unfolding the circle-map definition makes this a scalar identity; this vanishing proof permits compLp to lift the map without an integrability assumption on a nonzero constant.

steps.title: characteristicLp
steps.body: Lift \(c_t\) to \(L^2\) by Lipschitz composition, then add the constant class one. Thus \(\operatorname{characteristicLp}(t,X)\) represents \(e^{itX}\). The probability assumption makes the constant function square integrable.

steps.title: characteristicLp coe
steps.body: Combine the almost-everywhere representative identities for lifted composition, \(L^2\) addition, and the constant class. Their intersection has full measure; there the representative is \((e^{itX}-1)+1=e^{itX}\). This connects quotient-space operations with the random function used in the characteristic integral.

steps.title: charFun map eq inner characteristicLp
steps.body: The pushforward integral theorem gives \(\widehat{P_X}(t)=\int e^{itX}dP\). In complex \(L^2\), inner product with the constant one has exactly this integral because its conjugate is one. The representative identity above therefore yields \(\widehat{P_X}(t)=\langle1,\operatorname{characteristicLp}(t,X)\rangle\).

steps.title: continuous charFun map Lp
steps.body: Lipschitz composition is continuous on \(L^2\); adding the constant one preserves continuity. Pairing with one is a continuous linear functional. The preceding integral identity rewrites their composition as \(X\mapsto\widehat{P_X}(t)\), proving continuity of the actual-law characteristic function at every fixed frequency.

steps.title: continuous gaussianReal charFun Lp
steps.body: The centered Gaussian characteristic function is \(e^{-t^2\|X\|_2^2/2}\). Norm, squaring, conversion of a nonnegative real to ℝ≥0, and the exponential are continuous. Lean unfolds the Gaussian formula and composes these continuity facts; the variance is the actual squared \(L^2\) norm.

steps.title: hasLaw gaussianReal of tendsto Lp eventually
steps.body: At each frequency, \(L^2\) convergence makes the actual characteristic functions converge. It also makes the centered Gaussian characteristic functions with variances \(\|X_i\|_2^2\) converge to variance \(\|Y\|_2^2\). Eventual Gaussianity identifies the two nets eventually, so uniqueness of limits identifies their limits. Measure.ext_of_charFun then gives the claimed Gaussian law of \(Y\); a nontrivial filter is required for uniqueness.

steps.title: hasLaw gaussianReal of tendsto Lp
steps.body: If every approximant has the stated Gaussian law, then the law identity holds eventually for any filter. Feed Eventually.of_forall to the preceding closure theorem. This version is suited to finite orthogonal sums converging to an infinite Gaussian series.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianHilbert.lean.title: Construct an isonormal Gaussian family from product coordinates
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianHilbert.lean.summary: An explicit product of standard normal coordinates realizes a linear isometry \(I:H\to L^2\) with \(I(x)\sim\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\) and covariance \(\mathbb E[I(x)I(y)]=\langle x,y\rangle\).

steps.title: source
steps.body: Use the product probability \(Q=\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)\) on real coordinate families. The construction uses Measure.infinitePi; independence and coordinate marginals are properties of this concrete source rather than extra assumptions on an unspecified Gaussian process.

steps.title: coordinate hasLaw
steps.body: The coordinate projection \(\omega\mapsto\omega_i\) pushes the product measure to its \(i\)-th factor \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). The product marginal theorem proves both almost-everywhere measurability and the pushforward identity, packaged as HasLaw.

steps.title: coordinateLp
steps.body: A standard Gaussian has finite second moment, so the coordinate projection belongs to \(L^2(Q)\). Apply its MemLp.toLp construction to obtain the quotient class \(Z_i\); the definition stores the original coordinate function together with its integrability proof.

steps.title: coordinateLp coe
steps.body: The representative selected for \(Z_i\) agrees with \(\omega_i\) almost everywhere by the defining property of toLp. This equality is the bridge used to transfer coordinate laws, means, and independence calculations to the \(L^2\) classes.

steps.title: coordinates independent
steps.body: The coordinate projections of an infinite product measure are jointly independent. Invoke that product theorem for the scalar Gaussian factors. This is independence of every finite set of coordinates, which is precisely what finite Gaussian linear combinations require.

steps.title: coordinate mean
steps.body: Change variables through the coordinate law and use the centered Gaussian mean: \(\int\omega_i\,dQ=\int x\,d\mathcal N(0,1)=0\). Gaussian integrability makes this an ordinary expectation identity.

steps.title: coordinateLp inner
steps.body: For \(i=j\), the \(L^2\) inner product is \(\mathbb EZ_i^2=1\). For \(i\ne j\), independence factors \(\mathbb EZ_iZ_j=(\mathbb EZ_i)(\mathbb EZ_j)=0\). Almost-everywhere representative identities move between \(Z_i\) and the product coordinates. Thus \(\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle=\mathbf1_{i=j}\).

steps.title: coordinates orthonormal
steps.body: The preceding inner-product formula is the orthonormality criterion for a family in a real Hilbert space. Lean converts the diagonal value one and off-diagonal value zero into Orthonormal ℝ coordinateLp, the input for the orthogonal-series extension.

steps.title: source isProbabilityMeasure
steps.body: Each scalar Gaussian factor is a probability measure. The product-probability instance therefore gives \(Q(\Omega)=1\). This instance is what permits constant functions and integrable functions to be treated in the usual probability-space \(L^2\) theory below.

steps.title: synthesis
steps.body: Extend the orthonormal family \(Z_i\) to a linear isometry \(S:\ell^2(\iota)\to L^2(Q)\). The orthogonal-family extension theorem constructs the limit of finite sums and preserves squared norm, \(\|S(a)\|_2^2=\sum_i a_i^2\). It constructs an \(L^2\) limit rather than assuming pointwise convergence of a random series.

steps.title: synthesis hasSum
steps.body: The synthesis extension theorem states \(\sum_i a_iZ_i=S(a)\), with convergence of finite partial sums in \(L^2\). In Lean HasSum is convergence along finite subsets, so the identity does not require choosing an enumeration of the basis index set.

steps.title: isonormal
steps.body: For a Hilbert basis \(b\), compose its coordinate isometry \(b.\mathrm{repr}:H\to\ell^2(\iota)\) with synthesis. The resulting linear isometry \(I_b\) sends \(x\) to the Gaussian series with coefficients \(\langle b_i,x\rangle\), and preserves all inner products.

steps.title: isonormal hasSum
steps.body: Apply synthesis_hasSum to the coefficient family \(b.\mathrm{repr}(x)\). Unfolding the composition gives \(I_b(x)=\sum_i\langle b_i,x\rangle Z_i\) in \(L^2\). This is the exact series represented by the bundled isonormal isometry.

steps.title: integral eq inner one
steps.body: On a probability space, the constant one is in \(L^2\). The definition of the real \(L^2\) inner product gives \(\mathbb EX=\langle1,X\rangle\), after replacing the selected constant representative by one almost everywhere. This exhibits expectation as a continuous functional.

steps.title: coordinateLp mean
steps.body: Use \(Z_i=\omega_i\) almost everywhere to replace the \(L^2\) representative inside the integral. The already established centered coordinate expectation then gives \(\mathbb EZ_i=0\).

steps.title: synthesis mean
steps.body: Each finite partial sum \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\) has mean zero by linearity and the coordinate means. Pair the \(L^2\)-convergent series with the constant one; continuity of the inner product passes the zero expectations to the limit, giving \(\mathbb ES(a)=0\).

steps.title: isonormal mean
steps.body: The isonormal variable is synthesis applied to the Hilbert-basis coefficients of \(x\). Specialize the synthesis mean theorem to these coefficients to get \(\mathbb EI_b(x)=0\), without redoing the infinite-series limit.

steps.title: variance eq norm sq
steps.body: For an \(L^2\) random variable with mean zero, the variance formula reduces to \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\int X^2dQ\). The \(L^2\) norm identity identifies this with \(\|X\|_2^2\). The explicit mean premise is used to remove the centering term.

steps.title: partial sum coe
steps.body: Induct over the finite set. The zero sum has zero representative almost everywhere; addition and scalar multiplication of \(L^2\) classes agree almost everywhere with the corresponding pointwise operations. Intersect the finitely many full-measure sets to obtain \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i\omega_i\) almost everywhere.

steps.title: partial sum hasGaussianLaw
steps.body: Independent scalar standard Gaussians remain Gaussian after a finite linear combination. Apply that finite-sum Gaussian theorem to \(a_i\omega_i\), and transfer the law across partial_sum_coe. This proves Gaussianity of the actual \(L^2\) partial sum, not merely of a formally similar expression.

steps.title: partial sum mean
steps.body: The integral of a finite \(L^2\) sum is the sum of its integrals, because every summand is integrable. Each coordinate mean is zero, hence \(\mathbb E\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i=0\). This supplies the centering parameter needed to identify its Gaussian law.

steps.title: partial sum hasLaw
steps.body: A scalar Gaussian law is determined by its mean and variance. The finite sum is Gaussian and centered; its variance is its squared \(L^2\) norm. Therefore its law is \(\mathcal N(0,\|\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\|_2^2)\), with the variance converted to a nonnegative real.

steps.title: synthesis hasLaw
steps.body: Finite partial sums converge in \(L^2\) to \(S(a)\), and each has the centered Gaussian law with its own squared norm as variance.
