Apply hasLaw_gaussianReal_of_tendsto_Lp; the isometry then rewrites the limiting variance as \(\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2\). This proves Gaussianity of the completed infinite series.

steps.title: isonormal hasLaw
steps.body: Apply the synthesis law theorem to \(b.\mathrm{repr}(x)\). The Hilbert-basis coordinate map preserves norm, so the variance becomes \(\|x\|^2\). Hence \(I_b(x)\sim\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\), including the degenerate law for \(x=0\).

steps.title: isonormal hasGaussianLaw
steps.body: The exact law theorem identifies \(I_b(x)\) with a scalar Gaussian probability. Forgetting its explicit mean and variance parameters yields the bundled HasGaussianLaw predicate used by the finite-dimensional Gaussian-process construction.

steps.title: isonormal covariance
steps.body: Both variables are centered, so their covariance is \(\mathbb E[I_b(x)I_b(y)]\), the \(L^2\) inner product. The linear isometry preserves that inner product, giving \(\operatorname{Cov}(I_b(x),I_b(y))=\langle x,y\rangle_H\). Lean checks integrability through their \(L^2\) membership.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianLinearProcess.title: Scalar Gaussian linear maps give jointly Gaussian processes
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianLinearProcess.summary: If a linear map \(T:H\to L^2(P;\mathbb R)\) sends every input to a Gaussian variable, all finite collections of its evaluations are jointly Gaussian.

steps.title: hasGaussianLaw pi of linearMap Lp
steps.body: Use the finite-dimensional Gaussian criterion: every scalar linear functional of \((T(f_i))_i\) must be Gaussian. A finite linear combination equals \(T(\sum_i a_if_i)\) as an \(L^2\) class by linearity, hence agrees almost everywhere as a random variable. The assumed Gaussianity of every \(T(x)\) proves the criterion.

steps.title: isGaussianProcess of linearMap Lp
steps.body: For each finite set of times, apply the preceding joint-Gaussian theorem to the corresponding finite family of vectors \(f(t)\). This verifies the finite-dimensional-law definition of IsGaussianProcess. The index set may be uncountable; this statement alone asserts no sample-path continuity.

UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalBrownian.lea.title: An explicit Gaussian construction of pre-Brownian coordinates
UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalBrownian.lea.summary: The isonormal family on the time Hilbert space constructs a Gaussian process with covariance \(\min(s,t)\). Independent product copies supply the Brownian coordinates required by the canonical ULA theorem. The construction proves pre-Brownian laws; continuous sample paths are not asserted or needed, because continuity is established in \(L^2\).

steps.title: TimeHilbert
steps.body: Take the deterministic Hilbert space \(L^2(\mathbb R,dt)\). Its vectors will encode time intervals before an isonormal map turns their inner products into covariances. It is distinct from the random-variable \(L^2\) space on the Gaussian source.

steps.title: timeIndicator
steps.body: Let \(e_t=\mathbf1_{(0,t]}\) as a class in \(L^2(dt)\), for \(t\ge0\). Lean constructs it with indicatorConstLp and the finite Lebesgue measure of Ioc 0 t. Endpoints do not affect this Lebesgue \(L^2\) class, but this half-open convention makes interval intersection identities direct.

steps.title: timeIndicator inner
steps.body: The product of the two indicators is the indicator of \([0,\min(s,t)]\) almost everywhere. Integrating it gives \(\langle e_s,e_t\rangle=\min(s,t)\). The proof evaluates the Lebesgue measure of that finite interval, producing the Brownian covariance before introducing randomness.

steps.title: basisIndex
steps.body: Choose the index type supplied by a Hilbert basis of the time Hilbert space. It is a set of Hilbert-space vectors used as a type; no explicit countable enumeration is required by the orthogonal-family construction.

steps.title: basis
steps.body: Select a Hilbert basis for TimeHilbert by Hilbert-space basis existence. This basis supplies the coordinate isometry for the explicit isonormal Gaussian family; all subsequent covariance identities follow from isometry and do not depend on which basis was selected.

steps.title: Sample
steps.body: A sample is a real family indexed by the chosen time-Hilbert basis. This concrete product space stores the independent standard Gaussian coefficients used to synthesize all Brownian times.

steps.title: probability
steps.body: Use GaussianHilbert.source on the basis index type, namely the product of standard scalar Gaussians. Its established probability instance provides normalization and independent coordinate laws for the Brownian construction.

steps.title: instance at 53
steps.body: The scalar source is the Gaussian coordinate product probability. Reuse GaussianHilbert.source_isProbabilityMeasure to provide normalization for the chosen basis index. This instance enables the \(L^2\) expectation and covariance theorems for the constructed Brownian process.

steps.title: valueLp
steps.body: Apply the isonormal isometry to \(e_t\), obtaining \(B_t=I(e_t)\) as an \(L^2\) random variable. The construction immediately gives a centered Gaussian with variance \(\|e_t\|^2=t\); joint Gaussianity follows from linearity.

steps.title: process
steps.body: At each time select the strongly measurable representative of valueLp. This defines an actual function \(B_t(\omega)\) for use in HasLaw and finite-dimensional distributions. Equalities of \(L^2\) classes still translate to almost-everywhere equalities of these representatives.

steps.title: process measurable
steps.body: The representative selected for an \(L^2\) class is measurable in this setting. Apply the representative measurability theorem to valueLp t, obtaining measurability of the actual time-\(t\) random variable.

steps.title: process mean
steps.body: The isonormal mean theorem gives \(\mathbb EI(e_t)=0\). Since process t is precisely the selected representative of this class, this is the expectation of the displayed random function \(B_t\).

steps.title: process covariance
steps.body: The isonormal covariance formula gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(I(e_s),I(e_t))=\langle e_s,e_t\rangle\). Substitute timeIndicator_inner to obtain \(\min(s,t)\). This calculation establishes the Brownian covariance for the concrete source and representatives.

steps.title: isGaussianProcess
steps.body: The isonormal isometry is linear and every output is scalar Gaussian. Apply isGaussianProcess_of_linearMap_Lp to the family \(t\mapsto e_t\). Every finite collection of the selected random variables is therefore jointly Gaussian.

steps.title: isPreBrownian
steps.body: Combine centered Gaussian finite-dimensional laws with covariance \(\min(s,t)\). The Gaussian-process Brownian characterization yields IsPreBrownianReal. This proves Brownian finite-dimensional laws; the prefix “pre” records that sample-path continuity is not part of this predicate.

steps.title: VectorSample
steps.body: For a coordinate index type \(I\), take one scalar Brownian sample for each \(i\in I\). This is the product sample type \(I\to\mathrm{Sample}\), allowing independent entire coordinate processes rather than only independent values at one time.

steps.title: vectorProbability
steps.body: Equip the vector sample space with the infinite product of the scalar Brownian source probabilities. The coordinate processes inherit independence from this actual product construction.

steps.title: coordinate
steps.body: Define the \(i\)-th coordinate process by \(B_i(t,\omega)=B(t,\omega_i)\). It first projects to the \(i\)-th scalar sample, then evaluates the already constructed scalar process at \(t\).

steps.title: coordinate isPreBrownian
steps.body: The product coordinate projection has the scalar Brownian source as its law. Pull the scalar pre-Brownian process back along this projection; its finite-dimensional distributions, mean, and covariance are preserved. Thus each vector coordinate has the established scalar Brownian laws.

steps.title: coordinate paths independent
steps.body: The product coordinate projections are independent as sample-valued maps. Compose each projection with the map sending a scalar sample to its entire time-indexed process. Independence is preserved under these coordinatewise functions, giving independence of the whole coordinate paths.

steps.title: coordinate grid paths independent
steps.body: Restrict each independent coordinate path to the deterministic grid \(nh\). This is a coordinatewise function of the path, so independence is preserved. The result supplies exactly the countable grid-path hypothesis used in the innovation theorems.

steps.title: instance at 89
steps.body: Each scalar Brownian sample source has mass one. The infinite product over vector coordinates therefore also has mass one. This instance concerns the actual vector sample measure, not an assumed normalization of an abstract process law.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianInnovations.l.title: Normalized increments are independent standard Gaussians
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianInnovations.l.summary: For a pre-Brownian coordinate and positive grid spacing \(h\), \(Z_n=(B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh})/\sqrt h\) has standard normal law. Across independent coordinate paths, the entire coordinate-time family is independent.

steps.title: normalizedBrownianIncrement
steps.body: Define \(\xi_n=(B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh})/\sqrt h\). The denominator is interpreted as real scalar division; positive-step law results below explicitly require \(h>0\), so that the variance rescaling is legitimate.

steps.title: normalizedBrownianIncrement hasLaw
steps.body: A Brownian increment over an interval of length \(h\) is \(\mathcal N(0,h)\). Scaling by \(1/\sqrt h\) multiplies its variance by \(1/h\), producing \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). The proof rewrites \((n+1)h-nh=h\) and uses \((\sqrt h)^2=h\), justified by \(h>0\).

steps.title: normalizedBrownianIncrement memLp
steps.body: The exact standard Gaussian law provides every finite moment, in particular the second. Pull this square integrability back through normalizedBrownianIncrement_hasLaw to prove \(\xi_n\in L^2(P)\).

steps.title: normalizedBrownianIncrement second moment
steps.body: Transfer the integral of \(x^2\) along the standard Gaussian law of \(\xi_n\). Its mean is zero and variance one, hence \(\mathbb E\xi_n^2=1\). This is an exact second-moment identity for the normalized increment.

steps.title: normalizedBrownianIncrement independent
steps.body: Brownian increments on the consecutive grid intervals are independent. Normalizing each by the same deterministic scalar is a coordinatewise measurable transformation and preserves independence. The formulation permits \(h=0\), where every increment is the constant zero and the independence assertion remains valid.

steps.title: iIndepFun uncurry nat of aemeasurable
steps.body: Assume the row-valued random maps \((X_{i,n})_n\) are independent and each row is internally independent. Replace the almost-everywhere measurable coordinates by measurable versions; countability of \(\mathbb N\) lets all replacements in a row hold on one full-measure set. Apply independence of independent families, then transfer the result back across the coordinatewise almost-everywhere equalities.

steps.title: normalizedBrownianIncrements independent
steps.body: Each grid increment depends measurably on two entries of its coordinate grid path. Independence of those paths gives independence across coordinate rows, while Brownian independent increments gives independence within each row. Apply iIndepFun_uncurry_nat_of_aemeasurable to obtain joint independence of all \((i,n)\) innovations.

steps.title: normalizedBrownianIncrements independent of paths
steps.body: Restrict each independent full coordinate path to the grid \(nh\), preserving independence under composition. The preceding theorem then yields joint coordinate-time independence of the normalized increments. This avoids requiring a separate measurable map into an uncountable path space.

steps.title: The entire innovation law
steps.body: Every coordinate-time innovation has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), and the family is jointly independent. The countable product-law theorem therefore identifies the whole innovation map with \(\bigotimes_{(i,n)}\mathcal N(0,1)\). Countability supplies measurability of the path-valued map from coordinatewise almost-everywhere measurability.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianInnovationVec.title: From scalar coordinate laws to independent Gaussian vectors
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianInnovationVec.summary: For finitely many spatial coordinates, independent standard normal scalar innovations assemble into independent standard Gaussian vectors. Scalar normal laws without joint independence would not suffice for this conclusion.

steps.title: gaussianInnovations pathLaw
steps.body: Regroup the jointly independent scalar coordinates indexed by \((n,i)\) into vector blocks \(W_n\). A finite block with independent standard Gaussian coordinates has the standard Euclidean Gaussian law. Product-measure identification and reindexing then show that the full vector path has law \(\bigotimes_n\mathcal N(0,I)\).

steps.title: gaussianInnovations vectorLaw
steps.body: Project the established whole-path product law to its \(n\)-th vector coordinate. Product marginals give \(P\circ W_n^{-1}=\mathcal N(0,I)\). This derives the multivariate law from the scalar coordinate assumptions rather than adding it as an algorithm hypothesis.

steps.title: gaussianInnovations vectorIndependent
steps.body: The coordinate maps of the vector product law are independent. Pull that independence back through the actual innovation-path map using gaussianInnovations_pathLaw. Thus the vector-valued \(W_n\) are independent over time, not just uncorrelated.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianCoordinates.l.title: Coordinate Gaussian moments and L² Brownian continuity
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianCoordinates.l.summary: Coordinatewise Gaussian laws suffice for the second moment \(\mathbb E\|X\|^2=dv\). This module carefully obtains Brownian \(L^2\) continuity and increment norms without assuming independence between spatial coordinates.

steps.title: gaussian coordinates memLp
steps.body: Each centered Gaussian coordinate has a finite second moment. In finite Euclidean dimension, \(\|X\|^2=\sum_iX_i^2\), so the finite sum is integrable. Coordinatewise measurability also assembles to vector measurability, giving \(X\in L^2\). Coordinate independence is unnecessary for this moment statement.

steps.title: gaussian coordinates second moment
steps.body: Use \(\|X\|^2=\sum_iX_i^2\) and finite-sum integral linearity. The coordinate law \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(0,v)\) gives \(\mathbb EX_i^2=v\), hence \(\mathbb E\|X\|^2=|\iota|v\). The dimension factor is exactly the cardinality of the finite coordinate set.

steps.title: gaussian coordinates Lp norm sq
steps.body: For the given \(L^2\) class, its squared norm is the integral of the squared norm of its representative. Apply the preceding Gaussian coordinate moment formula to obtain \(\|X\|_2^2=|\iota|v\).

steps.title: gaussian coordinates Lp norm
steps.body: Take nonnegative square roots in \(\|X\|_2^2=|\iota|v\). Norm nonnegativity selects the positive root, giving \(\|X\|_2=\sqrt{|\iota|v}\), including zero variance and zero dimension.

steps.title: gaussian coordinates toLp coordinateLaw
steps.body: The representative of MemLp.toLp X agrees almost everywhere with \(X\). Coordinate evaluation preserves that equality, so each coordinate law transfers to the canonical \(L^2\) representative by almost-everywhere invariance of pushforwards.

steps.title: gaussian coordinates toLp norm
steps.body: Apply the exact \(L^2\) Gaussian norm theorem to toLp X, using its transferred coordinate laws. This gives \(\|[X]\|_2=\sqrt{|\iota|v}\) for the class constructed from the original random vector.

steps.title: gaussian coordinates scaled l2 norm
steps.body: The scalar-norm identity gives \(\|\sqrt2[X]\|_2=\sqrt2\sqrt{|\iota|v}\). Nonnegativity permits the square-root product rules, producing \(\sqrt{2|\iota|}\sqrt v\). This is the precise Langevin noise constant used in the local error estimate.

steps.title: brownianCoordinates
steps.body: Assemble the scalar coordinate processes into \(B_t(\omega)=(W_i(t,\omega))_{i\in\iota}\). Finite Euclidean coordinates determine the vector; no new random source or independence is introduced by this definition.

steps.title: brownianCoordinates coordinateLaw
steps.body: At a fixed time \(t\ge0\), each scalar pre-Brownian coordinate has law \(\mathcal N(0,t)\). Unfolding the assembled vector shows that its \(i\)-th coordinate is exactly that scalar variable, giving the required coordinate law.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesIncrement
steps.body: Define the vector increment \(\Delta_aB_t=B_{a+t}-B_a\) coordinate by coordinate. This records both the starting time and elapsed nonnegative time, matching the local noise input on an arbitrary Langevin segment.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesIncrement coordinateLaw
steps.body: The scalar Brownian increment law depends only on elapsed time: \(W_i(a+t)-W_i(a)\sim\mathcal N(0,t)\). Simplify \((a+t)-a=t\) in the variance and unfold the vector increment to obtain its coordinate law.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesIncrement memLp
steps.body: Apply gaussian_coordinates_memLp to the increment's coordinate laws of variance \(t\). The assembled Brownian vector increment is square integrable even without independence between different coordinate processes.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesIncrement scaled l2 norm
steps.body: Apply the exact scaled Gaussian-coordinate norm theorem with variance \(t\). It yields \(\|\sqrt2[\Delta_aB_t]\|_2=\sqrt{2|\iota|}\sqrt t\), establishing the noise radius from Brownian laws alone.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp
steps.body: Convert the assembled Brownian vector at time \(t\) to its \(L^2\) class using its Gaussian-coordinate square-integrability proof. This places the time-indexed process in the Hilbert space where the deterministic integral equation is solved.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp coe
steps.body: The toLp representative theorem gives \([B_t](\omega)=B_t(\omega)\) almost everywhere for each fixed time. This is the bridge from class-valued continuity statements to coordinate laws of the original Brownian process.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp sub coordinateLaw
steps.body: The difference of two selected representatives agrees almost everywhere with \(B_t-B_s\). Brownian increment laws, including the sign reversal when \(t<s\), give a centered Gaussian with variance \(|t-s|\); centered Gaussian symmetry handles the reversed order.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp norm sub
steps.body: Apply the Gaussian \(L^2\) norm formula to the difference class, whose coordinates have variance \(|t-s|\). Thus \(\|[B_t]-[B_s]\|_2=\sqrt{|\iota|\,|t-s|}\). This exact increment norm is stronger than the continuity statement derived from it.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp continuous
steps.body: As \(s\to t\), \(|t-s|\to0\), hence the exact norm formula gives \(\|[B_t]-[B_s]\|_2\to0\). Lean uses continuity of the square root and the metric characterization of continuity. This needs finite-dimensional Brownian laws, with no sample-path continuity premise.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp increment scaled norm
steps.body: Set the two times in the difference-norm identity to \(a+t\) and \(a\). Their distance is \(t\), and scalar multiplication by \(\sqrt2\) gives \(\sqrt{2|\iota|}\sqrt t\). This is the class-valued version of the earlier increment estimate.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp zero
steps.body: At time zero every coordinate has the degenerate centered Gaussian law of variance zero. Equivalently its \(L^2\) norm is zero by the moment formula. Norm-zero equivalence proves that the whole class is zero, irrespective of the chosen pointwise representative.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesRealLp
steps.body: Extend the nonnegative-time \(L^2\) process to real times by \(t\mapsto[B_{\max(t,0)}]\), implemented with Real.toNNReal. It is constant zero for negative times and agrees with the original class at nonnegative times.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesRealLp continuous
steps.body: The clipping map \(t\mapsto\max(t,0)\) into nonnegative reals is continuous. Compose it with the established \(L^2\)-continuous Brownian map to obtain continuity of the real-time extension, including at zero.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesRealLp zero
steps.body: At real time zero the clipping map returns nonnegative zero. The previously proved zero-time \(L^2\) identity therefore simplifies the real-time extension to zero.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesRealLp increment scaled norm
steps.body: For \(a,t\ge0\), clipping leaves \(a\) and \(a+t\) unchanged. Rewrite the real-time extension at both endpoints as the nonnegative-time Brownian classes, then apply their scaled increment formula. This supplies \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) in the real interval-integral formulation.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianProposalDensi.title: Identify Gaussian proposals with their radial density
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianProposalDensi.summary: For \(h>0\), the affine standard Gaussian proposal \(c+\sqrt{2h}\,Z\) has density proportional to \(e^{-\|y-c\|^2/(4h)}\). The proof identifies probability measures by characteristic functions and does not require a preselected coordinate formula for the Gaussian normalizer.

steps.title: radialGaussianIntegral
steps.body: Set \(J(a)=\int_H e^{-a\|z\|^2}dz\) as an ordinary real integral. The positive-precision results below prove its integrability and positivity before using \(J(a)^{-1}\) as a normalizing constant.

steps.title: radialGaussianNormalizer
steps.body: Define \(C(a)=J(a)^{-1}\). This is an actual integral normalizer on the given finite-dimensional Hilbert space, avoiding a coordinate-dependent choice of a formula for Lebesgue density.

steps.title: radialGaussianIntegral pos
steps.body: For \(a>0\), Gaussian integrability was established in integrable_exp_neg_mul_norm_sq. The integrand is strictly positive, so its ordinary integral is strictly positive by integral_exp_pos.

steps.title: radialGaussianNormalizer pos
steps.body: The inverse of a strictly positive real number is strictly positive. Apply this to \(J(a)\), whose positivity was proved immediately above. This also proves the normalizer is nonzero for later cancellation.

steps.title: radialGaussianDensity
steps.body: Define \(q_{a,c}(z)=C(a)e^{-a\|z-c\|^2}\), embedded in extended nonnegative scalars. The center changes the translated argument, while the normalizer depends only on precision and dimension.

steps.title: integrable radialGaussianDensity real
steps.body: Translation by \(c\) preserves Lebesgue measure, so \(e^{-a\|z-c\|^2}\) is integrable whenever \(a>0\). Multiply by the finite real constant \(C(a)\) to obtain integrability of the displayed real density.

steps.title: integral radialGaussianDensity real
steps.body: Translate \(z\mapsto z-c\) in the integral and pull out \(C(a)\). The result is \(C(a)J(a)=1\), justified by \(J(a)>0\). Thus normalization is independent of the center.

steps.title: radialGaussianDensity isProbability
steps.body: The total mass of the with-density measure is the extended integral of its density. Nonnegativity and the proved real integrability identify it with ofReal of the real integral, which is one. This constructs probability normalization, including finiteness.

steps.title: integral complex radialGaussian
steps.body: For real \(a\), \(e^{-(a:\mathbb C)\|z\|^2}\) is the complex embedding of the real Gaussian exponential. Rewrite the integrand with Complex.ofReal_exp; the continuous real embedding commutes with integration, giving the complex embedding of \(J(a)\).

steps.title: integral radialGaussian character
steps.body: Apply the finite-dimensional complex Gaussian Fourier integral with imaginary linear coefficient. Combining the two exponentials and using \(i^2=-1\) gives \(\int e^{-a\|z\|^2}e^{i\langle z,t\rangle}dz=J(a)e^{-\|t\|^2/(4a)}\). The zero-frequency Gaussian formula identifies the normalization factor with the same real integral \(J(a)\).

steps.title: charFun radialGaussianDensity
steps.body: Change from the density measure to a weighted Lebesgue integral. Translate \(z=u+c\); the character splits into \(e^{i\langle u,t\rangle}e^{i\langle c,t\rangle}\). The Fourier formula gives a factor \(J(a)\), canceled by \(C(a)\), leaving \(e^{-\|t\|^2/(4a)}e^{i\langle c,t\rangle}\).

steps.title: gaussianProposalNormalizer
steps.body: Specialize the precision to \(a=1/(4h)\). The resulting constant normalizes a Gaussian with covariance \(2hI\). Its independence of the current state is essential when the same factor cancels in the forward and reverse Metropolis ratio.

steps.title: gaussianProposalDensity
steps.body: Define \(q_h(c,y)=C(1/(4h))e^{-\|y-c\|^2/(4h)}\). For \(h>0\), this is the density of a covariance-\(2hI\) Gaussian centered at \(c\). The density identification is proved later rather than built into the definition.

steps.title: gaussianProposalNormalizer pos
steps.body: For \(h>0\), the precision \(1/(4h)\) is positive. Apply positivity of the radial Gaussian normalizer at that precision. This nonzero constant is used in detailed-balance cancellation.

steps.title: radialGaussianDensity eq proposalDensity
steps.body: Unfold the two density definitions and the proposal normalizer. Their exponents agree by \(-(1/(4h))\|y-c\|^2=-\|y-c\|^2/(4h)\). Function extensionality gives equality of the density functions, with no probabilistic argument needed.

steps.title: gaussian proposal density
steps.body: Compute characteristic functions on both sides. The affine image \(c+\sqrt{2h}Z\) has character \(e^{-h\|t\|^2}e^{i\langle c,t\rangle}\); the radial-density formula with \(a=1/(4h)\) gives the same expression. Both measures are probabilities, so Measure.ext_of_charFun identifies them. The square-root identity uses \(h>0\).

steps.title: gaussian proposal radial density
steps.body: Rewrite the proposal density using radialGaussianDensity_eq_proposalDensity in the established affine-Gaussian law equality. This yields the equivalent precision-parameter form used in the detailed-balance proof.

steps.title: ula proposal radial density
steps.body: Set the affine Gaussian center to \(c=x-h\nabla U(x)\). The fixed-state density theorem then gives \(x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}Z\) its exact radial density. No regularity of \(U\) is required because \(x\) is fixed throughout this statement.

steps.title: ula proposal density
steps.body: Expand the radial density at center \(x-h\nabla U(x)\). The exponent becomes \(-\|y-x+h\nabla U(x)\|^2/(4h)\), with the same positive normalizer. This is the explicit ULA transition density used in the Metropolis acceptance ratio.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianProposalPairD.title: The joint initial-state and proposal density
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianProposalPairD.summary: For a measurable center \(c(x)\), independent \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) produce the joint law \(\mu(dx)q_h(c(x),y)dy\).

steps.title: Disintegrate the Gaussian change of variables
steps.body:
For \(X\sim\mu\) and independent \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), fix \(x\) and apply the proved proposal-density identity to \(c(x)+\sqrt{2h}Z\). It gives conditional integration against \(q_h(c(x),y)dy\).

To obtain equality of joint measures, evaluate a measurable set \(A\subset H\times H\). Tonelli writes both sides as integrals over \(x\) of their \(y\)-sections. The fixed-center density theorem identifies each section, hence the measures agree. Measurability of \(c\) supplies measurability of the pair update and joint density; no probability or moment condition on \(\mu\) is added.

UnadjustedLangevin/Metropolis.lean.title: Detailed balance through accepted and rejected flows
UnadjustedLangevin/Metropolis.lean.summary: The Metropolis correction preserves the initial marginal whenever the accepted proposal flow is invariant under swapping its two states. A positive proposal-pair density makes this symmetry explicit.

steps.title: acceptedFlow
steps.body: Weight the current/proposal joint measure \(\nu(dx,dy)\) by acceptance probability \(a(x,y)\). Thus \(A(dx,dy)=a(x,y)\nu(dx,dy)\), with ofReal embedding its real nonnegative weight. The bounds \(0\le a\le1\) are supplied in the conservation theorems below.

steps.title: rejectedFlow
steps.body: The rejected pair measure is \(R(dx,dy)=(1-a(x,y))\nu(dx,dy)\). It retains the proposed state as an auxiliary coordinate; the eventual output maps it to the original state \(x\), preserving all rejection mass.

steps.title: metropolisOutput
steps.body: Define the output as \(\operatorname{snd}_*A+\operatorname{fst}_*R\). Accepted moves output \(y\), while rejected moves output \(x\). This is the complete transition measure and requires no renormalization of accepted moves.

steps.title: acceptedFlow add rejectedFlow
steps.body: Since \(0\le a\le1\), the two nonnegative weights add to one after embedding in extended scalars. Additivity of with-density measures then gives \(A+R=\nu\). The proof checks both nonnegativity guards before combining ofReal values.

steps.title: marginals eq of swap invariant
steps.body: The identity \(\operatorname{fst}\circ\operatorname{swap}=\operatorname{snd}\) and pushforward composition give \(\operatorname{snd}_* u=\operatorname{fst}_*(\operatorname{swap}_* u)\). If the pair measure is swap invariant, this is \(\operatorname{fst}_* u\), proving equality of its marginals.

steps.title: metropolisOutput eq initial
steps.body: Detailed balance makes the two marginals of the accepted flow equal. Replace its second marginal by its first, then combine the accepted and rejected first marginals using \(A+R=\nu\). The output is therefore \(\operatorname{fst}_*\nu\), exactly the original state law.

steps.title: map weighted comp
steps.body: For a measurable \(f\) and weight \(w\), prove \(f_*((w\circ f)\mu)=w(f_*\mu)\). On each measurable set, the pushforward definition and nonnegative change-of-variables formula turn both sides into \(\int\mathbf1_A(f(x))w(f(x))d\mu(x)\). This is the weight-transport identity used by the actual MALA proposal map.

steps.title: map weighted comp equiv
steps.body: Specialize the preceding pushforward/weight identity to a measurable equivalence. Its bundled measurability supplies the required hypothesis. The application below uses the coordinate swap equivalence to prove symmetry of an accepted density.

steps.title: metropolisAcceptance
steps.body: For positive joint density \(w(x,y)\), define \(a(x,y)=\min(1,w(y,x)/w(x,y))\). The ratio is reverse flow divided by forward flow; positivity ensures both its meaning and nonnegative acceptance.

steps.title: weight mul metropolisAcceptance
steps.body: Distribute the positive factor \(w(x,y)\) through the minimum. Cancellation of the nonzero denominator gives \(w(x,y)a(x,y)=\min(w(x,y),w(y,x))\). This algebra is the reason the accepted joint density is symmetric.

steps.title: acceptedFlow density
steps.body: Two successive changes of density multiply their weights. Combine the original positive density \(w\) and acceptance \(a\), then apply the weight/minimum identity. The accepted flow becomes the base measure weighted by \(\min(w,w\circ\operatorname{swap})\), a visibly symmetric density.

steps.title: metropolisOutput density eq initial
steps.body: The base measure is swap invariant, and the accepted minimum density is unchanged by swapping its arguments. The weight-transport theorem therefore proves accepted-flow detailed balance. The general accepted/rejected conservation theorem then identifies the output with the initial marginal.

UnadjustedLangevin/MALAError.lean.title: A finite O(h³ᐟ²) rejected-displacement bound
UnadjustedLangevin/MALAError.lean.summary: The Metropolis-adjusted Langevin proposal provides an exactly invariant approximation to the diffusion. This module proves that its mean rejected displacement under Gibbs initialization is at most \(Ch\sqrt h\), with a finite constant derived from the potential assumptions.

steps.title: malaProposal
steps.body: Define \(T_h(x,\xi)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\xi\). This is the same Euler proposal used by ULA; MALA applies an accept/reject rule to this proposed state.

steps.title: malaLogRatio
steps.body: The log acceptance ratio is \(R_h(x,y)=U(x)-U(y)+(\|y-x+h\nabla U(x)\|^2-\|x-y+h\nabla U(y)\|^2)/(4h)\). The common Gaussian normalizers cancel in the reverse/forward proposal density ratio.

steps.title: malaLogRatio expansion
steps.body: Expand both squared norms using the real inner-product norm identity. The \(\|y-x\|^2\) terms cancel, and division by \(4h\) gives \(R_h=U(x)-U(y)+ rac12\langle abla U(x)+ abla U(y),y-x angle- rac h4(\| abla U(y)\|^2-\| abla U(x)\|^2)\). The premise \(h e0\) justifies denominator cancellation.

steps.title: gradient norm sq difference bound
steps.body: Factor \(|\|g_y\|^2-\|g_x\|^2|=|\|g_y\|-\|g_x\||(\|g_y\|+\|g_x\|)\). The reverse triangle inequality bounds the first factor by \(\|g_y-g_x\|\), then Lipschitzness bounds it by \(L\|y-x\|\). The other factor is nonnegative, so multiplication preserves the estimate.

steps.title: potential trapezoid bound
steps.body: Use the smooth upper and lower first-order models for the potential increment at the two endpoints. Compare the increment with the average endpoint directional derivative, and use the Lipschitz bound on the derivative difference. The resulting trapezoid error is at most \(L\|y-x\|^2\); no second derivative of \(U\) is assumed.

steps.title: malaLogRatio abs bound
steps.body: Insert the exact log-ratio expansion and use the triangle inequality. Bound its potential trapezoid term by \(L\|y-x\|^2\) and its squared-gradient difference by \(L\|y-x\|(\|g_x\|+\|g_y\|)\). Positivity of \(h\) gives the displayed coefficient \(hL/4\) without an absolute value on the step.

steps.title: metropolis rejection le abs
steps.body: If \(r\ge0\), \(e^r\ge1\), so rejection is zero. If \(r<0\), \(1-e^r\le-r=|r|\) by \(e^r\ge1+r\). Both cases also give \(0\le1-\min(1,e^r)\), establishing a nonnegative rejection probability and its log-ratio bound.

steps.title: rejected displacement le
steps.body: Multiply \(1-\min(1,e^r)\le|r|\) by the nonnegative displacement norm \(\|y-x\|\). This yields the rejection-weighted coupling error bound with no condition on the states.

steps.title: malaAmplitude
steps.body: Use the step-independent amplitude \(A(x,\xi)=\|\nabla U(x)\|+\sqrt2\|\xi\|\). For \(0\le h\le1\), it bounds the proposal displacement after extracting \(\sqrt h\); its cubic integrability will give a uniform rejection-error constant.

steps.title: malaRejectionDisplacement
steps.body: Define \(D_h(x,\xi)=\|T_h(x,\xi)-x\|(1-\min(1,e^{R_h(x,T_h(x,\xi))}))\). This is the acceptance-variable-averaged distance lost on rejection, so no additional uniform random variable appears in its integral.

steps.title: malaAmplitude nonneg
steps.body: Both score and noise norms are nonnegative, and \(\sqrt2\ge0\). Their sum defining \(A\) is therefore nonnegative. This sign permits later powers, products, and integral comparisons without absolute-value ambiguity.

steps.title: malaRejectionDisplacement nonneg
steps.body: The proposal displacement norm is nonnegative and the rejection factor is nonnegative by metropolis_rejection_le_abs. Their product is nonnegative, permitting use of extended integrals and domination by an integrable envelope.

steps.title: malaProposal displacement le
steps.body: The triangle inequality gives \(\|T_h-x\|\le h\|g_x\|+\sqrt{2h}\|\xi\|\). For \(0\le h\le1\), \(h\le\sqrt h\) and \(\sqrt{2h}=\sqrt2\sqrt h\). Factor out \(\sqrt h\) to obtain \(\|T_h-x\|\le\sqrt h A(x,\xi)\).

steps.title: malaRejectionDisplacement pointwise
steps.body: Use rejection \(\le|R_h|\), the log-ratio estimate, and \(\|g_{T_h}\|\le\|g_x\|+L\|T_h-x\|\). Replace the displacement by \(\sqrt hA\), and absorb the remaining step factors with \(h\le1\). The result is \(D_h\le h\sqrt h\,L(2+L)A^3\), whose envelope has no step-size dependence.

steps.title: integrable norm fourth mul exp neg mul norm sq
steps.body: A polynomial of degree four can be absorbed by part of Gaussian decay: \(\|x\|^4e^{-a\|x\|^2}\le C e^{-(a/2)\|x\|^2}\) for \(a>0\). Gaussian integrability and measurable domination therefore prove the fourth weighted moment is finite.

steps.title: integrable norm fourth mul exp neg of strongConvex
steps.body: The quadratic strong-convexity lower bound gives \(e^{-U(x)}\le C e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\). Multiply by \(\|x\|^4\) and invoke the fourth Gaussian weighted-moment theorem. This derives the unnormalized Gibbs fourth moment from the original potential assumptions.

steps.title: integrable norm fourth gibbsMeasure
steps.body: Change measure to the normalized Gibbs density. Integrability of \(\|x\|^4\) under \(\pi_U\) reduces to the just-proved integrability of \(\|x\|^4e^{-U(x)}\) times a finite normalization factor. No fourth-moment premise is added.

steps.title: memLp three id gibbsMeasure
steps.body: The fourth-moment theorem gives the identity variable in \(L^4(\pi_U)\). On a probability space, \(L^4\subset L^3\), so the identity belongs to \(L^3\). This supplies the cubic moment needed for the rejection envelope.

steps.title: malaPairMeasure
steps.body: Take \(\pi_U\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\), representing a Gibbs state and an independent standard Gaussian proposal innovation. This is the joint law under which the local rejection error is averaged.

steps.title: malaAmplitude memLp three
steps.body: The Gibbs state is in \(L^3\); Lipschitz growth \(\|\nabla U(x)\|\le\|\nabla U(0)\|+L\|x\|\) puts its score in \(L^3\). Gaussian noise also belongs to \(L^3\). Lift both to their independent product and add their norm envelopes to obtain \(A\in L^3\).

steps.title: malaAmplitude cube integrable
steps.body: For nonnegative \(A\), its third power is \(\|A\|^3\). The \(L^3\) characterization gives integrability of this function. This is the finite ordinary integral used to define the rejection constant.

steps.title: malaRejectionConstant
steps.body: Set \(C_{U,L}=L(2+L)\int A(x,\xi)^3d(\pi_U\otimes\gamma)\). The preceding declaration proves the integral is finite under the potential assumptions. All dependence on the positive step size has been removed from this constant.

steps.title: malaRejectionConstant nonneg
steps.body: The cubic amplitude integrand is nonnegative and its integral is nonnegative. Since \(L\ge0\), the factor \(L(2+L)\) is nonnegative as well. Their product gives \(C_{U,L}\ge0\).

steps.title: malaRejectionDisplacement integrable
steps.body: Continuity of the potential and gradient makes the rejection-displacement function measurable. Its absolute value equals itself by nonnegativity, and its pointwise bound is the integrable function \(h\sqrt h\,L(2+L)A^3\). Apply measurable domination to prove ordinary integrability.

steps.title: malaRejectionDisplacement integral bound
steps.body: Integrate the pointwise rejection envelope using the established integrability of both sides. Pull the step-independent factors out of the integral and recognize \(C_{U,L}\). This gives \(\mathbb ED_h\le C_{U,L}h\sqrt h\) for \(0<h\le1\).

steps.title: exists malaRejectionConstant
steps.body: Choose the explicitly defined malaRejectionConstant U L. Its nonnegativity and the integrated envelope theorem verify the existential statement for every \(0<h\le1\) simultaneously. The same constant works throughout the small-step limit.

UnadjustedLangevin/MALACoupling.lean.title: Couple ULA to an invariant Metropolis chain
UnadjustedLangevin/MALACoupling.lean.summary: A common Gaussian proposal couples unadjusted ULA with MALA. Under a stable small step, their expected distance grows by at most the Gibbs-average rejected displacement at each step. This is an auxiliary approximation for stationarity.

steps.title: malaAcceptance
steps.body: Define \(a_h(x,y)=\min(1,e^{R_h(x,y)})\), with the proved target/proposal log ratio. The minimum caps acceptance at one and the exponential ensures nonnegativity; these bounds justify the accepted/rejected measure split.

steps.title: malaProposalAcceptance
steps.body: Compose \(a_h\) with \((x,\xi)\mapsto(x,T_h(x,\xi))\). The resulting \(a_h(x,T_h(x,\xi))\) is the acceptance weight on the original state/noise product space, prior to pushing to state/proposal pairs.

steps.title: malaAcceptance nonneg
steps.body: Both entries of the minimum, one and the exponential, are nonnegative. Their minimum is nonnegative. This direct order proof is used when combining real weights through ENNReal.ofReal.

steps.title: malaAcceptance le one
steps.body: The minimum \(\min(1,e^{R_h})\) is at most its first entry. This proves \(a_h\le1\), so the rejection weight \(1-a_h\) is nonnegative.

steps.title: malaProposal measurable
steps.body: The gradient is continuous by Lipschitzness. Projections, scalar multiplication, subtraction, and addition preserve continuity, so the joint proposal map \((x,\xi)\mapsto x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\xi\) is measurable.

steps.title: malaProposalAcceptance measurable
steps.body: Differentiability makes \(U\) continuous, and Lipschitzness makes its gradient continuous. The log-ratio formula is assembled from continuous norms, inner products, and arithmetic; exponentiation and minimum preserve measurability. Composing with the measurable proposal gives the state/noise acceptance weight.

steps.title: ulaLawStep
steps.body: Define \(P_h\mu\) as the pushforward of \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) by the Euler proposal \(T_h\). The product measure encodes that the fresh Gaussian is independent of the current state. This transition is the actual independent-noise ULA step on laws.

steps.title: malaOneStep
steps.body: Split \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) into acceptance- and rejection-weighted measures. Map the accepted part to \(T_h(x,\xi)\), and the rejected part to \(x\), then add them. This defines one full MALA transition with all rejection mass retained.

steps.title: malaCoupledStep
steps.body: For a pair \((x,y)\), draw one shared Gaussian \(\xi\). ULA always moves to \(T_h(x,\xi)\); MALA moves to \(T_h(y,\xi)\) with weight \(a_h(y,T_h(y,\xi))\), otherwise stays at \(y\). The two weighted pushforwards define the explicit coupling measure.

steps.title: weighted accept reject add
steps.body: For a measurable \(a\in[0,1]\), combine the two with-density measures using \(a+(1-a)=1\). Nonnegativity of both terms justifies the ofReal addition identity, so their sum is exactly the original measure.

steps.title: malaCoupledStep fst
steps.body: The first-coordinate update is identical on acceptance and rejection. Combine those two weights to one before pushing forward. The remaining product marginal is the original first marginal times a fresh Gaussian, so the first output law is \(P_h(\operatorname{fst}_*\rho)\).

steps.title: malaCoupledStep snd
steps.body: Project both branches of the explicit coupling to the second state. They are exactly the accepted proposal and rejected current-state branches of MALA. Product marginal identities replace \(\rho\) by its second marginal, giving \(\operatorname{snd}_*\rho'=M_h(\operatorname{snd}_*\rho)\).

steps.title: malaCoupledStep isProbability
steps.body: The first marginal is a measurable pushforward of a probability product by malaCoupledStep_fst. It has mass one, and a measure and its first-coordinate pushforward have the same total mass. Therefore the joint coupling also has total mass one.

steps.title: malaCoupledChain
steps.body: Initialize on the diagonal \((X_0,Y_0)=(X,X)\) with \(X\sim\mu\), then recursively apply the explicit coupled step. Equal starting states give zero initial transport cost, while subsequent first and second marginals follow ULA and MALA respectively.

steps.title: malaCoupledChain isProbability
steps.body: The diagonal pushforward of the initial probability is a probability. Induct on the number of transitions, using probability preservation of malaCoupledStep at each successor. This produces the instance needed for product noise and finite-cost arguments at every iteration.

steps.title: malaCoupledChain fst
steps.body: At zero, diagonal initialization has first marginal \(\mu\). In the successor step apply malaCoupledStep_fst and the induction hypothesis. The resulting recursion is precisely the iteration \(P_h^n\mu\).

steps.title: malaCoupledChain snd
steps.body: At zero the second marginal is \(\pi\). The successor marginal theorem gives \(M_h\) applied to the current second marginal; substitute the induction hypothesis and the supplied one-step invariance \(M_h\pi=\pi\). Thus the second coordinate remains stationary through the coupling.

steps.title: malaProposal nonexpansive
steps.body: Shared noise cancels in \(T_h(x,\xi)-T_h(y,\xi)\). The sharp strong-convexity/smoothness contraction theorem for the deterministic gradient map bounds the remaining norm by \(\|x-y\|\) when \(0\le h\le2/(m+L)\). No Gaussian moment is used in this pointwise comparison.

steps.title: malaCoupledStep pointwise
steps.body: The accepted distance is at most \(\|x-y\|\) by nonexpansiveness. On rejection, insert \(T_h(y,\xi)\) and use the triangle inequality to bound the distance by \(\|x-y\|+\|T_h(y,\xi)-y\|\). Weight the two branches; their common old-distance coefficients add to one, and the remaining term is the rejection displacement.

steps.title: malaL1Cost
steps.body: Define \(\mathcal C(\rho)=\int\|x-y\|d\rho\) as a nonnegative extended integral. Keeping it extended avoids assuming integrability before the cost recurrence proves it. Subsequent theorems establish finiteness and then convert it to an ordinary expected distance.

steps.title: lintegral weighted map
steps.body: Pull an extended nonnegative integral through a measurable pushforward, then through a with-density measure. Multiplication of the two nonnegative real factors becomes the embedded product \(a(x)b(f(x))\). This gives an exact integration formula for each branch of the coupling.

steps.title: malaCoupledStep cost formula
steps.body: Apply lintegral_weighted_map to accepted and rejected branches of the coupled measure. Their cost is the integral of the acceptance-weighted proposal distance plus rejection-weighted stay distance over \(\rho\otimes\gamma\). The formula exposes exactly the pointwise expression bounded by malaCoupledStep_pointwise.

steps.title: malaCoupledStep cost le
steps.body: Integrate the pointwise coupling bound. The old distance integrates to \(\mathcal C(\rho)\); the error depends only on the second state and innovation. Its second marginal is Gibbs by hypothesis, so that integral is bounded by \(C_{U,L}h\sqrt h\). Thus \(\mathcal C(\rho')\le\mathcal C(\rho)+C_{U,L}h\sqrt h\), valid initially as an extended inequality.

steps.title: malaCoupledChain cost le
steps.body: Induct from zero diagonal cost. The second marginal remains Gibbs by the supplied one-step MALA invariance, so the one-step cost bound applies at every iteration. Summing the same local error gives \(\mathcal C(\rho_n)\le nC_{U,L}h\sqrt h\).

steps.title: malaCoupledChain distance integrable
steps.body: The quantitative extended cost estimate bounds \(\int\|x-y\|d\rho_n\) by a finite embedded real number. The distance is measurable and nonnegative, so finite extended integral is equivalent to ordinary integrability. This discharges the moment condition rather than assuming it.

steps.title: malaCoupledChain distance integral le
steps.body: Convert the finite extended cost inequality to real scalars using ENNReal.toReal. The newly proved integrability identifies the real value of the extended integral with the ordinary expected distance. Consequently \(\mathbb E_{\rho_n}\|X-Y\|\le nC_{U,L}h\sqrt h\).

UnadjustedLangevin/MALAInvariance.lean.title: Exact Gibbs invariance of the Metropolis-adjusted step
UnadjustedLangevin/MALAInvariance.lean.summary: The Gaussian proposal density identifies the MALA pair flow. Its reversed-to-forward density ratio is precisely the exponential of the implemented log ratio, so the Metropolis balance theorem proves exact Gibbs invariance.

steps.title: malaProposalJoint
steps.body: Push \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) through \((x,\xi)\mapsto(x,T_h(x,\xi))\). Its first coordinate retains the current state, and its second records the actual Gaussian proposal. This joint measure is the input to the accepted-flow detailed-balance theorem.

steps.title: malaJointWeight
steps.body: Set \(w_h(x,y)=\exp(-U(x)-\|y-x+h\nabla U(x)\|^2/(4h))\). The Gibbs and Gaussian normalization constants are kept in a separate symmetric base measure, so \(w_h\) is strictly positive and its reverse/forward ratio is easy to compute.

steps.title: malaJointWeight ratio
steps.body: Divide the two positive exponentials and use \(e^a/e^b=e^{a-b}\). Expanding the definition of \(w_h\) shows the exponent difference is exactly malaLogRatio. Thus \(w_h(y,x)/w_h(x,y)=e^{R_h(x,y)}\).

steps.title: malaOneStep eq metropolisOutput
steps.body: Transport acceptance and rejection weights through the measurable pair map using map_weighted_comp. Projecting the accepted pair to its second coordinate gives the proposal; projecting rejected pairs to the first gives the unchanged state. These are precisely the two branches defining malaOneStep.

steps.title: malaProposalJoint gibbs density
steps.body: Apply the Gaussian joint-density theorem with center \(x-h\nabla U(x)\), then multiply its density by the Gibbs density. Combine the exponential factors into \(w_h(x,y)\). Pull the two state-independent normalizers into the base measure \(Z_U^{-1}C_h(dx\,dy)\), which is invariant under coordinate swap.

steps.title: malaOneStep gibbs invariant
steps.body:
The joint proposal measure has a positive density \(w_h\) against a symmetric base. Its acceptance rule is \(\min(1,w_h(y,x)/w_h(x,y))\) by malaJointWeight_ratio. Hence its accepted density is the symmetric minimum \(\min(w_h(x,y),w_h(y,x))\).

Apply metropolisOutput_density_eq_initial and the exact step/output identity. The initial marginal of the proposal pair is Gibbs, since projecting \(\pi_U\otimes\gamma\) to its state returns \(\pi_U\). Thus \(M_h\pi_U=\pi_U\) is proved with no stationarity input.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianLangevin.lean.title: Construct the L² Langevin equation from Brownian-coordinate laws
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianLangevin.lean.summary: Coordinate pre-Brownian laws produce the continuous \(L^2\) additive noise needed by the deterministic integral-equation existence theorem. The exact noise norm is \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\).

steps.title: brownianLangevinNoise
steps.body: Define \(N_a(t)=\sqrt2([B_{a+t}]-[B_a])\) in \(L^2\), using the real-time Brownian extension. The subtraction fixes the input at zero at local time zero, and the \(\sqrt2\) factor gives the overdamped Langevin diffusion normalization.

steps.title: brownianLangevinNoise continuous
steps.body: The real-time Brownian map is continuous in \(L^2\) from its Gaussian increment moments. Composition with \(t\mapsto a+t\), subtraction of the fixed class \([B_a]\), and scalar multiplication preserve continuity. Thus the additive input satisfies the deterministic Picard theorem's continuity requirement.

steps.title: brownianLangevinNoise zero
steps.body: At local time zero both Brownian terms are \([B_a]\), so they cancel and their scalar multiple is zero. Lean unfolds the definition and uses additive identities; no exceptional-set statement is needed because this is equality in \(L^2\).

steps.title: brownianLangevinNoise norm
steps.body: For \(a,t\ge0\), apply the exact real-time Brownian increment moment formula. It gives \(\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\), with \(d=|\iota|\). The Gaussian laws prove this value; it is not an additional noise-bound hypothesis.

steps.title: exists lp langevin integral of brownian small
steps.body: Supply the continuous, zero-starting \(N_a\) to exists_lp_langevin_integral_small. It constructs \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t\operatorname{lpDrift}(\nabla U)(Y_s)ds+N_a(t)\) for \(Lh\le1/2\). Attach the exact noise norm theorem to the existential package. Neither the integral equation nor its noise estimate is assumed.

steps.title: exists lp langevin integral of brownian
steps.body: Use the unrestricted finite-horizon \(L^2\) existence theorem with the same constructed Brownian input. The resulting solution is continuous in \(L^2\), starts at the prescribed random variable, and satisfies the actual gradient integral equation. The exact \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) noise formula is included as a proved property.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianReference.lea.title: Assemble continuous Brownian reference segments
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianReference.lea.summary: Construct consecutive \(L^2\) Langevin segments from actual Brownian-coordinate noise and package them as an analytic reference. At this intermediate stage Gibbs stationarity remains an explicit premise, later discharged in CanonicalULA.

steps.title: brownianSegmentFrom
steps.body: Choose the integral solution supplied by exists_lp_langevin_integral_of_brownian for the segment starting at absolute time \(nh\), with the supplied initial \(L^2\) variable. Classical choice selects data from a proved existence theorem; its defining equation and continuity are recovered by the specification theorem.

steps.title: brownianSegmentFrom spec
steps.body: Apply the choice specification to obtain continuity, the time-zero initial value, the gradient integral equation on \([0,h]\), and the exact noise norm. These four properties describe the selected segment independently of its noncomputable implementation.

steps.title: brownianKnots
steps.body: Set the zeroth knot to the prescribed initial variable. Define the next knot to be the endpoint at local time \(h\) of the segment started at the current knot. This recursion ensures consecutive segments meet exactly as \(L^2\) classes.

steps.title: brownianSegments
steps.body: At index \(n\), select brownianSegmentFrom with the recursively constructed \(n\)-th knot as initial state. The absolute noise start is \(nh\), so all segments are driven by increments of the same Brownian process.

steps.title: brownianSegments start
steps.body: The chosen-segment specification states its value at zero equals its supplied initial state. Here that state is the \(n\)-th knot, so \(Y^{(n)}_0=K_n\) follows directly by specialization.

steps.title: brownianSegments initial
steps.body: Apply the segment-start identity at \(n=0\), then unfold the zeroth knot. The actual constructed reference therefore begins at exactly the prescribed random variable, preserving its chosen joint realization with the numerical initialization.

steps.title: brownianEulerNoise
steps.body: Normalize the actual segment endpoint noise by \(1/\sqrt{2h}\). This defines the \(L^2\) innovation used by the Euler chain, so it shares the exact Brownian increment driving the reference segment.

steps.title: brownianEulerNoise endpoint
steps.body: For \(h>0\), \(\sqrt{2h}\ne0\). Multiply the normalized noise class by \(\sqrt{2h}\) and cancel the inverse scalar. The resulting equality identifies the Euler noise contribution with the same Brownian endpoint input in the integral equation.

steps.title: brownianReference
steps.body: Populate L2Reference with the constructed segments. Their specification proves continuity and the integral equation; recursive knots prove endpoint compatibility; normalized noise proves endpoint matching; Gibbs-score moment transfer proves the drift bound. The supplied all-time Gibbs-law premise remains visible and is later discharged by the stationarity construction.

steps.title: brownianReference of strongConvex
steps.body: Use strong convexity to derive finiteness of the Gibbs partition, then call brownianReference. All analytic, normalization, moment, and noise fields are proved internally. The all-time law premise is still explicit in this constructor and must be provided by the stationary-law theorem.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianSegmentsGloba.title: Identify chosen reference segments with one global solution
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianSegmentsGloba.summary: The segment construction is compatible with the unique global integral solution. This lets stationarity of a global Brownian Langevin solution prove stationarity of every chosen reference segment.

steps.title: brownianLangevinNoise increment
steps.body: Expand the two increments from zero and subtract them. Their common \([B_0]\) term cancels, leaving \(\sqrt2([B_{a+t}]-[B_a])=N_a(t)\). This is an algebraic cocycle identity in \(L^2\), valid for the real-time extension as defined.

steps.title: lp brownian integral shift
steps.body: Subtract the global integral equations at \(a+t\) and \(a\). Integral additivity gives the drift integral over \([a,a+t]\), and time translation turns it into \(\int_0^t\nabla U(Y_{a+s})ds\). The noise cocycle gives \(N_a(t)\), yielding the local segment equation with initial state \(Y_a\).

steps.title: brownianSegmentFrom eq global
steps.body: The shifted global path and the selected local segment are continuous solutions of the same \(L^2\) integral equation with the same initial value and noise input. Apply \(L^2\) uniqueness to identify them on \([0,h]\). The horizon premise ensures the shifted interval lies inside the global solution interval.

steps.title: brownianKnots eq global
steps.body: Induct on the knot index. At zero, the global equation and zero-starting noise give the prescribed initial state. If the current knot equals \(Y_{nh}\), segment/global uniqueness makes its endpoint equal \(Y_{(n+1)h}\), establishing the next knot identity.

steps.title: brownianSegments eq global
steps.body: The knot/global theorem supplies the matching initial value for the \(n\)-th segment. Apply brownianSegmentFrom_eq_global to conclude \(Y^{(n)}_t=Y_{nh+t}\) on \([0,h]\). This is a deterministic identification of the constructions, with no stationarity premise.

UnadjustedLangevin/ChainLaw.lean.title: A noise-driven recursion has a law independent of its realization
UnadjustedLangevin/ChainLaw.lean.summary: For measurable \(F(x,z)\), the recursion \(X_{n+1}=F(X_n,Z_n)\) has a law determined by the initial law and the full noise law when the initialization and noise are independent.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain
steps.body: Define \(X_0=x\), \(X_{n+1}=F(X_n,w_n)\) for any update and noise path. No distribution assumptions are part of the recursion; they enter only when a law is assigned to its inputs.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain zero
steps.body: The zero clause of the recursion evaluates to the supplied initial state. This definitional identity is the base case for all law and measurability inductions.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain succ
steps.body: The successor clause unfolds to \(X_{n+1}=F(X_n,w_n)\). This exact recursion lets the generic construction later be identified with ULA by induction.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain measurable
steps.body: Induct on \(n\). The base map is the initial-state projection. At the successor, pair the measurable current state with the measurable coordinate evaluation \(w\mapsto w_n\), then compose with the measurable uncurried update. Thus each iterate is a measurable function of initialization and the full noise path.

steps.title: chainLaw
steps.body: Push \(\mu\otimes Q\) through the measurable recursion output at index \(n\). The product gives independent initialization and noise path. This canonical law depends only on the initial law, noise-path law, and update, not on a particular sample-space implementation.

steps.title: chainLaw zero
steps.body: At index zero the output map is first-coordinate projection. Since \(Q\) has mass one, the first marginal of \(\mu\otimes Q\) is exactly \(\mu\). This proves that the canonical law starts from the supplied initial law.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain law of indep
steps.body: Independence gives the joint input law \(P_{(X,W)}=P_X\otimes P_W\). Push that identity through the measurable recursion output and use pushforward composition. The resulting output law is exactly chainLaw F (P.map X) (P.map W) n.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain law of iid
steps.body: Joint independence of the innovations and their common law \(\eta\) identify the entire noise-path law with \(\bigotimes_n\eta\). Substitute this identity into the independent-initialization law theorem. Countability of the time index supplies path-valued measurability.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain law unique
steps.body: Apply the canonical iid-law formula on both probability spaces. Equality of their initial laws and the shared innovation law makes the right sides identical, so their iterate laws agree. The theorem compares distributions without coupling the two implementations.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain eq ulaChain
steps.body: Induct on the index with \(F=\operatorname{ulaUpdate}\). The zero values agree, and the successor equations apply the same update to equal previous states and the same noise vector. This proves pointwise equality of the generic recursion and the repository's ULA chain.

steps.title: ulaUpdate measurable
steps.body: Lipschitzness makes \(\nabla U\) continuous. The joint ULA update is obtained from coordinate projections and that gradient by scalar multiplication and addition, hence is measurable. This discharges the generic recursion's update-measurability premise.

steps.title: ulaChain law of iid
steps.body: Use measurability of ulaUpdate in the generic iid law theorem, then rewrite the generic recursion using noiseDrivenChain_eq_ulaChain. The result identifies the actual ULA implementation with its canonical product-noise law.

steps.title: lpUlaChain law of iid
steps.body: The \(L^2\) chain representative agrees almost everywhere with the pointwise ULA recursion of the input representatives. Apply the pointwise law theorem and transfer pushforwards across that almost-everywhere equality. Quotient representative choices therefore do not change the algorithm law.

UnadjustedLangevin/MarkovLaw.lean.title: Identify recursive sampling laws with iterated Markov transitions
UnadjustedLangevin/MarkovLaw.lean.summary: The path-space law of an iid-noise recursion agrees with the repeated one-step transition \(\mu\mapsto F_\#(\mu\otimes\eta)\). The proof explicitly establishes independence of the current state and the fresh innovation.

steps.title: finiteNoiseChain
steps.body: Evaluate the same recursion using only a finite prefix \((w_0,\ldots,w_{n-1})\). At the successor, recurse on the first \(n\) coordinates and use the final coordinate as the next innovation. This makes finite dependence explicit for the fresh-noise independence proof.

steps.title: finiteNoiseChain eq
steps.body: Induct on prefix length. Restricting an infinite path to its first \(n\) entries gives the same previous state, and the final finite coordinate is \(w_n\). The successor updates thus agree, identifying finite-prefix and infinite-path implementations pointwise.

steps.title: finiteNoiseChain measurable
steps.body: The zero map is the initial projection. At the successor, restriction to the earlier finite coordinates and evaluation of the last coordinate are measurable; combine them with the measurable update and the induction hypothesis. This proves the state depends measurably on a finite prefix.

steps.title: iid prefix independent fresh
steps.body: The index sets \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and \(\{n\}\) are disjoint. Independence of the coordinate family on the iid product source therefore gives independence of the whole prefix vector and the next coordinate. This is stronger than pairwise independence of individual past entries.

steps.title: markovStep
steps.body: Define \(M_\eta(\mu)=F_*(\mu\otimes\eta)\). Its product measure means the innovation is fresh and independent of the current state. The subsequent theorem derives that independence for the canonical recursion, rather than assuming it at each step.

steps.title: markovLaws
steps.body: Set \(\mu_0=\mu\), \(\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n)\). These are iterated independent-noise transition laws. The recursion alone does not yet assert that a previously defined sample-path algorithm realizes them.

steps.title: chainLaw joint fresh
steps.body: The current state is a measurable function of initialization and the first \(n\) noises. Product-source independence and prefix/fresh independence make it independent of \(w_n\). Its marginal is chainLaw, and the innovation marginal is \(\eta\); their joint law is therefore the product of those actual marginals.

steps.title: chainLaw succ iid
steps.body: The pointwise successor is \(F(X_n,w_n)\). Push the proved product joint law of \((X_n,w_n)\) through \(F\); this yields \(\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n)\) for the canonical recursion laws. No later-time state/noise independence is assumed.

steps.title: chainLaw eq markovLaws
steps.body: The canonical path law and the iterated Markov law have the same initial value and the same successor equation. Induction on \(n\) identifies them at every index. This closes the connection between sample-path and transition-law definitions.

steps.title: markovStep isProbability
steps.body: The independent product of two probability measures has mass one. A measurable pushforward preserves that total mass, so markovStep is again a probability measure.

steps.title: markovLaws isProbability
steps.body: Induct from the initial probability and apply markovStep_isProbability at each successor. This proves normalization of every transition iterate and provides the probability instances used in later law comparisons.

steps.title: noiseDrivenChain law eq markovLaws
steps.body: First identify the independent iid realization with the canonical product-path output law. Then apply chainLaw_eq_markovLaws. Every realization satisfying the original initialization/noise assumptions consequently has the same proved Markov iterate law.

UnadjustedLangevin/InitialExtension.lean.title: Realize every initial coupling independently of the noise
UnadjustedLangevin/InitialExtension.lean.summary: Given any coupling \(\gamma\) of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\), extend it to \(\gamma\otimes Q\). This preserves its quadratic cost and supplies independent noise without requiring an optimal coupling.

steps.title: Coupling.isProbabilityMeasure
steps.body: The coupling's first marginal is the initial probability. Pushforward preserves total mass, so \(c(H\times H)=\mu(H)=1\). This constructs normalization of the joint measure using a marginal identity already stored in Coupling.

steps.title: initialExtension
steps.body: Extend an initial coupling \(c(dx,dy)\) by an independent noise sample \(s\sim Q\), using \(c\otimes Q\) on \((H\times H)\times S\). Both algorithms retain the prescribed initial joint law while sharing fresh noise independent of the pair.

steps.title: initialExtension isProbabilityMeasure
steps.body: The coupling is a probability by its first marginal, and \(Q\) is a probability by hypothesis. Their product therefore has total mass one. This instance supports all subsequent \(L^2\) constructions on the extension.

steps.title: initialExtension joint
steps.body: Projecting \(c\otimes Q\) to the first factor integrates out the probability noise coordinate. Since \(Q(S)=1\), the resulting measure is exactly \(c\), preserving the entire initial dependence structure.

steps.title: initialExtension initial
steps.body: Compose the joint projection with its first state projection. The extension's joint marginal is \(c\), whose first state marginal is \(\mu\). Pushforward composition therefore yields the specified algorithm initialization law.

steps.title: initialExtension reference
steps.body: Compose projection to the initial pair with its second state projection. The coupling's second marginal is \(\pi\), so the reference initialization on the extension has exactly law \(\pi\).

steps.title: initialExtension noise
steps.body: The coupling measure has mass one. Projecting its product with \(Q\) to the noise factor therefore returns \(Q\). The SFinite hypothesis supplies the product marginal theorem's measure-theoretic condition.

steps.title: initialExtension independent
steps.body: The two coordinate projections of a product probability measure are independent. Here those coordinates are the full coupled initial pair and the fresh noise sample. Independence of either individual initial state from any noise-derived random object follows by composition.

steps.title: initialExtension initial noise
steps.body: Map \(((x,y),s)\) to \((x,s)\). Product pushforward and the first marginal identity of \(c\) give \(\mu\otimes Q\). Thus removing the reference coordinate leaves the same algorithm input law for every initial coupling.

steps.title: initialExtension map
steps.body: Factor the map through \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,s)\), whose law is \(\mu\otimes Q\). Pushforward composition proves that every measurable output depending only on algorithm initialization and noise has the coupling-independent law \(f_*(\mu\otimes Q)\).

steps.title: initialExtension chainLaw
steps.body: Apply initialExtension_map to the measurable recursion output. Its canonical pushforward is exactly chainLaw, so the same output law is realized on every initial-coupling extension. This equality is derived rather than made a field of the coupling.

steps.title: initialExtension iid noiseLaw
steps.body: First project the extension to its product-path noise law, then evaluate coordinate \(n\). The marginal of \(\bigotimes_k\eta\) at that coordinate is \(\eta\), giving the requested noise law on the extension.

steps.title: initialExtension iid independent
steps.body: The iid path has independent coordinate evaluations. Pull this independence back along the extension's measure-preserving noise projection. The resulting innovation sequence remains jointly independent on the coupled initialization space.

steps.title: initialExtension initial independent
steps.body: The algorithm's initial state is a projection of the initial pair. Compose the pair/noise independence theorem with this state projection. This proves independence from the entire noise sample, not just from each individual noise vector.

steps.title: initialExtension cost
steps.body: The difference \(x-y\) depends only on the initial pair. Its \(L^2\) extended norm under \(c\otimes Q\) equals the same norm under \(c\), because the noise factor has mass one. The latter is exactly couplingCost c.joint.

steps.title: initialExtension memLp difference
steps.body: The state-difference function is measurable. Its extended \(L^2\) norm equals the finite initial coupling cost by the previous theorem. These two facts prove MemLp for the difference on the extension.

steps.title: initialExtension memLp reference
steps.body: The reference coordinate has law \(\pi\). Pull its supplied \(L^2(\pi)\) identity moment back through this law to get square integrability on the extension. This establishes the reference initialization without choosing a separate realization.

steps.title: initialExtension memLp initial
steps.body: Write \(x=(x-y)+y\). The difference is in \(L^2\) by finite coupling cost and the reference coordinate is in \(L^2\) by its law. Closure of \(L^2\) under addition gives square integrability of the initial algorithm state; no independent moment premise on \(\mu\) is introduced.

steps.title: initialExtension lpInitial
steps.body: Use initialExtension_memLp_initial to convert the first state coordinate into an actual \(L^2\) class. The class is represented almost everywhere by \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x\), preserving its concrete relation to the coupling coordinates.

steps.title: initialExtension lpReference
steps.body: Convert the square-integrable second state coordinate into an \(L^2\) class. Its representative equals \(((x,y),s)\mapsto y\) almost everywhere, with law \(\pi\), and it shares the same product probability space as the algorithm initialization.

steps.title: initialExtension lpInitial law
steps.body: The representative chosen by toLp agrees almost everywhere with the first state coordinate. Pushforwards are unchanged by such an equality. Combine this with initialExtension_initial to obtain the initial law \(\mu\).

steps.title: initialExtension lpReference law
steps.body: Replace the selected \(L^2\) representative by the second state projection almost everywhere. Its already proved marginal is \(\pi\), hence the class used as reference initialization has exactly that law.

steps.title: initialExtension lp cost
steps.body: The representative of the class difference equals \(x-y\) almost everywhere. The norm of that \(L^2\) difference is the real value of its extended norm; initialExtension_cost identifies it with \((\operatorname{couplingCost}c)_{\mathbb R}\). The finite-cost premise justifies this real conversion.

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsStationarity.lea.title: Prove Gibbs stationarity by refining invariant Metropolis chains
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsStationarity.lea.summary: A Brownian Langevin integral solution started from Gibbs stays Gibbs. The proof uses convergent Euler approximations and exactly invariant MALA chains, with no weak-PDE uniqueness assumption.

steps.title: hilbert lpChain coe
steps.body: Induct over the chain recursion. The representative of the lifted gradient equals the pointwise gradient almost everywhere, and the representative formulas for addition and scalar multiplication give the same Euler successor. Intersect the finite set of null-set complements needed at each index to identify the \(L^2\) chain with the ordinary recursion.

steps.title: hilbert lpChain law eq ulaLawStep
steps.body: Use the almost-everywhere pointwise-chain identification, the independent-iid realization law theorem, and the canonical path/Markov-law identity. With innovation law \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), the generic independent-noise step is exactly ulaLawStep. Thus the \(L^2\) implementation has law \(P_h^n(P_{X_0})\).

steps.title: additiveEulerChain eq hilbert lpChain
steps.body: Induct on the mesh index. Both chains start at the same \(L^2\) variable. Their successor equations agree because the supplied additive increment equals \(\sqrt{2h}W_k\), making the noise terms identical as classes.

steps.title: brownianLangevinNoise grid increment
steps.body: Apply the Brownian input cocycle at \(a=kh\), \(t=h\). The elementary identity \((k+1)h=kh+h\) matches its endpoints to the grid notation. This supplies the exact additive increment used by the normalized Euler noise.

steps.title: brownian additiveEulerChain eq lpChain
steps.body: The Brownian grid-increment identity and brownianEulerNoise_endpoint verify the increment premise of the generic chain equality. Therefore the deterministic matching-noise Euler approximation is exactly the already defined Brownian-normalized \(L^2\) Euler chain.

steps.title: brownianEulerNoise vectorGaussian
steps.body: Each normalized coordinate is standard Gaussian. The supplied joint scalar-coordinate independence lets gaussianInnovations_vectorLaw and gaussianInnovations_vectorIndependent assemble those coordinates into iid standard multivariate Gaussian vectors. These are the exact law hypotheses needed by the Markov-recursion theorem.

steps.title: Pass the invariant Gibbs marginal to the continuous limit
steps.body:
Fix \(T>0\) and choose meshes \(h_n=T/N_n\to0\) small enough for the nonexpansive MALA coupling. Matching-noise Euler approximations converge in \(L^2\) to \(Y_T\). Their laws are exactly \(P_{h_n}^{N_n}\pi_U\), by the proved iid Brownian innovation laws and initialization independence.

Couple each Euler law to \(N_n\) MALA steps started from Gibbs. Exact MALA invariance makes the second marginal \(\pi_U\). The rejection bound gives expected coupling distance at most \(N_nC h_n\sqrt{h_n}=TC\sqrt{h_n}\to0\); integrability of this distance is proved from the finite extended-cost estimate.

Apply measure_map_Lp_eq_of_coupling_cost_tendsto: characteristic functions of the Euler endpoints converge to those of \(Y_T\) by \(L^2\) convergence, and to those of \(\pi_U\) by the vanishing coupling cost. Equality of characteristic functions proves \(P_{Y_T}=\pi_U\). The zero-horizon case follows directly from the integral equation.

UnadjustedLangevin/CouplingLimit.lean.title: A vanishing coupling distance determines the limiting law
UnadjustedLangevin/CouplingLimit.lean.summary: If \(X_n\to X\) in \(L^2\) and each \(\operatorname{Law}(X_n)\) couples to a fixed probability \(\pi\) with mean distance tending to zero, then \(\operatorname{Law}(X)=\pi\).

steps.title: characteristicTest norm sub le
steps.body: The unit-circle map is \(1\)-Lipschitz, so the difference of the two characters is at most \(|\langle x-y,t\rangle|\). Cauchy–Schwarz then bounds this by \(\|t\|\|x-y\|\). Thus characteristic tests have an explicit Lipschitz constant at each fixed frequency.

steps.title: charFun marginals norm sub le
steps.body: Pull both marginal characteristic integrals back to the coupling space and subtract. Each character is bounded by one, hence integrable under the probability coupling. The integral norm inequality and the pointwise Lipschitz estimate give \(|\widehat\mu(t)-\widehat\pi(t)|\le\|t\|\mathbb E\|X-Y\|\), with the distance's integrability explicitly supplied.

steps.title: continuous charFun map Lp hilbert
steps.body: Apply the continuous linear functional \(x\mapsto\langle t,x\rangle\) to an \(H\)-valued \(L^2\) variable. Its lifted map is continuous on \(L^2\). The Hilbert-valued characteristic function at \(t\) is the scalar projected characteristic function at frequency one, so the scalar continuity theorem proves the claim.

steps.title: measure map Lp eq of coupling cost tendsto
steps.body: For each \(t\), the coupling inequality forces the approximating characteristic functions toward \(\widehat\pi(t)\), since the expected distance tends to zero. Independently, \(L^2\) convergence forces them toward \(\widehat{P_X}(t)\). Uniqueness of limits along a nontrivial filter identifies these values, and Measure.ext_of_charFun yields \(P_X=\pi\).

UnadjustedLangevin/ProductReference.lean.title: A reference for every initial coupling with one output law
UnadjustedLangevin/ProductReference.lean.summary: This construction turns the analytic reference estimate into an exact initial Wasserstein term by realizing each finite initial coupling on a product with one fixed noise source.

steps.title: pointwiseUpdate
steps.body: Define the ordinary Euler update \(F_h(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}z\) in an arbitrary Hilbert-space presentation. It is the pointwise function whose lifted composition gives the \(L^2\) numerical chain.

steps.title: pointwiseUpdate measurable
steps.body: The Lipschitz gradient is continuous. Compose it with the first coordinate projection and combine the remaining continuous scalar and vector operations. The uncurried map \((x,z)\mapsto F_h(x,z)\) is therefore measurable.

steps.title: productNoise memLp
steps.body: The noise projection from \(c\otimes Q\) to \(Q\) is measure preserving because the coupling is a probability. Pull back the supplied \(L^2(Q)\) noise function along this projection. Its square integrability is unchanged.

steps.title: productNoise
steps.body: Use the preceding square-integrability proof to form the class of \(((x,y),s)\mapsto W_n(s)\) on the concrete extension. Both the numerical chain and reference use this same \(L^2\) innovation.

steps.title: productNoise coe
steps.body: The representative selected by toLp agrees almost everywhere with the pulled-back original noise \(W_n(s)\). This identity connects quotient-space noise arithmetic to the actual source random functions.

steps.title: productOutputLaw
