steps.body: Push \(\mu\otimes Q\) through the pointwise noise-driven chain starting at \(x\) with source path \(W(s)\). This definition omits the reference coupling entirely, making explicit the common algorithm output law for all coupling realizations.

steps.title: product chain coe
steps.body: Induct through the lifted chain and use the representative identities for initial state, product noise, lifted drift, addition, and scalar multiplication. At each fixed index the result agrees almost everywhere with the ordinary recursion driven by \(x\) and \(W(s)\).

steps.title: product chain outputLaw
steps.body: Replace the \(L^2\) chain by its almost-everywhere pointwise recursion. That recursion depends only on the algorithm's initial coordinate and noise sample, so initialExtension_map gives its coupling-independent law. The result is exactly productOutputLaw.

steps.title: productProbability
steps.body: A coupling of the initial probability with the reference measure is itself a probability, and its product with the fixed probability noise source is a probability. This local instance supplies normalization on every extension separately.

steps.title: ProductReference
steps.body: For every finite-cost initial coupling, the structure supplies a concrete L2Reference on that coupling's product extension, with its initial state matching the second coordinate. Algorithm output laws and initial costs are proved outside the structure; no convergence estimate is a field.

steps.title: ProductReference.output finite
steps.body: Finite initial Wasserstein distance supplies at least one finite-cost initial coupling. On its concrete extension, the numerical and reference variables belong to \(L^2\), giving a finite-cost output coupling. Their established laws identify its marginals with the common output law and \(\pi\), hence the output Wasserstein distance is finite.

steps.title: dalalyan small step of product reference
steps.body:
For each finite-cost initial coupling \(c\), apply the analytic \(L^2\) Dalalyan theorem on \(c\otimes Q\). The initial class-distance theorem identifies its initial error exactly with the real coupling cost, and the common output-law theorem identifies its numerical law.

The resulting bound holds for every finite \(c\), with coefficient \((1-mh)^n\ge0\). Infimizing their costs gives the genuine \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\), without selecting an optimal coupling. Output finiteness is proved first so the final real-valued inequality cannot conceal infinity.

steps.title: dalalyan large step of product reference
steps.body: Repeat the couplingwise analytic argument for the stable large-step branch, whose contraction factor is \(Lh-1\in[0,1)\). The geometric error sum has denominator \(2-Lh>0\). The finite-coupling infimum theorem replaces the initial class distance by the actual initial Wasserstein distance and yields the displayed large-step bias term.

UnadjustedLangevin/ProductBrownian.lean.title: Pull Brownian noise onto every coupled initialization
UnadjustedLangevin/ProductBrownian.lean.summary: Brownian-coordinate laws, innovation independence and their L² realizations survive passage to the product \(\gamma\otimes Q\). This builds all reference fields except the explicitly displayed stationarity premise, discharged by the later canonical assembly.

steps.title: preBrownian comp measurePreserving
steps.body: A measure-preserving map leaves the law of every measurable random variable unchanged after pullback. Apply this to every finite-dimensional Brownian vector. Their Gaussian laws and covariance data are therefore preserved, giving a pre-Brownian process on the new sample space.

steps.title: brownianCoordinatesLp pullback
steps.body: Both sides represent the vector \((B_i(t,f(\omega)))_i\) almost everywhere. Pull back the source representative equality using measure preservation and combine it with the target toLp equality. Lp.ext identifies the two quotient classes.

steps.title: brownianEulerNoise pullback
steps.body: The \(L^2\) pullback is linear, hence commutes with subtraction and scalar multiplication. Apply the preceding Brownian-vector pullback identity to the two endpoints in the normalized increment. This identifies the pulled-back Euler noise with the noise constructed after pullback.

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise
steps.body: Take the actual selected representative of the previously constructed \(L^2\) Brownian Euler noise on the source space. This is the random function supplied to the generic product algorithm before choosing any initial coupling.

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise memLp
steps.body: Every representative of a given \(L^2\) class is square integrable by Lp.memLp. Apply that fact to the Brownian Euler noise class. This avoids assuming an extra noise-moment condition in the product construction.

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise coe
steps.body: Unfold the nested class-valued noise definition and apply representative equalities for scalar multiplication, subtraction, and the Brownian vector classes. Almost everywhere the result is \((\sqrt{2h})^{-1}\sqrt2(B_{nh+h}-B_{nh})\), with real-time clipping as in the original definition.

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise coordinate coe
steps.body: Evaluate the vector representative formula in coordinate \(i\). For \(h>0\), use \(\sqrt{2h}=\sqrt2\sqrt h\) and cancel the nonzero \(\sqrt2\), obtaining \((B_i((n+1)h)-B_i(nh))/\sqrt h\).

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise coordinate coe nnreal
steps.body: For nonnegative mesh times, Real.toNNReal leaves their real values unchanged. Rewrite both clipped grid endpoints into the corresponding nonnegative-real products. The coordinate formula becomes the ordinary Brownian grid increment divided by \(\sqrt h\).

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise normalized coordinate
steps.body: The nonnegative-grid formula is exactly the definition of normalizedBrownianIncrement. After converting the positive real step to its nonnegative-real form, the two random functions agree almost everywhere. This gives a direct bridge to the established innovation-law theorems.

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise coordinateLaw
steps.body: A normalized Brownian increment has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Transfer this law across sourceEulerNoise_normalized_coordinate using almost-everywhere invariance of laws. Hence the actual source noise representative has the required Gaussian coordinate law.

steps.title: sourceEulerNoise independent
steps.body: The Brownian grid-path theorem gives independence of all normalized coordinates indexed by \((i,n)\). Reindex by the injective coordinate swap to \((n,i)\), then transfer across the almost-everywhere coordinate identities. This matches the index order expected by the vector innovation theorem.

steps.title: productPreBrownian
steps.body: Projection from an initial-coupling product extension to the noise source is measure preserving. Pull each scalar Brownian coordinate back along it using preBrownian_comp_measurePreserving. The actual coordinate processes on the extension retain their Brownian finite-dimensional laws.

steps.title: productNoise eq brownianEulerNoise
steps.body: The lifted source noise and the extension's constructed Brownian noise are both the measure-preserving pullback of the source \(L^2\) Brownian Euler noise. Use representative extensionality to identify the former with this pullback, then apply brownianEulerNoise_pullback to identify the latter.

steps.title: productEulerNoise coordinateLaw
steps.body: Pull the source standard-Gaussian coordinate law through the extension's noise projection. The lifted product-noise representative agrees almost everywhere with the raw pulled-back source noise. Transfer the law across that equality to obtain the coordinate law for the exact classes used by the numerical chain.

steps.title: productEulerNoise independent
steps.body: Identify the source coordinate-time path law as the product of standard Gaussians. Pull that law to the extension; its coordinate family is independent by the product-law independence criterion. Finally replace raw source pullbacks by the almost-everywhere equal product-noise representatives.

steps.title: productEulerNoise independentInitial
steps.body: The raw first initial coordinate depends only on the coupling factor, while the whole source noise sequence depends only on the noise factor. Product independence therefore applies. Countability of the sequence lets representative equalities hold simultaneously at all indices; transport independence to the selected \(L^2\) initialization and noise representatives.

steps.title: productEulerNoise independentReference
steps.body: Use the same product independence argument with the second initial coordinate. Both initialization and whole noise-path representative equalities are transferred almost everywhere, proving the actual reference class is independent of all fresh Euler noise.

steps.title: brownianProductProbability
steps.body: The coupling is a probability by its marginal identity and the Brownian source measure is a probability. Their product extension is normalized. This local instance supplies the probability-space hypotheses of the Brownian pullback and \(L^2\) reference constructors.

steps.title: productGibbsMemLp
steps.body: Name the already proved finite-second-moment theorem for the strongly convex Gibbs law. The abbreviation supplies exactly the \(L^2(\pi_U)\) identity moment needed to construct the reference initialization on every coupling extension.

steps.title: brownianProductL2Reference
steps.body: Construct the Brownian reference on the extension using the supplied stationarity of its selected segments. Replace its Brownian-defined Euler noise by the common lifted source noise using productNoise_eq_brownianEulerNoise. All remaining continuity, integral, score, and noise fields come from the established constructors.

steps.title: productReference of constructed brownian
steps.body: For each finite initial coupling, use brownianProductL2Reference. Its initial reference equals the second-coordinate \(L^2\) class by the segment-initial identity. These constructions fill the ProductReference fields. Only the explicitly quantified segment-stationarity premise remains an input at this intermediate stage.

steps.title: dalalyan of constructed product brownian
steps.body: Derive \(m\le L\) from strong convexity and smoothness, construct the product reference from the stated stationary segment laws, and apply the small-step product-reference theorem. This intermediate endpoint has the genuine initial \(W_2\) term; the later independent Brownian construction discharges its stationarity premise.

UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalULA.lean.title: Dalalyan’s theorem for the actual Gaussian ULA transition
UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalULA.lean.summary: Let \(U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. The canonical Brownian source derives all stochastic reference obligations and proves the Wasserstein bound for the iterated Gaussian transition \(P_h\), with finite initial \(W_2\).

steps.title: Identify the canonical output law
steps.body: The Brownian source provides jointly independent standard Gaussian innovations; the product extension makes initialization independent of the entire sequence. The realization/Markov-law theorem identifies its output with \(P_h^k\mu\). The product output-law identity removes the chosen finite coupling from this law equality.

steps.title: productReference of independent brownian
steps.body:
On each finite-coupling extension, pull back the independent Brownian coordinates and use the product independence theorems for the reference initialization. Construct a global \(L^2\) integral solution over the required finite horizon.

The proved MALA/Euler stationarity theorem gives Gibbs law for that global solution at every needed absolute time. Segment/global uniqueness identifies each recursively constructed reference segment with that solution. Thus the segment-stationarity premise of productReference_of_constructed_brownian is discharged, filling every reference field from the stated source and potential assumptions.

steps.title: canonicalEulerNoise
steps.body: Specialize the source Euler noise to the explicitly constructed independent coordinate Brownian source. This abbreviation fixes one concrete implementation of the standard Gaussian innovations for the unconditional law theorem.

steps.title: canonicalProductReference
steps.body: The canonical Brownian construction supplies the coordinate Brownian laws and independence of their grid paths for every positive step. Apply productReference_of_independent_brownian. No stochastic reference structure or stationary-law assertion remains an external premise.

steps.title: canonicalOutput eq ulaLawStep
steps.body: Finite initial transport provides a finite-cost coupling, and Gibbs has a finite second moment. Apply the general Brownian output-law identity on that extension with the canonical independent Brownian source. It proves the canonical product implementation has exactly the ordinary ULA law \(P_h^k\mu\).

steps.title: dalalyan output finite
steps.body: The canonical product reference supplies a finite-cost output coupling for every iteration whenever initial transport is finite. Its output law is \(P_h^k\mu\). Substituting this law proves \(W_2(P_h^k\mu,\pi_U)<\infty\), legitimizing the real Wasserstein notation used in the final estimates.

steps.title: dalalyan
steps.body:
Construct canonicalProductReference from differentiability, \(m\)-strong convexity, and \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Nontriviality of the finite coordinate space proves \(m\le L\); the finite-coupling product theorem gives the small-step bound with bias \((33/20)(L/m)\sqrt{hd}\).

Finally replace the canonical product output by \(P_h^k\mu\) using canonicalOutput_eq_ulaLawStep. The resulting inequality is about the actual Gaussian ULA laws, and output finiteness has already been proved. The independent Brownian construction and stationary reference are internal parts of this proof.

steps.title: dalalyan large step
steps.body: Use the same fully constructed canonical reference in the large-step product theorem. The step assumptions give \(0\le Lh-1<1\) and \(2-Lh>0\), so the bias is \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}/(2-Lh)\). Rewrite its output law as the actual iterated Gaussian ULA law.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianULA.lean.title: Dalalyan bounds for an implemented L² Gaussian recursion
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianULA.lean.summary: This endpoint applies the canonical-law theorem to an actual chain on a supplied probability space. Its inputs are the original potential assumptions, a square-integrable initialization, independent standard Gaussian scalar innovations and independence of the initial variable from the innovation sequence.

steps.title: initialLaw probability
steps.body: The representative of the \(L^2\) initialization is measurable. Its pushforward of a probability measure therefore has total mass one, giving the probability instance required by the law-level canonical ULA theorem.

steps.title: gaussianULA initial transport finite
steps.body: The actual initialization is in \(L^2\), so its law has a finite second moment. Strong convexity proves the same for Gibbs and proves its normalization. The independent product coupling of these two laws has finite quadratic cost, hence their Wasserstein distance is finite.

steps.title: dalalyan of gaussian innovations
steps.body: Assemble the jointly independent standard scalar Gaussian coordinates into iid multivariate standard innovations. Initialization independence and the \(L^2\) representative theorem identify the implementation's law with \(P_h^k(P_{X_0})\). Derive finite initial transport from its moments, then apply the unconditional canonical small-step theorem and rewrite the law back to the implementation.

steps.title: dalalyan large step of gaussian innovations
steps.body: Use the same implementation/Markov-law identification and derived finite initial transport, then apply the canonical large-step theorem. The numerical implementation therefore inherits contraction factor \(Lh-1\) and bias \((33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}/(2-Lh)\) throughout the stated stable large-step regime.

UnadjustedLangevin/PotentialAssumptions..title: Strong convexity forces m ≤ L
UnadjustedLangevin/PotentialAssumptions..summary: On a nontrivial Hilbert space the numerical compatibility \(m\le L\) follows from strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient of the same differentiable potential.

steps.title: Compare monotonicity with Cauchy–Schwarz
steps.body: Choose \(x e0\), possible because the Hilbert space is nontrivial. Strong monotonicity gives \(m\|x\|^2\le\langle abla U(x)- abla U(0),x angle\), while Cauchy–Schwarz and Lipschitzness bound the same quantity by \(L\|x\|^2\). Cancel the strictly positive \(\|x\|^2\) to prove \(m\le L\). No positivity premise on \(m\) is needed here.

UnadjustedLangevin/TransportMoments.lean.title: Finite quadratic transport transfers second moments
UnadjustedLangevin/TransportMoments.lean.summary: Finite \(W_2\) distance to a finite-second-moment law supplies the other second moment automatically. This removes a redundant integrability premise when passing an initial law to the L² formulation.

steps.title: memLp id of wasserstein2 ne top
steps.body: Finite Wasserstein distance supplies a finite-cost coupling. On that coupling space the second coordinate is in \(L^2\) by the reference moment, and the coordinate difference is in \(L^2\) by finite coupling cost. Their sum is the first coordinate, so its law \(\mu\) has a finite second moment. No optimal coupling is selected.

steps.title: wasserstein2 ne top of memLp
steps.body: Use the explicit independent coupling \(\mu\otimes\pi\). Each coordinate is in \(L^2\), hence their difference is in \(L^2\) and has finite cost. Wasserstein distance is at most this coupling cost, proving finiteness.

steps.title: memLp of law of wasserstein2 ne top
steps.body: The finite-transport theorem first proves \(\mathrm{id}\in L^2(\mu)\). Replace \(\mu\) by the supplied pushforward law of \(X\), then use the change-of-law \(L^2\) criterion to pull this moment back to \(X\) on its original sample space.

steps.title: memLp of wasserstein2 map ne top
steps.body: Specialize the preceding theorem to \(\mu=P\circ X^{-1}\), whose law identity is reflexive. Finite transport of the actual pushforward to a finite-moment reference therefore gives \(X\in L^2(P)\).

UnadjustedLangevin/Projection.lean.title: Project transport convergence into parameter RMS error
UnadjustedLangevin/Projection.lean.summary: For a continuous linear contraction \(T:H\to K\), reference point \(b\), and equilibrium projected radius \(c\), the parameter error obeys \((\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\le W_2(\mu,\pi)+c\). This derives the estimate directly from couplings.

steps.title: projectedRMS
steps.body: Define the extended projected error \(R_{T,b}(\mu)=\|x\mapsto Tx-b\|_{L^2(\mu)}\). Using an extended norm retains infinity for a divergent second moment and allows the following transport comparison before any finiteness assumption.

steps.title: projectedRMSReal
steps.body: Take the real value of the extended projected norm. Later estimates first prove that the extended quantity is finite; that guard is essential because ENNReal.toReal alone does not distinguish infinity from its totalized real value.

steps.title: projectedDifference le
steps.body: If \(\|T\|\le1\), then \(\|T(x-y)\|\le\|x-y\|\) pointwise. Monotonicity of the extended \(L^2\) norm bounds the projected difference norm by the original coupling cost.

steps.title: projectedRMS le coupling
steps.body: On a coupling write \(Tx-b=T(x-y)+(Ty-b)\). Minkowski bounds its \(L^2\) norm by the sum of the two norms; the contraction estimate controls the first by coupling cost. Marginal identities rewrite the outer norms as \(R_{T,b}(\mu)\) and \(R_{T,b}(\pi)\).

steps.title: projectedRMS le wasserstein2
steps.body: The preceding bound holds for every coupling, with the same equilibrium radius. Take the infimum of coupling costs to obtain \(R_{T,b}(\mu)\le W_2(\mu,\pi)+R_{T,b}(\pi)\). Nonemptiness supplies the indexed-infimum identity; no minimizing plan is assumed.

steps.title: projectedRMS ne top
steps.body: Finite transport guarantees a coupling exists and makes \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\) finite. The assumed equilibrium radius is bounded by a finite real embedding. The transport-radius inequality therefore bounds the current projected norm by a sum of two finite extended values, proving its finiteness.

steps.title: projectedRMSReal eq sqrt integral
steps.body: The explicit finite extended norm and measurability give \(x\mapsto Tx-b\in L^2(\mu)\). The \(L^2\) norm formula then identifies its real norm with \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu}\). This derivation guards both the real integral and the toReal conversion against hidden divergence.

steps.title: projectedRMS le of secondMoment
steps.body: The supplied \(L^2\) membership makes the squared-norm integral genuine. Its bound by \(c^2\), together with \(c\ge0\), implies the root-mean-square norm is at most \(c\). Re-embed this finite real inequality to obtain the extended radius bound.

steps.title: Convert the finite bound to real quantities
steps.body: First prove current-radius finiteness using finite transport and the finite equilibrium bound. Then convert the extended transport-radius inequality to real values, using finiteness of every summand. The result is \(R_{T,b}^{\mathbb R}(\mu)\le W_2^{\mathbb R}(\mu,\pi)+c\).

UnadjustedLangevin/ReferenceFamily.lean.title: An abstract family of compatible finite-coupling references
UnadjustedLangevin/ReferenceFamily.lean.summary: This interface isolates the passage from a bound for each initial coupling to a theorem with the exact initial Wasserstein distance. A concrete product construction later supplies this interface without assuming an optimal plan.

steps.title: FiniteCoupling
steps.body: Restrict the coupling type to those with \(\operatorname{couplingCost}\ne\infty\). This subtype records the integrability needed to realize initial class distances and convert them to real values while taking the Wasserstein infimum.

steps.title: ReferenceFamily
steps.body: For each finite coupling, supply initial and noise \(L^2\) variables and an L2Reference. The fields identify initial law, bound initial class distance by that coupling's cost, and require one common output law across the family. These are explicit construction obligations, with no convergence estimate among them.

steps.title: ReferenceFamily.output finite
steps.body: Choose one finite initial coupling using the finite initial Wasserstein premise. Its supplied numerical/reference \(L^2\) variables yield a finite-cost output coupling. The output-law and stationary-reference fields identify its marginals, proving \(W_2(\nu_n,\pi)<\infty\).

steps.title: Pass the analytic bound through the infimum
steps.body: Apply the analytic \(L^2\) estimate to every finite coupling realization in the family. Replace its initial error by the coupling cost and its numerical law by the common \(\nu_n\). Because \((1-mh)^n\ge0\), the affine finite-coupling infimum theorem gives the displayed bound with the true initial Wasserstein distance.

UnadjustedLangevin/ULAFromBrownian.lean.title: An intermediate bound with a supplied stationary Brownian reference
UnadjustedLangevin/ULAFromBrownian.lean.summary: This auxiliary endpoint already derives the integral equation, continuity and moment bounds from the Brownian coordinates and potential assumptions. It keeps stationarity of the constructed reference segments as an explicit premise.

steps.title: Apply the reference estimate to the constructed segments
steps.body: Build the reference from actual Brownian segments using the displayed all-time Gibbs-law premise. Strong convexity proves finite partition and \(m\le L\), while Brownian laws prove the noise radius and the Gibbs score theorem proves its drift bound. Apply the analytic \(L^2\) theorem with the supplied joint initialization, yielding its actual initial class distance. This intermediate theorem retains its explicit stationarity premise.

UnadjustedLangevin/Degenerate.lean.title: Zero-dimensional state spaces have zero transport cost
UnadjustedLangevin/Degenerate.lean.summary: On a subsingleton state space every two states coincide, so every coupling has zero quadratic difference cost. Probability laws on such a space therefore have zero Wasserstein distance.

steps.title: couplingCost eq zero of subsingleton
steps.body: In a subsingleton state space every pair satisfies \(x=y\), so the displacement function is identically zero. Its extended \(L^2\) norm is zero under every pair measure, hence every coupling cost vanishes.

steps.title: wasserstein2 eq zero of subsingleton
steps.body: The independent product of two probabilities is a coupling, so the coupling type is nonempty. Every coupling has zero cost by the preceding result; taking their infimum gives \(W_2(\mu,\pi)=0\).

steps.title: wasserstein2Real eq zero of subsingleton
steps.body: Rewrite the extended Wasserstein distance as zero using the subsingleton theorem. Its real conversion is also zero. This covers dimension-zero spaces without invoking the nontrivial-space comparison \(m\le L\).

UnadjustedLangevin/Check.lean.title: Kernel dependency audit for the ULA library
UnadjustedLangevin/Check.lean.summary: This file imports the public ULA library and asks Lean to print the axioms of the central contraction, integrability, Brownian construction, stationarity and Gaussian-algorithm endpoints. It introduces no new mathematical declarations.

steps.title: What the audit verifies
steps.body:
After building the library, run lake env lean UnadjustedLangevin/Check.lean. Each #print axioms reports transitive logical dependencies of its named theorem; the intended output consists only of the standard Lean logical axioms, with no sorryAx and no added mathematical axiom. The audit spans the route

\[\text{potential geometry}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{Brownian reference and Gibbs stationarity}\;\longrightarrow\;W_2\text{ bounds}.\]

The final #check commands expose the complete endpoint types. An axiom audit confirms kernel dependencies; theorem hypotheses still govern every application, including the explicitly conditional weak-PDE interface.

This module imports the assembled strong-convexity theory and queries the kernel-visible axiom dependencies of its public endpoints. A successful run checks that the named proof terms elaborate from the imported declarations. The mathematical arguments are given on the linked theorem modules; this audit file introduces no additional mathematical hypothesis or theorem.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Check.lean.title: Kernel dependency audit for the conditional LSI proof
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Check.lean.summary: This file checks the entropy-calculus, one-step, recurrence and regular-interpolation endpoints. It adds no declarations and does not discharge their analytic premises.

steps.title: Audit hypotheses and logical dependencies separately
steps.body:
Run lake env lean UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Check.lean after the library build. The audit prints the axioms of the chain

\[\text{relative density calculus}\;\longrightarrow\;H\prime\le-\tfrac34J+\mathcal E\;\longrightarrow\;H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+8hdL^2/\alpha.\]

The desired reports contain standard logical axioms and no sorryAx. This is compatible with a conditional theorem: interpolation densities, regularity, weak identities, drift-error control and the stated gradient-moment bridge remain premises wherever present. Inspect the theorem types alongside their dependency reports.

The #check commands print the exact formal types of the entropy endpoints, and #print axioms audits their transitive proof dependencies. Compiling this file verifies the imported proofs and exposes their hypotheses, including the regular-interpolation premises. The mathematical derivations are in the density, calculus, one-step and recurrence modules.

UnadjustedLangevin.lean.title: The public ULA import surface
UnadjustedLangevin.lean.summary:
This umbrella module imports the deterministic contraction argument, its probability and Brownian foundations, the unconditional Gaussian ULA endpoints and the conditional LSI development. It contains no additional theorem or proof.

This umbrella file has no local proof body. Its import declarations assemble the proved deterministic, probabilistic and entropy modules into one library entry point. To inspect an individual mathematical argument, follow the corresponding module page; to verify the assembled library, run lake build from the repository root.

steps.title: The strongly convex Wasserstein route
steps.body:
The imported modules prove Gibbs normalization and score moments, construct independent Brownian coordinates and \(L^2\) Langevin solutions, establish Gibbs stationarity by invariant Metropolis approximation, and assemble a stationary coupling reference for every finite initial coupling. Infimizing the resulting cost gives

\[W_2(P_h^k\mu,\pi)\le(1-mh)^kW_2(\mu,\pi)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{hd}\]

under differentiability, \(m>0\) strong convexity, \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(0

steps.title: The conditional entropy route and verification
steps.body: The LSI imports establish the entropy mechanism and recurrence under their explicit interpolation and analytic data, giving the bound \(H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+8hdL^2/\alpha\). Their hypotheses are not removed by this import. Use lake build for the compiled library, then lake env lean UnadjustedLangevin/Check.lean and lake env lean UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Check.lean for the two kernel-dependency audits. The generated module pages show the source declarations and their mathematical explanations.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ConditionalDrift..title: Construct the conditional Gaussian drift and transfer its energy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ConditionalDrift..summary: The actual frozen Gaussian interpolation is \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\), where \((X,Z)\) has the independent law \(P=\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\). Write \(D_t= abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\). This module constructs a measurable field \(e_t\) satisfying \(e_t(Y_t)=\mathbb E[D_t\mid Y_t]\), proves its flux identities, and derives its squared-energy bound by conditional Jensen. Thus the state-dependent error is a consequence of the joint Gaussian construction. The entropy weak equation is a separate analytic obligation.

steps.title: Construct a conditional mean on the observed state space
steps.body:
Let \(Y:\Omega\to S\) be measurable, let \(P\) be a probability measure, and let the Banach-valued vector \(D\) satisfy \(\mathbb E_P\|D\|^2<\infty\). The theorem constructs a strongly measurable \(e:S\to F\) such that

\[e(Y)=\mathbb E_P[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\quad P\text{-almost surely},\qquad \int_S\|e(y)\|^2\,d(Y_\#P)(y)\le\int_\Omega\|D\|^2\,dP.\]

The proof first applies Doob–Dynkin factorization to the strongly measurable conditional expectation. In Lean, stronglyMeasurable_condExp and exists_eq_measurable_comp produce e, its strong measurability he, and the exact factorization hfactor. The equality hcomp writes that factorization in the pointwise function form needed for later rewrites.

Next hD.condExp proves that the conditional expectation is in \(L^2(P)\). Its squared norm is therefore integrable. The pushforward integrability theorem converts this to integrability of \(\|e\|^2\) under \(Y_\#P\); this is hint. Finally, integral_map_of_stronglyMeasurable identifies the left energy with \(\int\|\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\|^2dP\). The conditional Jensen theorem integral_norm_condExp_rpow_le, with exponent \(2\), bounds that integral by \(\int\|D\|^2dP\). The real-power notation in that library theorem is converted to the ordinary square by Real.rpow_two.

steps.title: Identify the vector flux on every measurable set
steps.body:
Suppose a strongly measurable field \(e\) satisfies the conditional-mean identity \(e(Y)=\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\), with \(D\) integrable. For every measurable \(A\subseteq S\),

\[\int_A e(y)\,d(Y_\#P)(y)=\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}D(\omega)\,dP(\omega).\]

The first step, setIntegral_map, pulls the left integral back to \(\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}e(Y)dP\). The almost-sure conditional-mean identity changes its integrand to the conditional expectation. Because \(Y^{-1}(A)\) belongs to the pulled-back sigma algebra, setIntegral_condExp replaces that expectation by \(D\) in the set integral. The probability assumption guarantees the finite-measure hypotheses for conditional expectation. This proves a vector-valued identification of the flux, extending beyond the energy estimate.

steps.title: Transfer integrable inner-product tests through the conditional mean
steps.body:
Let \(\varphi:S\to F\) be strongly measurable and suppose \(\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\) is integrable. Then

\[\int_S\langle e(y),\varphi(y)\rangle\,d(Y_\#P)(y)=\int_\Omega\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\,dP.\]

This is the flux identity needed when the test depends on the current interpolated state. The proof gives \(Y\) its pulled-back sigma algebra and observes that \(\varphi\circ Y\) is strongly measurable for that algebra; the Lean witnesses are hYpull and hφ.comp_measurable hYpull. Conditional expectation can therefore pull this factor out of the continuous bilinear inner product:

\[\mathbb E[\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\mid Y]=\langle\mathbb E[D\mid Y],\varphi(Y)\rangle.\]

condExp_bilin_of_stronglyMeasurable_right proves this equality as hpull, using innerSL ℝ as the continuous bilinear map. The pushforward integral is pulled back, hcond substitutes the conditional expectation, and integrating hpull removes the conditioning. The statement allows noncompact tests whenever its displayed product is integrable; it does not prove a Fokker–Planck equation or the integrability of an arbitrary entropy test.

steps.title: Specify the discrepancy on the actual independent joint law
steps.body:
For \(p=(x,z)\), define

\[D_t(p)= abla U\!\left(x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}\,z ight)- abla U(x).\]

This is exactly frozenGradientDiscrepancy U t p: ULA.malaProposal supplies the interpolated state and the two gradient terms are subtracted in the displayed order. Its sign agrees with the additional relative-density drift \(e_t(y)= abla U(y)-\mathbb E[ abla U(X)\mid Y_t=y]\). No conditional expectation, density, or error bound is part of this definition. For \(t\ge0\), the later energy theorem uses the actual independent Gaussian product law.

steps.title: Record precisely what is observed at interpolation time
steps.body:
The observed variable is \(Y_t(x,z)=x-t\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\). The sigma algebra \(\sigma(Y_t)\) consists of preimages \(Y_t^{-1}(A)\) of measurable subsets of the state space. Lean writes it as MeasurableSpace.comap of the proposal map.

The abbreviation frozenDriftSigmaAlgebra U t makes the conditional expectation statements refer to this exact observation. Conditioning retains the interpolated position and averages out information about the starting point and Gaussian innovation that the position alone does not determine. Lipschitzness of the gradient later proves that this pulled-back sigma algebra lies inside the ambient measurable structure.

steps.title: Construct the actual interpolation error and prove its energy bound
steps.body:
Assume \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu<\infty\). For each \(t\ge0\), the theorem constructs a strongly measurable \(e_t:E\to E\) with

\[e_t(Y_t)=\mathbb E[D_t\mid Y_t],\qquad \int\|e_t(y)\|^2\,d\rho_t(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2,\]\[\rho_t=(Y_t)_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)),\qquad n=\dim E.\]

The proof names the actual proposal map Y and discrepancy D. ULA.malaProposal_measurable proves measurability of \(Y\). frozen_gradient_error_energy gives square-integrability of \(D\) and the joint bound \(\mathbb E\|D\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2tn)\). The continuity of the Lipschitz gradient gives hDmeas, so memLp_two_iff_integrable_sq_norm turns that bound into the \(L^2\) input hD.

The general conditional-mean theorem now constructs err. Its pushforward measure is definitionally the actual interpolationLaw, so the field is integrable on the required marginal. Conditional Jensen followed by the joint Gaussian estimate gives the result; the final ring step expands \(L^2(t^2G_0+2tn)\) into the exact coefficient order used by the entropy interface. Neither the error field nor its numerical energy estimate is a hypothesis.

steps.title: Express the constructed error energy in relative-density coordinates
steps.body:
Suppose a measurable nonnegative \(r\) identifies the actual interpolation law as \( ho_t=r u\). The preceding construction gives a field \(e_t\) satisfying both the conditional-mean identity and

\[\int r(y)\|e_t(y)\|^2\,d u(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2.\]

The weighted integrand is also proved integrable. In Lean, exists_frozen_drift_error first supplies the state-space field. The law identity hlaw changes its integrability and energy conclusions from the interpolation law to tiltedMeasure ν r. integrable_withDensity_iff_integrable_smul' then converts integrability under \(r u\) into integrability of \(r\|e_t\|^2\) under \( u\). Nonnegativity of \(r\) makes the real conversion of ENNReal.ofReal r equal to \(r\).

Finally integral_tiltedMeasure converts the energy integral itself. The density-law identity is a displayed input to this corollary; at positive times InterpolationDensity.lean constructs such a relative density explicitly for a normalized Gibbs target. This corollary does not assume entropy production or prove the remaining weak differential equation.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InteriorEntropy.l.title: Compare entropy using derivatives only at positive times
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InteriorEntropy.l.summary: Gaussian regularization naturally supplies derivatives for positive times. The scalar comparison here uses ordinary derivatives on \(0<t<T\) and continuity on \([0,T]\); neither endpoint needs a derivative. A second theorem computes actual KL derivatives from local relative-density data only in that open interval. The existing global ULA endpoint retains its earlier interface; these lemmas provide a more flexible route for a future positive-time construction.

steps.title: Use an integrating factor without differentiating at the endpoints
steps.body:
Let \(a>0\), let \(H\) be continuous on \([0,T]\), and suppose it has derivative \(H'(t)\le-aH(t)+b\) for \(0<t<T\). Then for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba(1-e^{-at}).\]

Define \(F(t)=e^{at}(H(t)-b/a)\). The product and chain rules give

\[F'(t)=e^{at}\bigl(a(H(t)-b/a)+H'(t)\bigr)\le0.\]

The Lean proof calls the transformed function F, proves its endpoint continuity as hFcont, calculates its derivative in hFderiv, and proves the sign in hFnonpos. The division cancellation \(a(b/a)=b\) uses \(a\ne0\). The mean-value theorem antitoneOn_of_deriv_nonpos then proves that \(F\) is nonincreasing on the closed interval. Its derivative hypotheses concern only the interior, identified with \((0,T)\) by interior_Icc.

Consequently \(F(t)\le F(0)=H(0)-b/a\). Multiplication by the positive factor \(e^{-at}\), together with \(e^{-at}e^{at}=1\), yields the stated affine comparison. The final arithmetic rearrangement is nlinarith. Endpoint continuity is essential in this proof; endpoint differentiability is unnecessary.

steps.title: Differentiate actual KL at an interior interpolation time
steps.body:
Fix \(0<t<T\). Assume that, at every interior time \(u\), \(r_u\) is positive, continuously differentiable, normalized relative to the probability target \( u\), and has the local dominated entropy regularity recorded in LocalEntropyRegularity. Then

\[ rac d{dt}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r_t u\Vert u)=\int \dot r_t(x) igl(\log r_t(x)+1 igr)\,d u(x).\]

The local regularity theorem already differentiates the ordinary integral \(\int r_u\log r_u\,d u\). To identify that integral with actual KL in a whole neighborhood of \(t\), the proof uses \((0,T)\in\mathcal N(t)\). For each nearby \(u\), densityEntropy_eq_integral applies using positivity, normalization, measurability, and integrability from data u hu. This gives the eventual equality hnear.

HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq transfers the already proved integral derivative to actual KL. The statement requests no density or local domination information at time zero. To combine it with the preceding scalar theorem, continuity of the actual entropy at the two endpoints still has to be justified separately.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GradientMoment.le.title: Transfer the Gibbs score moment through a transport coupling
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GradientMoment.le.summary: For any finite-cost coupling of \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Y\sim u\), an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient gives \(\mathbb E_\mu\| abla U\|^2\le2L^2\mathbb E\|X-Y\|^2+2\mathbb E_ u\| abla U\|^2\). This module proves that estimate together with gradient square integrability. For a normalized Gibbs target the second term is bounded by \(2nL\). An explicit entropy-cost coupling then supplies the exact gradient-moment bound used by the ULA proof. The final Gaussian ULA theorem instead derives its moment directly from entropy in EntropyMoment.lean; no transport implication is needed there.

steps.title: Derive both integrability and the coupling moment estimate
steps.body:
Let \(c\) be a joint measure with marginals \(\mu\) and \( u\). Assume \(\int\|x-y\|^2dc<\infty\), that the gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and that \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u<\infty\). The theorem proves square integrability under \(\mu\) and

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2\,dc(x,y)+2\int\| abla U\|^2d u.\]

At a pair \((x,y)\), write \( abla U(x)=( abla U(x)- abla U(y))+ abla U(y)\). The triangle inequality and Lipschitzness give \(\| abla U(x)\|\le L\|x-y\|+\| abla U(y)\|\). Squaring and applying \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) proves the pointwise bound hpoint. Lean obtains the last elementary inequality from the nonnegative square \((a-b)^2\).

Before integrating the inequality, the proof establishes integrability: hsecond pulls the target squared-gradient integrand to the second marginal, while hmajor combines it with the integrable coupling cost. This dominating function and continuity of the gradient prove hfirst, integrability of the first-coordinate squared gradient. The map-integrability equivalence and the first-marginal identity then prove hμ. Thus a missing moment is derived, rather than represented by a possibly undefined real integral.

Finally integral_mono integrates hpoint. The identities hfirst_marginal and hsecond_marginal, proved by the pushforward integral formula, replace the joint-coordinate integrals by their marginal integrals and give exactly the displayed estimate.

steps.title: Insert the derived target score bound
steps.body:
For the normalized Gibbs probability \( u=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dx\), differentiability of \(U\) and an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient imply the target estimate \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u\le nL\). Consequently every finite-cost coupling gives

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2dc+2nL.\]

The proof first derives \(Z<\infty\) from probability normalization, using gibbsPartition_ne_top_of_probability. The shared theorem ULA.memLp_gradient_gibbsMeasure then supplies target square integrability; its \(L^2\) conclusion is converted into the integrability input for the preceding coupling theorem. The sharp target moment itself comes from ULA.integral_norm_sq_gradient_gibbs_le.

Those shared Gibbs results use translation invariance and a sub-Gaussian score argument under first-order smoothness, so strong convexity is unnecessary here. Substituting their target bound into the coupling estimate proves the stated result and retains the newly derived square integrability under \(\mu\).

steps.title: Obtain the exact entropy-dependent coefficient from transport control
steps.body:
Suppose the preceding finite-cost coupling additionally satisfies

\[\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)\le rac2\alpha D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\Vert u),\qquad \alpha>0,\quad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\Vert u)<\infty.\]

Substitution into the coupling bound gives

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le rac{4L^2}{\alpha}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\Vert u)+2nL.\]

The Lean hypothesis htransport is exactly the displayed cost estimate for the supplied coupling. It is multiplied by the nonnegative factor \(2L^2\); heq verifies the coefficient identity \(2L^2(2/\alpha)=4L^2/\alpha\). The result also returns gradient square integrability from the previous theorem. Separate hypotheses record positive \(\alpha\) and finite extended KL before its real value is used.

This theorem completes the coupling-to-moment calculation and connects it to the already proved target score bound. It does not assert that LSI constructs this coupling or prove the LSI-to-Talagrand implication. The existing ULA endpoint still displays its gradient-moment input in this reusable coupling-based interface. The complete endpoint uses the direct score-exponential estimate in EntropyMoment.lean.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationDens.title: Construct the positive Gaussian mixture and Gibbs-relative density
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationDens.summary: At positive time the actual update has an explicit Gaussian mixture density, even if its initial law is singular. Let \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\) and let \(C_t>0\) be the Gaussian normalizer. The Lebesgue density is \(q_t(y)=\int C_t\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\,d\mu(x)\). This module proves its law identity, everywhere positivity, pointwise finiteness and spatial continuity. For the normalized Gibbs target, \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}q_t(y)\) is then a positive continuous relative probability density. GaussianEntropy, GaussianTimeDerivative, GaussianWeakEquation and GaussianEntropyIdentity extend this construction to the full positive-time entropy calculus used by the final theorem.

steps.title: Define the explicit Gaussian mixture before taking real values
steps.body:
For the state-dependent center \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\), let

\[K_t(x,y)=C_t\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-c_t(x)\|^2}{4t}\right),\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=\int K_t(x,y)\,d\mu(x).\]

interpolationDensity is this mixture as an extended nonnegative integral: Lean integrates ULA.gaussianProposalDensity t (x - t • gradient U x) y. The normalizer \(C_t\) is the inverse of the actual radial Gaussian integral, already identified with the standard-noise proposal law in GaussianProposalDensity.lean.

The definition is total in time and potential, but the Gaussian density interpretation is used only for \(t>0\). Keeping the integral in \(\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\}\) makes nonnegativity immediate and preserves a genuine finiteness obligation before taking a real density. The later normalizer bound discharges that obligation at every proposed state.

steps.title: Apply measurable parameter integration to the mixture
steps.body:
If \(\nabla U\) is Lipschitz, its state-dependent center \(c_t\) is continuous and measurable. The joint Gaussian integrand \((x,y)\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is therefore measurable: subtraction, scalar multiplication, squared norm and exponential preserve the required measurability.

The theorem Measurable.lintegral_prod_left now proves that \(y\mapsto q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\) is measurable. Lean unfolds only the Gaussian proposal density, records gradient measurability as hg, and lets fun_prop assemble the elementary operations. The mixing probability measure supplies the finite, hence sigma-finite, hypothesis for parameter integration. No positive-time assumption is needed for this measurability statement.

steps.title: Prove the Gaussian mixture is the density of the actual update
steps.body:
For every \(t>0\),

\[\rho_t=(Y_t)_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I))=q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}\,dy.\]

To prove equality of measures, fix a measurable set \(A\). The pushforward formula and Tonelli express the actual proposal probability as

\[\rho_t(A)=\int \mathbb P\bigl(c_t(x)+\sqrt{2t}Z\in A\bigr)\,d\mu(x).\]

For each fixed \(x\), ULA.gaussian_proposal_density already identifies the affine Gaussian proposal with density \(K_t(x,\cdot)\). The local identity hinner therefore changes the inner probability to \(\int_AK_t(x,y)\,dy\). The joint integrand is measurable, as proved by hd, so lintegral_lintegral_swap interchanges the two nonnegative integrals:

\[\rho_t(A)=\int_A\left(\int K_t(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\right)dy=\int_Aq_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\,dy.\]

The Lean proof mirrors these three steps with Measure.map_apply, Measure.prod_apply, the fixed-state density identity, and Tonelli under the restricted volume measure on \(A\). It assumes no density for \(\mu\).

steps.title: Use positivity of every Gaussian component
steps.body:
At every positive time and every point \(y\), the mixture density is strictly positive:

\[q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)>0.\]

The normalizer is positive by ULA.gaussianProposalNormalizer_pos, and the real exponential is positive. Thus the component density \(K_t(x,y)\) is positive for every initial point \(x\). Lean proves this as hqpos, using positivity of ENNReal.ofReal.

The support of \(x\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is consequently all of \(E\); this is hsupp. Its measurability is hq. The characterization lintegral_pos_iff_support reduces positivity of its integral to positive mass of that support. Since \(\mu(E)=1\), the integral is positive. The assertion holds pointwise in \(y\), not only almost everywhere.

steps.title: Bound every mixture value by the common Gaussian peak
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the Gaussian exponent is nonpositive, hence

\[0\le K_t(x,y)\le C_t,\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\le C_t.\]

Lean proves the exponential bound with Real.exp_le_one_iff: the numerator \(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonpositive and the denominator \(4t\) is positive. Multiplication by the nonnegative normalizer preserves the inequality, as does ENNReal.ofReal.

lintegral_mono integrates this pointwise bound. The integral of the constant \(C_t\) equals \(C_t\mu(E)=C_t\) because \(\mu\) is a probability measure. This theorem requires no regularity of the gradient: its bound concerns the nonnegative integrand at every point, and the upper nonnegative integral remains monotone even before measurability is established.

steps.title: Derive pointwise finiteness before real conversion
steps.body:
The preceding bound gives \(q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\le\operatorname{ofReal}(C_t)<\infty\) for each \(t>0\) and \(y\). The extended density therefore never equals infinity.

The Lean proof is the order argument ne_top_of_le_ne_top, applied to the universal fact ENNReal.ofReal_ne_top and interpolationDensity_le_normalizer. This small theorem is the explicit finiteness witness used by every later conversion from the extended mixture density to an ordinary real function. It prevents the total operation toReal from silently turning an infinite density into zero.

steps.title: Choose the finite real representative of the mixture
steps.body:
The real density is defined by

\[q_t(y)=\bigl(q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\bigr).\mathrm{toReal}.\]

This is interpolationLebesgueDensity U μ t y. The definition itself is total; its positive-time interpretation uses the pointwise finiteness theorem above. Once \(q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\ne\infty\) is supplied, converting \(q_t(y)\) back with ENNReal.ofReal recovers the original extended density exactly. The subsequent law identity, positivity argument, ordinary integral formula and continuity theorem all retain the positive-time hypotheses that justify this interpretation.

steps.title: Identify the actual law with the finite real density
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the actual proposal law satisfies

\[\rho_t(A)=\int_Aq_t(y)\,dy\quad\text{for every measurable }A.\]

The extended-density law identity is already proved. The present proof changes only its integrand representative: ENNReal.ofReal_toReal and interpolationDensity_ne_top prove \(\operatorname{ofReal}(q_t(y))=q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\) for every \(y\). Function extensionality then gives equality of the two density functions and hence of their withDensity measures.

The separate finiteness theorem is invoked at the exact point where it is needed. This is why the real-valued representative still denotes the genuine Gaussian mixture, including from an initial law that has no Lebesgue density.

steps.title: Deduce absolute continuity for every positive time
steps.body:
The law identity \(\rho_t=q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}dy\) immediately implies \(\rho_t\ll dy\): every Lebesgue-null set has zero integral against the density and thus zero proposal probability.

Lean rewrites the actual interpolationLaw using interpolationLaw_eq_withDensity, then applies the general theorem withDensity_absolutelyContinuous. The result holds for any initial probability law when the gradient is Lipschitz. In particular, positive-time Gaussian smoothing produces absolute continuity from a Dirac or other singular initial law. This conclusion alone does not imply finite KL relative to a particular target, nor entropy continuity at the initial time.

steps.title: Convert the nonnegative mixture to its ordinary real integral
steps.body:
The real density has the expected ordinary integral formula:

\[q_t(y)=\int C_t\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-c_t(x)\|^2}{4t}\right)d\mu(x).\]

The proof records nonnegativity of the real integrand as hnonneg and the uniform bound by \(C_t\) as hbound. Because \(\mu\) is a probability measure, the constant majorant is integrable. Continuity of the Lipschitz gradient supplies measurability, and Integrable.mono' proves hint, integrability of the displayed real Gaussian integrand.

ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal can now identify its ordinary integral with the extended mixture integral after applying ofReal. Taking toReal reverses this conversion because the real integral is nonnegative. This proves the formula without treating a nonintegrable Bochner integral as an ordinary expectation.

steps.title: Pass spatial continuity through the probability mixture
steps.body:
At a fixed positive time, \(q_t:E\to\mathbb R\) is continuous. For every fixed initial state \(x\), the Gaussian kernel \(y\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is continuous, and its absolute value is bounded by the same constant \(C_t\), independent of \(x\) and \(y\).

The proof first replaces interpolationLebesgueDensity by the ordinary integral formula from the previous theorem. It applies continuous_of_dominated with constant majorant \(x\mapsto C_t\). Measurability in \(x\) follows from gradient continuity. The nonpositive Gaussian exponent proves \(\|K_t(x,y)\|=K_t(x,y)\le C_t\); probability normalization makes this majorant integrable. Pointwise continuity in \(y\) is then assembled from subtraction, norm, square and exponential.

These are exactly the four inputs of dominated convergence for continuous parameters. The result proves spatial continuity of the actual mixture, while GaussianEntropy.lean and GaussianTimeDerivative.lean prove the corresponding spatial and time derivatives.

steps.title: Derive finite partition from target normalization
steps.body:
Recall \( u=Z^{-1}(e^{-U}dy)\) with the extended partition function \(Z=\int e^{-U}dy\). If this measure is a probability measure, then \(Z e\infty\).

Indeed, \(Z=\infty\) would give \(Z^{-1}=0\), and hence \( u=0\). Its mass on the whole space would then be zero, contradicting \( u(E)=1\). Lean names the hypothetical zero-measure equality hzero, rewrites the probability mass identity hmass, and closes the contradiction by arithmetic.

No strong convexity or LSI estimate is used. This matters because LSI already includes probability normalization of its target, so its finite partition requirement can be recovered from that normalization rather than imported through a stronger convexity hypothesis.

steps.title: Write the explicit density relative to Gibbs
steps.body:
The normalized Gibbs target has Lebesgue density \(Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\). Therefore the relative density corresponding to the mixture \(q_t(y)dy\) is

\[r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}q_t(y).\]

interpolationRelativeDensity is exactly this product, with \(Z\) represented by (ULA.gibbsPartition U).toReal and \(q_t\) by interpolationLebesgueDensity. The later theorems separately prove finite partition, positivity and the density-law identity before using this expression as a normalized relative density.

The definition makes the coordinate conversion explicit: the ratio to the target is obtained by multiplying the Lebesgue density by the reciprocal target density. It does not package an entropy derivative, convergence bound or weak PDE as part of the meaning of a density.

steps.title: Multiply measurable factors to obtain relative-density measurability
steps.body:
Differentiability of \(U\) implies continuity and measurability of \(e^U\). The extended Gaussian mixture is measurable by interpolationDensity_measurable, and its real conversion remains measurable by ennreal_toReal. Multiplication by the constant \(Z^{\mathrm{toReal}}\) therefore proves measurability of \(r_t\).

The Lean expression follows these factors in order: measurable_const.mul combines the partition scalar with Real.measurable_exp.comp hU.continuous.measurable, then the final .mul inserts the real Gaussian mixture. This statement concerns measurability only, so it does not need a positive-time assumption or a finiteness conversion.

steps.title: Obtain relative-density continuity at positive time
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), spatial continuity of \(q_t\) and continuity of \(e^U\) give continuity of \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}q_t(y)\).

The proof assembles three continuous factors directly: the constant partition scalar, Real.continuous_exp.comp hU.continuous, and interpolationLebesgueDensity_continuous. Its two applications of Continuous.mul mirror the two products in the definition. The conclusion is a property of the explicit actual-law density. It supplies continuity, and GaussianEntropy.lean proves the C¹ regularity needed to apply the declared LSI.

steps.title: Retain all finiteness guards when proving strict positivity
steps.body:
When the target Gibbs measure is a probability measure and \(t>0\), all three factors of \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}q_t(y)\) are strictly positive. The partition is positive by ULA.gibbsPartition_pos and finite by gibbsPartition_ne_top_of_probability. The mixture is positive by interpolationDensity_pos and finite by interpolationDensity_ne_top.

For each of these two extended-valued quantities, ENNReal.toReal_pos requires both nonzero value and finiteness. The Lean witnesses hZpos, hZfin, hqpos and hqfin provide exactly those hypotheses. The ordinary exponential is positive independently. Two applications of mul_pos prove strict positivity of the relative density at every spatial point.

steps.title: Cancel the target density and identify the exact relative law
steps.body:
The constructed relative density satisfies

\[r_t\nu=q_tdy=\rho_t\qquad(t>0).\]

The proof first records positive finite partition and measurability of the Gibbs weight and relative density. The actual-law mixture theorem changes \(\rho_t\) to its Lebesgue density. On the left, withDensity_smul_measure, withDensity_mul and withDensity_smul' combine multiplication by the relative density with multiplication by the Gibbs density into one density with respect to volume.

The remaining equality is pointwise. The real-to-extended conversion hrel proves

\[\operatorname{ofReal}(r_t(y))=Z\,\operatorname{ofReal}(e^{U(y)})\,q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y).\]

Its uses of ofReal_toReal invoke the finite partition and pointwise finite mixture bounds. Next hexp proves \(e^{-U(y)}e^{U(y)}=1\) in the extended nonnegative representation. The full density product is rearranged into \((Z^{-1}Z)(e^{-U(y)}e^{U(y)})q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\). Both cancellation steps are justified explicitly, leaving exactly the mixture density.

This theorem constructs law identification at positive times; no density is supplied as an assumption. Spatial \(C^1\) regularity, time derivatives, entropy domination and the entropy weak equation are not conclusions of this algebraic density identity.

steps.title: Transfer normalization from the actual proposal law
steps.body:
The measure induced by the constructed relative density is a probability measure:

\[\int r_t\,d\nu=1\qquad(t>0).\]

Lean expresses this as IsProbabilityMeasure (tiltedMeasure ν r_t). The proof rewrites that measure with tiltedMeasure_interpolationRelativeDensity, reducing normalization to the already proved probability preservation of the actual independent-Gaussian update. interpolationLaw_isProbability supplies the result from probability of the initial law and measurability of the Lipschitz-gradient proposal.

Thus positivity, continuity, law identification and normalization all refer to the same explicitly constructed density. Normalization alone does not prove finite entropy or Fisher information, and GaussianEntropy.lean derives those finiteness properties for the actual positive-time interpolation.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/BoundedLog.lean.title: Bounded logarithmic tests and their entropy primitives
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/BoundedLog.lean.summary: The unbounded logarithm in entropy production is replaced by a smooth bounded function. The replacement has derivative between zero and one, converges to the identity, and admits an entropy primitive dominated by the actual KL integrand. These properties separately justify the spatial test, the time chain rule, and the limit in the entropy identity.

steps.title: Choose the bounded test and its weight
steps.body:
For a natural number \(m\), write \(c=m+1>0\). Define

\[\chi_m(z)=c\arctan(z/c),\qquad w_m(z)=\frac1{1+(z/c)^2},\qquad\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du.\]

The positive offset in \(c\) prevents division by zero even for \(m=0\). The interval integral is oriented: when \(r<1\), its sign reverses. Lean defines these expressions for every real argument; the entropy claims below explicitly require \(r>0\).

steps.title: Differentiate and bound the test
steps.body:
The arctangent chain rule gives \(\chi_m(0)=0\) and \(\chi_m^{\prime}(z)=w_m(z)\). The denominator is at least one, so \(0\le w_m\le1\). The derivative bound implies that \(\chi_m\) is 1-Lipschitz, hence \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). Independently, \(|\arctan u|<\pi/2\) gives \(|\chi_m(z)|\le c\pi/2\). This last bound controls the time derivative integrand without any log-integrability requirement. Since arctangent has the sign of its argument, \(\chi_m\) does too.

ContDiff ℝ ⊤ records smoothness of the scalar test. HasDerivAt gives its exact derivative; the proof multiplies the derivative of arctangent by \(1/c\) and cancels the outer factor \(c\).

steps.title: Recover the logarithm and its primitive
steps.body:
As \(m\to\infty\), \(z/(m+1)\to0\). The derivative of arctangent at zero is one; its difference quotient therefore gives \(\chi_m(z)\to z\). At \(z=0\) the claim is exact at every index. Continuity of inversion at the positive denominator one gives \(w_m(z)\to1\).

The function \(u\mapsto\chi_m(\log u)\) is measurable and bounded, hence integrable on every finite interval, including intervals containing zero. When \(r>0\), continuity in a neighborhood of \(r\) and the fundamental theorem of calculus imply \(\Phi_m^{\prime}(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\).

steps.title: Dominate the entropy endpoints
steps.body:
We have \(\Phi_m(1)=0\). For \(r\ge1\), both \(\log u\) and its test are nonnegative on \([1,r]\), giving \(\Phi_m(r)\ge0\). For \(0

On the positive side, \(0\le\chi_m(\log u)\le\log u\). On the negative side, \(\log u\le\chi_m(\log u)\le0\); reversing the interval preserves the corresponding upper bound for the primitive. In both cases,

\[0\le\Phi_m(r)\le\int_1^r\log u\,du=r\log r-r+1.\]

Pointwise convergence of the test and domination by \(|\log u|\), integrable on the finite interval between 1 and \(r\), prove \(\Phi_m(r)\to r\log r-r+1\). These are exactly the hypotheses for dominated convergence against the finite-KL relative density later.

steps.title: Identify the spatial gradient of the test
steps.body:
For a differentiable scalar field \(f\), the Fréchet chain rule gives \(D(\chi_m\circ f)=w_m(f)Df\). Applying the Hilbert-space identification of linear derivatives with gradients yields

\[ abla(\chi_m\circ f)(x)=w_m(f(x)) abla f(x),\qquad\| abla(\chi_m\circ f)(x)\|\le\| abla f(x)\|.\]

The inequality uses \(0\le w_m\le1\). With \(f=\log r_t\), it supplies square-integrability of the bounded log test gradient from the actual Fisher bound.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianMeasurabi.title: Jointly measurable density and relative score
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianMeasurabi.summary: Spacetime integration requires joint measurability in time and state, rather than measurability separately at each fixed time. This module constructs a single measurable extension of the actual positive-time relative score and proves that it agrees with the gradient used in Fisher information.

steps.title: Integrate a jointly measurable Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
The density is a nonnegative parameter integral \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\). The normalizer, affine center, norm, and exponential are measurable in \((t,y,x)\). The parameterized nonnegative integral is therefore measurable. Passing from the extended integral to its real value preserves measurability. Multiplication by \(Z e^{U(y)}\) gives the joint measurability of \(r_t(y)\).

The definitions cover all real times using Lean’s total real operations; only positive times are used for density and score identities. This avoids defining a different measurable representative for each interval.

steps.title: Measurability of the spatial derivative
steps.body:
The derivative kernel is a continuous linear functional proportional to the inner product with the Gaussian residual:

\[D_yK_t(x,y)[v]=-\frac{K_t(x,y)}{2t}\langle y-x+t\nabla U(x),v\rangle.\]

The inner-product-to-dual map is continuous, so this is jointly strongly measurable as a continuous-linear-map-valued function. Its Bochner integral in \(x\), denoted \(A_t(y)\), remains strongly measurable. At positive times the earlier differentiation theorem identifies \(A_t=D p_t\).

steps.title: One relative-score field for all spacetime integrals
steps.body:
Define

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+p_t(y)^{-1}\mathcal R^{-1}(A_t(y)),\]

where \(\mathcal R^{-1}\) is the inverse Riesz identification of the continuous dual with the Hilbert space. Continuous scalar multiplication, inversion as a measurable real function, and the previous measurability results make \(\mathcal S\) jointly strongly measurable.

For \(t>0\), \(p_t>0\), so the log chain rule and \(r_t=Z e^U p_t\) give

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+ abla\log p_t(y)= abla\log r_t(y).\]

Thus the measurable field is the actual relative score wherever it is used. Its auxiliary extension at nonpositive time introduces no analytic premise into the proof.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GibbsInterpolatio.title: A Gaussian density comparison at the initial endpoint
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GibbsInterpolatio.summary: The entropy limit at zero is obtained by comparing the updated Gibbs density with the original Gibbs density. This calculation uses the differentiable potential and its Lipschitz gradient directly, with no initial density smoothness or change-of-variables theorem.

steps.title: The Gaussian normalizer ratio
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), integration of the radial Gaussian gives \(N_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Therefore for positive \(s,t\),

\[N_t/N_s=(s/t)^{d/2}.\]

The proof obtains the individual integrals from the finite-dimensional Gaussian integral, uses positivity to invert them, and applies the multiplication and division identities for real powers.

steps.title: Complete the square using only first derivatives
steps.body:
Write \(g_x=\nabla U(x)\), \(g_y=\nabla U(y)\), and choose positive \(s,t\) with \(s(1-4tL)=t\). The smooth upper model at \(y\) bounds \(U(y)-U(x)\) by \(\langle g_y,y-x\rangle+(L/2)\|y-x\|^2\). Lipschitzness gives \(\|g_x-g_y\|\le L\|x-y\|\). Expanding squares and bounding their cross term yields

\[U(y)-U(x)-\frac{\|y-x+tg_x\|^2}{4t}\le-\frac{\|x-y+sg_y\|^2}{4s}+\frac s4\|g_y\|^2.\]

The relation between \(s\) and \(t\) absorbs the Lipschitz error in the negative quadratic. Exponentiation preserves order. Multiplying by the positive Gaussian normalizer rewrites this as an upper bound on the Gibbs-weighted transition kernel.

steps.title: Integrate the comparison against the Gibbs start
steps.body:
The relative density of the updated Gibbs law is

\[r_{ u,t}(y)=\int N_t\exp\!\left(U(y)-U(x)- rac{\|y-x+t abla U(x)\|^2}{4t} ight)dx.\]

Insert the pointwise comparison. The remaining \(x\)-dependent expression is a normalized Gaussian with time \(s\) centered at \(y-s abla U(y)\), so its integral is one. The factors independent of \(x\) give

\[r_{ u,t}(y)\le(s/t)^{d/2}\exp\!\left( rac s4\| abla U(y)\|^2 ight).\]

Normalization of the original Gibbs probability cancels its partition function. Taking \(s=t/(1-4tL)\) later supplies an explicit reference-density bound whose logarithmic cost tends to zero.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/IntegratedEntropy.title: Integrating entropy dissipation with almost-everywhere derivatives
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/IntegratedEntropy.summary: The actual entropy chain rule yields local absolute continuity and a derivative inequality almost everywhere. These scalar lemmas use precisely that regularity, together with a continuous one-sided upper envelope at time zero. They do not require pointwise derivatives at every time.

steps.title: Integrate the affine differential inequality
steps.body:
Suppose \(H\) is absolutely continuous on \([s,t]\) and \(H^{\prime}\le-aH+b\) almost everywhere, with \(a>0\). Set \(F(u)=e^{au}(H(u)-b/a)\). Products of absolutely continuous functions on a compact interval are absolutely continuous. The product rule holds almost everywhere and gives \(F^{\prime}(u)=e^{au}(a(H(u)-b/a)+H^{\prime}(u))\le0\).

The fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions gives \(F(t)-F(s)=\int_s^tF^{\prime}\le0\). Multiply by \(e^{-at}>0\), cancel the exponentials, and rearrange:

\[H(t)\le e^{-a(t-s)}H(s)+\frac ba(1-e^{-a(t-s)}).\]

The proof removes no exceptional set by assuming a derivative there; both differentiability and the inequality are used only almost everywhere.

steps.title: Send the positive initial time to zero
steps.body:
Suppose \(H\) is absolutely continuous on every \([s,T]\), \(0\[H(T)\le e^{-a(T-s)}M(s)+\frac ba(1-e^{-a(T-s)}).\]

The right side tends to \(e^{-aT}M(0)+(b/a)(1-e^{-aT})\). Order is preserved under limits, giving the desired initial-endpoint bound. Single endpoints have zero Lebesgue measure, so an inequality on the open interval suffices. Continuity or differentiability of \(H\) at zero is not needed.

steps.title: Absorb the ULA forcing with its exact constants
steps.body:
Assume \(2\alpha H\le I\), \(H^{\prime}\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\), and \(G_0\le4L^2M(0)/\alpha+2dL\). Let \(0\[h^2L^2(4L^2/\alpha)\le\alpha/4,\qquad h^2L^2(2dL)\le hdL^2/2.\]

The derivative is therefore at most \(-3\alpha H/2+B\), where \(B=\alpha M(0)/4+(5/2)hdL^2\). The affine comparison and \(1-e^{-ah}\le ah\) imply \(H(h)\le e^{-3\alpha h/2}M(0)+Bh\). Finally \(e^{-x}\ge e^{-3x/2}+x/4\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\) absorbs the entropy part of \(Bh\). Bounding \(5/2\) by 6 gives

\[H(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}M(0)+6h^2dL^2.\]

The final actual-law theorem proves every analytic premise before invoking this scalar result.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Compatibility.lea.title: Why the LSI constant cannot exceed smoothness
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Compatibility.lea.summary: Write \(\nu(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\), with \(\nabla U\) globally \(L\)-Lipschitz, in a nonzero finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. The original positive \(C^1\) density formulation of LSI implies \(\alpha\le L\). The proof first derives a variance inequality for bounded smooth tests, then combines bounded sinusoidal tests with Gibbs integration by parts and the previously proved score bound. No position moment, transport inequality, Hessian, or strong convexity is assumed.

steps.title: integrable exp mul bounded
steps.body: If \(|f|\le B\), then \(tf\le |t|B\), so \(0<e^{tf}\le e^{|t|B}\). The right side is an integrable constant under every finite measure. Measurability follows from that of \(f\); mono' then proves actual integrability of the exponential. This establishes the whole real line as the domain of the moment generating function used below.

steps.title: exponential test
steps.body:
Let \(M(t)=\int e^{tf}\,d u\), \(\psi(t)=\log M(t)\), and \(r_t=e^{tf}/M(t)\). Boundedness of \(f\) proves \(0<M(t)<\infty\); the normalized tilt is therefore a probability measure. The proof constructs strict positivity and \(C^1\) regularity of r before testing the original LSI definition.

The logarithmic identity hl is \(\log r_t=tf-\psi(t)\). Integration against the tilted law and Mathlib's identity \(\int f\,r_t\,d u=\psi'(t)\) give the actual KL value \(H(r_t u\mid u)=t\psi'(t)-\psi(t)\); boundedness proves its finiteness first. The gradient identity hgrad gives \( abla\log r_t=t abla f\). If \(\| abla f\|\le D\), its squared norm is at most \(t^2D^2\). This is integrable under the probability tilt, so Fisher information is finite. LSI now yields \(2\alpha(t\psi'(t)-\psi(t))\le t^2D^2\). Both finiteness guards are retained when converting the extended-valued inequality to real numbers.

steps.title: tendsto entropy quotient
steps.body: For a \(C^3\) scalar function \(\psi\) with \(\psi(0)=0\), both numerator and denominator of \((t\psi'(t)-\psi(t))/t^2\) tend to zero as \(t\downarrow0\). The product rule cancels the two copies of \(\psi'(t)\), leaving numerator derivative \(t\psi''(t)\); the denominator derivative is \(2t\). On the punctured right neighborhood, their quotient equals \(\psi''(t)/2\). Continuity of the second derivative and one application of l'Hopital's rule prove the limit \(\psi''(0)/2\). The proof explicitly supplies the nonzero denominator derivative and both zero limits.

steps.title: variance le of bounded
steps.body:
For bounded \(f\), its moment and cumulant generating functions are analytic on all real parameters. Mathlib's second derivative formula at zero is \(\psi''(0)=\int f^2\,d u-(\int f\,d u)^2\), since \(M(0)=1\). Thus no unproved assertion that LSI implies a spectral gap is inserted.

Divide the exponential-test inequality by \(t^2>0\), for \(t>0\), and use tendsto_entropy_quotient. The left side tends to \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\), while the right side remains \(D^2\). Passing to the limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\le D^2\). The boundedness and gradient-bound hypotheses here describe this test function; they are not additional assumptions on the target.

steps.title: integral gibbs weighted
steps.body: Unfold \(\nu=Z^{-1}(e^{-U}dx)\). Scalar multiplication of a measure multiplies its real Bochner integral by \((Z^{-1})^{\mathrm{real}}\). The with-density integral formula then gives \(\int g\,d\nu=(Z^{-1})^{\mathrm{real}}\int e^{-U}g\,dx\). Continuity of \(U\) makes the weight measurable, and its pointwise value is finite. This equality concerns total integrals; integrability for its later uses is established separately.

steps.title: integrable gibbs weighted
steps.body: Strict positivity of the Gibbs partition follows from differentiability of \(U\); the hypothesis here also excludes an infinite partition. Consequently multiplication of the weighted Lebesgue measure by \(Z^{-1}\) preserves integrability in both directions. The with-density integrability equivalence then gives \(g\in L^1(\nu)\) exactly when \(e^{-U}g\in L^1(dx)\). This is the justification for moving the bounded-test integration-by-parts calculation to Lebesgue measure.

steps.title: gibbs stein bounded
steps.body:
For bounded \(C^1\) \(\psi\) with bounded gradient and any fixed \(v\), prove \(\mathbb E_ u[\psi\langle abla U,v angle]=\mathbb E_ u\langle abla\psi,v angle\). The already established score MGF implies integrability of \(\langle abla U,v angle\). Multiplying it by bounded \(\psi\) preserves integrability. Bounded \( abla\psi\) also makes its directional derivative integrable.

The three weighted functions required by Mathlib's global integration-by-parts theorem are therefore integrable: \(\psi e^{-U}\), \((D_v\psi)e^{-U}\), and \(\psi D_v(e^{-U})\). The explicit derivative hw is \(D_v(e^{-U})=-e^{-U}\langle abla U,v angle\). Integration by parts cancels the two minus signs; multiplying by the same Gibbs normalizer on both sides gives the identity. Boundary vanishing and coordinate moments are not separate hypotheses.

steps.title: integral mul sq le
steps.body: For real \(L^2\) functions \(f,g\), Holder's inequality proves \(fg\in L^1\); their squares are integrable as well. For every real \(c\), integrate \((cf+g)^2\ge0\) to obtain the quadratic \((\int f^2)c^2+2(\int fg)c+\int g^2\ge0\). Its discriminant is nonpositive. Dividing the resulting algebraic inequality by four gives \((\int fg)^2\le(\int f^2)(\int g^2)\). This elementary squared Cauchy-Schwarz form avoids square roots in the compatibility argument.

steps.title: logSobolev constant le smoothness
steps.body:
Choose \(\|v\|=1\), possible because the space is nontrivial. Put \(s(x)=\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\). The score MGF gives \(\mathbb E s^2\le L\); the bounded Stein identity with \(\psi=1\) gives \(\mathbb E s=0\).

For \(t>0\), use the bounded test \(f_t(x)=\sin(t\langle v,x\rangle)\). Its gradient is \(t\cos(t\langle v,x\rangle)v\), so its norm is at most \(|t|\). The bounded-test variance theorem gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\le t^2\). Stein's identity and score centering give \(\mathbb E[s(f_t-\mathbb Ef_t)]=t\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle)\). Squared Cauchy-Schwarz now yields \(t^2(\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle))^2\le L\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\).

Multiply by \(\alpha\ge0\), insert the variance bound, and cancel \(t^2>0\). This proves \(\alpha(\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle))^2\le L\). Dominated convergence applies because cosine is bounded by one and tends pointwise to one as \(t\downarrow0\). Its expectation tends to one, proving \(\alpha\le L\). No integrability of \(X\) itself is needed.

steps.title: constant le smoothness
steps.body: This wrapper removes two temporary restrictions from the previous proof. If \(\alpha<0\), then \(\alpha\le0\le L\) immediately. Otherwise, LSI includes the assertion that the Gibbs law is a probability measure. An infinite partition would make its normalizing scalar zero and hence make the Gibbs measure zero, contradicting mass one. Thus the partition is finite internally, and the nonnegative-constant compatibility theorem applies. The final hypotheses are precisely LSI, differentiability, Lipschitz gradient, finite dimension, and a nontrivial state space.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianTimeDeriv.title: Time derivatives and spacetime integrability of the Gaussian mixture
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianTimeDeriv.summary: Let \(g_x=\nabla U(x)\), \(c_t(x)=x-tg_x\), \(d=\dim E\), and \(K_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\). This module differentiates the actual normalized proposal, constructs \(\dot p_t(y)=\int\partial_tK_t(x,y)\,\mu(dx)\), and proves its local spacetime integrability. The only initial moment used is \(G_0=\int\|g_x\|^2d\mu<\infty\); this is derived from finite initial KL elsewhere.

steps.title: gaussianProposalNormalizer eq rpow
steps.body: The proposal normalizer is defined as the reciprocal of an actual Gaussian integral, not as a free scalar parameter.
