Gaussian Fourier integration evaluates \(\int e^{-a\|z\|^2}dz=(\pi/a)^{d/2}\) for \(a>0\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\), simplify \(\pi/a=4\pi t\), and invert the real power to obtain \(N_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Positivity of \(t\) justifies the Gaussian formula and the real-power inversion.

steps.title: hasDerivAt gaussianProposalNormalizer
steps.body: On a neighborhood of \(t>0\), all times remain positive, so the actual normalizer agrees locally with \((4\pi s)^{-d/2}\). The real-power chain rule gives derivative \((-d/2)(4\pi t)^{-d/2-1}(4\pi)\). Use \((4\pi t)^{p-1}=(4\pi t)^p/(4\pi t)\) to rewrite this as \(-dN_t/(2t)\). The local equality heq transfers the derivative back to the normalizer defined by the Gaussian integral.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernel
steps.body: The real component kernel is \(K_t(x,y)=N_t\exp(-\|y-x+tg_x\|^2/(4t))\). The gradient \(g_x\) is evaluated at the initial state \(x\), and is constant when differentiating in \(t\) or \(y\). Its integral over \(y\) is one at positive time by the previously proved Gaussian proposal normalization.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernelDot
steps.body: Define the explicit candidate derivative \(\dot K_t=K_t[-d/(2t)+\|y-x\|^2/(4t^2)-\|g_x\|^2/4]\). The dimension term comes from the normalizer; the remaining terms come from differentiating the exponent. In the expanded exponent, the mixed inner-product term is independent of time, which explains its absence from this expression. The following theorem verifies that this formula is the derivative.

steps.title: frozen exponent eq
steps.body: Set \(z=y-x\). The squared-norm identity gives \(\|z+sg_x\|^2=\|z\|^2+2s\langle z,g_x\rangle+s^2\|g_x\|^2\). For \(s\ne0\), division by \(-4s\) yields \(-\|z+sg_x\|^2/(4s)=-\|z\|^2/(4s)-\langle z,g_x\rangle/2-s\|g_x\|^2/4\). The vector identity and scalar denominator cancellation are proved separately in the Lean calculation.

steps.title: hasDerivAt frozenGaussianKernel
steps.body:
Write the expanded exponent as \(-A/s-B-sC\), where \(A=\|y-x\|^2/4\), \(B=\langle y-x,g_x\rangle/2\), and \(C=\|g_x\|^2/4\). Its derivative at positive \(t\) is \(A/t^2-C\). The expansion agrees with the original exponent on a neighborhood avoiding zero, so this is also the derivative of the original expression.

Apply the exponential chain rule and multiply by the actual normalizer. Its derivative contributes \(-dK_t/(2t)\); the exponential derivative contributes \(K_t(A/t^2-C)\). Collecting terms gives exactly frozenGaussianKernelDot. No derivative of \(g_x\), and therefore no Hessian, is taken.

steps.title: norm frozenGaussianKernelDot le
steps.body:
Put \(r=y-x+tg_x\) and \(e=e^{-\|r\|^2/(4t)}\). The triangle inequality and \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) give \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\). The Gaussian envelope gives \(\|r\|^2e\le4t\), while \(e\le1\). Consequently \(\|y-x\|^2e\le8t+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\).

Bound the absolute value of each derivative-coefficient term by their nonnegative sum, multiply by \(e\), and insert these bounds. The resulting convenient envelope is \(|\dot K_t(x,y)|\le N_t[(d+4)/t+\|g_x\|^2]\). It is uniform in \(y\), and is integrable in the initial variable whenever \(G_0<\infty\). Its purpose is time differentiation under the initial-state integral, rather than output-space integration.

steps.title: gaussianProposalNormalizer measurable
steps.body: The map \((t,z)\mapsto\exp(-(1/(4t))\|z\|^2)\) is jointly measurable. Parameter integration makes its real Gaussian integral measurable, even at parameters where the total integral takes its default value. Taking its reciprocal preserves measurability and gives the actual proposal normalizer. The all-time measurable extension is used only to form measurable parameter integrals; positive-time analysis uses the genuine finite normalization.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernelDot measurable
steps.body: Lipschitzness makes \(x\mapsto g_x\) continuous and measurable. Combine this with the measurable normalizer and the explicit algebraic formula for \(\dot K_t\). Products, norms, scalar inverses, and exponentials preserve measurability, giving joint measurability in \((t,y,x)\). This is the input needed to integrate out the initial variable while retaining measurable time-space dependence.

steps.title: interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative
steps.body: Define \(\dot p_t(y)=\int\dot K_t(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\). At this point it is an ordinary parameter integral. The subsequent differentiation theorem proves it is the actual derivative of \(p_t(y)\), and the energy estimates prove its integrability, so no analytic assertion is built into this definition.

steps.title: interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative measurable
steps.body: The component derivative is jointly measurable in \((t,y,x)\). Its strongly measurable parameter integral over the probability measure \(\mu\) is therefore measurable in \((t,y)\). This gives a single measurable version of \(\dot p\) for spacetime Fubini and the entropy chain rule.

steps.title: hasDerivAt interpolationLebesgueDensity time
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\). Continuity of \(N_t\) supplies a common neighborhood \(S\) on which \(s>t/2\) and \(N_s<N_t+1\). The pointwise derivative envelope then gives \(|\dot K_s(x,y)|\le(N_t+1)[2(d+4)/t+\|g_x\|^2]\) for every \(s\in S\). This bound is integrable in \(x\) by the initial gradient-energy hypothesis, and the component kernel at \(t\) is integrable because it is bounded by \(N_t\).

The parameter-integral derivative theorem now supplies both integrability of \(\dot K_t(\cdot,y)\) and the derivative of \(\int K_s(x,y)d\mu(x)\). On a positive-time neighborhood this integral equals the real density of the actual interpolation law. The local equality heq transfers the derivative to that density, proving \(\partial_t p_t(y)=\dot p_t(y)\) for every output state. No invertibility of the Euler map or step-size restriction is needed.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernel eq realGaussianKernel
steps.body: The spatial Fisher calculation uses precision notation \(q_a(c,y)=Z_a^{-1}e^{-a\|y-c\|^2}\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\) and \(c=x-tg_x\). The normalizers agree by definition, and \(-a\|y-c\|^2=-\|y-c\|^2/(4t)\). This pointwise identity makes the time and spatial calculations use precisely the same normalized Gaussian kernel.

steps.title: norm frozenGaussianKernelDot le weighted
steps.body: Retain the Gaussian factor instead of replacing it by its supremum. With \(r=y-x+tg_x\), the bound \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\) implies that the absolute derivative coefficient is at most \(d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2\). Multiplication by \(K_t\ge0\) yields \(|\dot K_t|\le K_t[d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2]\). Unlike the initial-variable envelope, this bound remains integrable in the output variable.

steps.title: frozenGaussianEnergy
steps.body: Use the common nonnegative envelope \(\mathcal E_t(x,y)=K_t(x,y)(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2)\). Its three terms correspond to Gaussian mass, initial gradient energy, and Gaussian displacement energy. This envelope can dominate the derivative with a time-dependent scalar coefficient and can also be reused in spatial integration by parts.

steps.title: frozenGaussianEnergy nonneg
steps.body: At positive time the actual normalizer and the Gaussian exponential are positive, so \(K_t\ge0\). Every term in \(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonnegative. Their product is nonnegative; this identifies its norm with itself in the Fubini integrability proof.

steps.title: frozenGaussianEnergy integral
steps.body: For fixed \(x\), Gaussian normalization gives \(\int K_t(x,y)dy=1\), and the centered Gaussian covariance gives \(\int K_t(x,y)\|y-c_t(x)\|^2dy=2td\). Both integrands are genuinely integrable. The initial gradient factor is constant in \(y\), so its integral is \(\|g_x\|^2\). Expand the common energy into these three integrable terms to obtain \(\int\mathcal E_t(x,y)dy=1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\).

steps.title: integrable frozenGaussianEnergy
steps.body: The common energy is jointly measurable. For every initial \(x\), its output section is integrable by the component energy theorem. Since the energy is nonnegative, the integral of its norm is exactly \(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\), an integrable function of \(x\) under the probability law \(\mu\). The product integrability criterion therefore proves \(\mathcal E_t\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\).

steps.title: integral frozenGaussianEnergy
steps.body: Joint integrability allows Fubini, giving \(\int\mathcal E_t\,d(\mu\otimes dy)=\int(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td)d\mu(x)\). Probability normalization and the definition of \(G_0\) reduce this to \(1+G_0+2td\). The displayed equality supplies a finite quantitative bound, rather than relying on an unspecified integrability witness.

steps.title: gaussianTimeCoefficient
steps.body: Set \(C_t=d/(2t)+1/(2t^2)+1\). It is positive for \(t>0\), and is bounded above on any interval \([a,b]\) with \(a>0\) by \(C_a\). The coefficient is deliberately coarse: only local spacetime integrability, rather than a sharp density-derivative estimate, is needed for the entropy chain rule.

steps.title: norm frozenGaussianKernelDot le energy
steps.body: In the weighted derivative bound, denote the three nonnegative coefficients by \(A=d/(2t)\), \(B=1/(2t^2)\), and \(1\). Each is at most \(C_t=A+B+1\). Therefore \(A+B\|r\|^2+\|g_x\|^2\le C_t(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|r\|^2)\). Multiply by \(K_t\ge0\) to prove \(|\dot K_t|\le C_t\mathcal E_t\).

steps.title: integrable frozenGaussianKernelDot
steps.body: The component time derivative is jointly measurable, and its norm is bounded by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The common energy is integrable on \(\mu\otimes dy\), and \(C_t\) is a finite scalar at positive time. Domination therefore proves joint integrability of \(\dot K_t\), which licenses the changes of integration order used in the time weak equation.

steps.title: integrable interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative
steps.body: Fubini applied to the jointly integrable component derivative first gives \(\dot p_t\in L^1(dy)\). The norm inequality for Bochner integration gives \(|\dot p_t(y)|\le\int|\dot K_t(x,y)|d\mu(x)\). Integrate in \(y\), exchange the two integrals, and dominate by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The exact envelope integral yields \(\int|\dot p_t(y)|dy\le C_t(1+G_0+2td)\).

steps.title: integrable interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative spacetime
steps.body: Joint measurability of \(\dot p\) permits the product integrability criterion on \([a,b]\times E\), where \(a>0\). Every time section is in \(L^1(dy)\). For times in the interval, \(C_t\le C_a\) and \(1+G_0+2td\le1+G_0+2bd\), giving the common finite scalar bound \(\int|\dot p_t|dy\le C_a(1+G_0+2bd)\). The time interval has finite measure, so the section norms are integrable. Hence \(\dot p\in L^1(dt\,dy)\) locally away from zero. If \(a>b\), the restricted time measure is zero and the same argument remains valid.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEnergyInt.title: Relative Fisher energy and the sharp frozen-gradient error
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEnergyInt.summary: Let \( ho_t\) be the actual frozen Gaussian interpolation, \(r_t=d ho_t/d u\), \(s_t= abla\log r_t\), and \(G_0=\mathbb E_\mu\| abla U\|^2\). This module proves \(I_t\le4(1+L^2t^2)G_0+8tdL^2+d/t\), local spacetime integrability of the weighted relative-score energy, and the exact pair-law error bound \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). These estimates provide domination for the unbounded entropy test and its truncation limits.

steps.title: norm add sq le two
steps.body: The triangle inequality gives \(\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|\). Square both nonnegative sides and use \(2\|x\|\|y\|\le\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2\), which follows from \((\|x\|-\|y\|)^2\ge0\). This proves \(\|x+y\|^2\le2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2\), the pointwise estimate used to split relative Fisher energy.

steps.title: interpolationRelativeScoreField energy le
steps.body:
The jointly measurable score field agrees at positive time with the actual relative score. Its decomposition is \(s_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t\). The propagated gradient is square integrable, and Gaussian smoothing gives \(\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le d/(2t)\). These facts also prove integrability of the relative-score square.

Apply the squared sum bound pointwise and integrate: \(I_t\le2G_t+2\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le2G_t+d/t\). The proof keeps the integrability witnesses for all terms before using integral monotonicity.

steps.title: interpolationRelativeScoreField energy bound
steps.body: The interpolation gradient-moment estimate is \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\). Substitute it into \(I_t\le2G_t+d/t\) and distribute the factor two. This gives \(I_t\le4(1+L^2t^2)G_0+8tdL^2+d/t\). Every quantity on the right is determined by the initial gradient energy and the original potential; no entropy-production assumption is used.

steps.title: interpolationRelativeScoreField weighted energy
steps.body: The explicitly constructed relative density satisfies \(r_t u= ho_t\). The with-density integrability equivalence therefore transports integrability of \(\|s_t\|^2\) under \( ho_t\) to integrability of \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\) under the fixed target \( u\). The corresponding integral identity is \(\int r_t\|s_t\|^2d u=\int\|s_t\|^2d ho_t\). Strict positivity and measurability of the constructed density justify the ordinary weighted-integral formulas.

steps.title: integrable interpolationRelativeScoreField energy spacetime
steps.body:
The relative density and the chosen relative-score field are jointly measurable in time and space. Their weighted energy is nonnegative. On a positive interval \([a,b]\), the section at every time is integrable by the density-change theorem.

Since \(0<a\le t\le b\), the quantitative estimate is bounded uniformly by \(4(1+L^2b^2)G_0+8bdL^2+d/a\). The integral of the section norm is exactly its nonnegative energy, so this finite scalar bound makes it integrable in time. The product criterion yields \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\in L^1(dt\,d\nu)\) on the interval. This is the spacetime dominating function required to pass from bounded entropy tests to the full relative Fisher term.

steps.title: frozenGradientErrorField
steps.body: For the fixed independent pair \((X,Z)\sim\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\), define \(e_t(X,Z)= abla U(X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z)- abla U(X)\). The underlying probability space is independent of time. This avoids assuming a jointly measurable choice of a state-space conditional expectation when integrating the error energy over time.

steps.title: integrable frozenGradientErrorField energy spacetime
steps.body: The proposal and Lipschitz gradient make \((t,X,Z)\mapsto\|e_t(X,Z)\|^2\) jointly measurable. For \(t\ge0\), the exact Gaussian calculation already gives integrability and \(\mathbb E\|e_t\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). On a compact nonnegative time interval this is at most \(L^2(b^2G_0+2bd)\). The time measure is finite, so Fubini's integrability criterion proves the squared error is integrable on the time/initial-state/noise product.

steps.title: frozenGaussianPair gradient error energy
steps.body: Map the independent initial/noise pair by \(T_t(x,z)=(x,x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z)\). The squared error as a function of the output pair is \(F(x,y)=\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2\). Its composition with \(T_t\) is exactly the frozen-gradient discrepancy from the Gaussian energy calculation. Measurability of \(T_t\) and continuity of \(F\) let the map-measure integrability and integral theorems transport both the integrability witness and the bound \(L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\) to the actual initial/output pair law.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernel gradient error energy
steps.body:
The actual pair law is identified with \(K_t(x,y)\,\mu(dx)dy\) by the previously proved Gaussian proposal pair-density theorem. The proof specializes its measurable center to \(x-t abla U(x)\); the precision and step-size versions of the kernel agree pointwise.

Rewrite the pair-law energy theorem using this exact density identity. The with-density integrability equivalence gives \(K_t\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\), and its integral formula gives the sharp bound \(\int K_t\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2d\mu\,dy\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). This transport preserves the exact constants needed in the final entropy recurrence; a cruder pointwise Gaussian envelope is not substituted for the error energy.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianScorePair.title: Averaging the Gaussian component score
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianScorePair.summary: The Gaussian component score \(S_{t,x}(y)=-(y-x+t\nabla U(x))/(2t)\) averages to the actual mixture score. This module establishes the vector identity \(p_t\nabla\log p_t=\int K_tS_{t,x}d\mu\), proves all joint integrability needed for pairing it with a continuous \(L^2(\rho_t)\) vector field, and transfers the resulting identity to the fixed independent initial/noise space used by entropy production.

steps.title: frozenGaussianScore
steps.body: For a fixed initial state \(x\), the Gaussian proposal has center \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\). Its score in the proposed state is \(S_{t,x}(y)=\nabla_y\log K_t(x,y)=-(y-c_t(x))/(2t)\). This definition is an explicit affine vector field. It is different from the mixture score, which averages this field over the posterior initial-state distribution.

steps.title: frozenGaussianScore memLp
steps.body: Represent the actual initial/output pair as \((X,Y_t)\), with \(Y_t=c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\) and independent standard Gaussian \(Z\). Substituting into the component score cancels the center: \(S_{t,X}(Y_t)=-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z\). The Gaussian identity random variable is square integrable; scalar multiplication and pullback to the product preserve this property. The map-measure theorem transfers it to the actual pair law. No initial position or gradient moment is needed for this component score.

steps.title: frozenGaussianJoint memLp state field
steps.body: If \(V\in L^2(\rho_t)\), then \(V(Y_t)\in L^2(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I))\), because \(\rho_t\) is the actual pushforward by the proposal. Map the independent pair to \((X,Y_t)\); a second application of the map-measure equivalence gives \((x,y)\mapsto V(y)\in L^2\) under the actual pair law. Continuity of \(V\) supplies the measurability required in both transfers.

steps.title: integrable frozenGaussianScore pairing
steps.body: The component score and the state field \(V(y)\) are both square integrable under the actual pair law. Holder's inequality makes the product of their norms integrable, and \(|\langle S,V\rangle|\le\|S\|\|V\|\) proves integrability of their inner product. The exact pair-density identity then rewrites this law as \(K_t(x,y)\mu(dx)dy\). The with-density equivalence gives joint integrability of \(K_t\langle S_{t,x},V(y)\rangle\) under \(\mu\otimes dy\), which is the hypothesis needed for Fubini in the averaging calculation.

steps.title: interpolationLebesgueDensity weighted score
steps.body: The already constructed spatial derivative of the Gaussian mixture identifies its score as the posterior mean of the component score. The posterior density in \(x\) is \(K_t(x,y)/p_t(y)\), where \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)>0\). Substitute this explicit with-density formula into the posterior integral and multiply by \(p_t(y)\). The common denominator cancels pointwise, giving \(p_t(y)\nabla\log p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)S_{t,x}(y)d\mu(x)\). The proof uses the actual Gaussian normalizers in both precision and step-size notation, rather than assuming a formal Bayes identity.

steps.title: integrable frozenGaussianScore weighted
steps.body: The component score is \(L^2\) under the actual pair probability law, hence is also \(L^1\). Identify that law with its explicit density \(K_t\) under \(\mu\otimes dy\). The vector-valued with-density integrability theorem gives \((x,y)\mapsto K_t(x,y)S_{t,x}(y)\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\). In particular, Fubini supplies integrability of the vector section in \(x\) for almost every output \(y\); this is needed before moving an inner product through its integral.

steps.title: integral frozenGaussianScore pairing
steps.body:
For almost every \(y\), vector-section integrability permits the linear functional \(w\mapsto\langle w,V(y)\rangle\) to commute with integration. The pointwise weighted-score identity then gives \(\int K_t(x,y)\langle S_{t,x}(y),V(y)\rangle d\mu(x)=p_t(y)\langle\nabla\log p_t(y),V(y)\rangle\).

The scalar pairing is jointly integrable by the preceding Holder argument, so Fubini exchanges the initial-state and output integrals. Integrate the displayed identity in \(y\). Finally \(p_t(y)dy=\rho_t(dy)\), with its explicit measurable finite density, changes the weighted Lebesgue integral into the actual-law integral. Thus \(\int K_t\langle S_{t,x},V\rangle d\mu\,dy=\int\langle\nabla\log p_t,V\rangle d\rho_t\).

steps.title: integral frozenGaussianScore pairing independent
steps.body:
Apply the measurable pair map \(T_t(x,z)=(x,Y_t(x,z))\) to the continuous pairing \(\langle S_{t,x}(y),V(y)\rangle\). The map-integral theorem expresses its actual pair-law integral as an integral over the fixed independent initial/noise space. The exact pair-density theorem expresses the same integral as the Gaussian-weighted Lebesgue pairing just evaluated.

Substitute \(Y_t=c_t(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\) in the component score. The residual becomes \(\sqrt{2t}z\), so the result is \(\mathbb E\langle-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z,V(Y_t)\rangle=\mathbb E_{\rho_t}\langle\nabla\log p_t,V\rangle\). With \(V=\nabla\log r_t\), this identity turns the Gaussian-noise part of the raw entropy flux into the Lebesgue-score pairing needed for the full Fisher term.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyMoment.lea.title: Finite entropy supplies the gradient moment directly
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyMoment.lea.summary: A finite initial KL divergence already controls the squared Gibbs score when \( abla U\) is Lipschitz. Gaussian averaging of the directional score MGF gives \(\mathbb E_ u e^{\| abla U\|^2/(4L)}\le e^{d/2}\). The entropy inequality then proves both integrability and \(G_\mu\le4L H(\mu\mid u)+2dL\). This direct argument closes the moment input to ULA without assuming an entropy-cost coupling or a transport inequality.

steps.title: mul le klFun add exp sub one
steps.body: Let \(\Phi(a)=a\log a-a+1\), with its continuous value \(\Phi(0)=1\). For \(a>0\), the elementary inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\), applied to \(u=b-\log a\), gives \(e^b\ge a+ab-a\log a\). Rearranging proves \(ab\le\Phi(a)+e^b-1\). The zero-density case is handled separately: its left side is zero, and its right side is \(e^b\ge0\). Thus this entropy/exponential Young inequality remains valid at zero Radon-Nikodym density.

steps.title: integrable of finite kl of integrable exp
steps.body:
Write \(a=d\mu/d u\). Finite KL supplies absolute continuity \(\mu\ll u\) and integrability of the actual log likelihood; equivalently \(\Phi(a)\) is integrable under \( u\). For a measurable nonnegative observable \(f\), the Young inequality gives \(0\le af\le\Phi(a)+e^f\). Both terms on the right are integrable by the finite-KL and exponential-moment hypotheses.

Domination proves \(af\in L^1( u)\). The Radon-Nikodym weighted-integrability equivalence then gives \(f\in L^1(\mu)\). In particular, the moment conclusion is derived before any ordinary expectation is manipulated; it is not an extra assumption hidden in the entropy inequality.

steps.title: integral le kl add of integral exp le
steps.body:
Assume \(\int e^f d u\le e^c\). First derive \(f\in L^1(\mu)\) with the preceding theorem. Apply the Young inequality to \(a=d\mu/d u\) and \(f-c\), and integrate: \(\int(f-c)d\mu\le\int\Phi(a)d u+\int e^{f-c}d u-1\).

Probability normalization identifies \(\int\Phi(a)d u\) with the genuine finite KL divergence and \(\int(f-c)d\mu=\int f d\mu-c\). The MGF hypothesis makes \(\int e^{f-c}d u\le1\), canceling the final two terms. Thus \(\int f d\mu\le H(\mu\mid u)+c\), together with the integrability witness used in its derivation. The proof explicitly justifies each weighted integral and subtraction.

steps.title: integrable radial gaussian
steps.body: For \(b>0\), the real radial Gaussian \(e^{-b\|v\|^2}\) is integrable on every finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. The proof specializes the complex Gaussian Fourier integrability theorem to real positive precision and takes its norm; the complex norm is exactly the displayed real exponential. This supplies the finite integral needed in the Gaussian linearization argument.

steps.title: lintegral radial gaussian
steps.body: Because the radial Gaussian is nonnegative and integrable, its nonnegative Lebesgue integral equals the embedded ordinary integral. The Gaussian Fourier formula evaluates the latter as \((\pi/b)^{d/2}\). Hence \(\int^- e^{-b\|v\|^2}dv=\operatorname{ofReal}((\pi/b)^{d/2})\), a positive finite normalization factor that can safely be canceled later.

steps.title: lintegral radial gaussian mul exp inner
steps.body: Complete the square in \(-b\|v\|^2+\langle g,v\rangle\): it equals \(\|g\|^2/(4b)-b\|v-g/(2b)\|^2\). Exponentiating separates the constant factor \(e^{\|g\|^2/(4b)}\) from a translated radial Gaussian. Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure and the radial normalization give \(\int^- e^{-b\|v\|^2}e^{\langle g,v\rangle}dv=e^{\|g\|^2/(4b)}(\pi/b)^{d/2}\). The identity is proved for nonnegative integrals before any integrability of a random score is assumed.

steps.title: lintegral exp norm sq le of directional mgf
steps.body:
Suppose \(\mathbb E e^{\langle g,v\rangle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\) for every direction \(v\). Multiply by \(e^{-L\|v\|^2}\) and integrate in \(v\). Tonelli applies to the nonnegative jointly measurable integrand, so the order of integration can be exchanged without assuming the desired exponential moment in advance.

Gaussian linearization identifies the left side with \((\pi/L)^{d/2}\mathbb E e^{\|g\|^2/(4L)}\). The directional MGF bound controls the right side by \(\int e^{-(L/2)\|v\|^2}dv=(2\pi/L)^{d/2}\). Cancel the positive finite factor \((\pi/L)^{d/2}\) in the extended nonnegative reals to obtain \(\mathbb E e^{\|g\|^2/(4L)}\le2^{d/2}\).

steps.title: gibbs score exponential moment
steps.body:
The smooth Gibbs score has the previously proved directional MGF bound \(\mathbb E_ u e^{\langle abla U,v angle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\), obtained from translation invariance and first-order smoothness. Apply Gaussian averaging with \(g= abla U\). This gives a finite nonnegative exponential integral bounded by \(2^{d/2}\); measurability and this finiteness prove ordinary integrability.

Convert the nonnegative integral back to its real expectation. Since \(\log2\le1\), \(2^{d/2}\le e^{d/2}\), giving the convenient bound \(\mathbb E_ u e^{\| abla U\|^2/(4L)}\le e^{d/2}\). Only differentiability, Lipschitz gradient, positive \(L\), and finite Gibbs normalization are used; neither convexity nor LSI enters this exponential-moment theorem.

steps.title: gibbs gradient moment bound of finite kl
steps.body:
Apply the entropy inequality with \(f(x)=\| abla U(x)\|^2/(4L)\) and \(c=d/2\). The Gibbs exponential-moment theorem provides both exponential integrability and the MGF bound; finite initial KL provides the absolute-continuity and entropy inputs. Therefore \(\mathbb E_\mu[\| abla U\|^2/(4L)]\le H(\mu\mid u)+d/2\), with this observable integrable under \(\mu\).

Multiply by \(4L>0\), proving \(G_\mu\le4L H(\mu\mid u)+2dL\) and actual square integrability of the score. The proof also derives finite Gibbs partition from its assumed probability normalization. This replaces the previously missing LSI-to-transport route by a stronger direct entropy/score estimate.

steps.title: gibbs gradient moment bound of finite kl of alpha le
steps.body: If \(0<\alpha\le L\), then \(4L\le4L^2/\alpha\). Finite KL is nonnegative, so replacing the direct estimate's coefficient \(4L\) by \(4L^2/\alpha\) preserves the inequality. Thus \(G_\mu\le(4L^2/\alpha)H(\mu\mid\nu)+2dL\), the coefficient used in the ULA one-step calculation. Integrability is inherited from the stronger direct theorem. Compatibility \(\alpha\le L\) is proved from LSI in a separate module.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyEndpoint.l.title: Data processing and a finite-entropy change of reference
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyEndpoint.l.summary: A Gaussian ULA interpolation applies the same transition to the input law and the Gibbs law. Data processing controls their mutual entropy. A one-sided upper bound on the updated Gibbs density then changes the reference back to the original target, proving finiteness as well as an upper bound. Propagated gradient moments make the logarithmic density correction integrable, without any initial position-moment assumption.

steps.title: klDiv prod same right
steps.body: Adjoin the same independent probability innovation \(\eta\) to two finite measures. The log likelihood of \(\mu\otimes\eta\) relative to \(\nu\otimes\eta\) depends only on the first coordinate, so KL is unchanged. The formal proof uses Mathlib's conditional-product KL identity with the constant Markov kernel \(x\mapsto\eta\); its conditional products are exactly the ordinary product measures. This equality supplies the independent-noise step in data processing.

steps.title: llr eq add of absolutelyContinuous
steps.body:
For \(\mu\ll ho\ll u\), the Radon-Nikodym chain rule gives \(d\mu/d u=(d\mu/d ho)(d ho/d u)\) almost everywhere under the integrated law \(\mu\). Each factor is positive and finite there: positivity is transported along absolute continuity, and finiteness uses the probability measures' finite Radon-Nikodym derivatives.

Convert the product of extended densities to real numbers, then apply the logarithm product rule. This proves \(\log(d\mu/d u)=\log(d\mu/d ho)+\log(d ho/d u)\), as an almost-everywhere identity under \(\mu\). The positivity and finiteness checks prevent using logarithm algebra at a zero or infinite density.

steps.title: integrable exp neg llr
steps.body: For \(\mu\ll u\), the reciprocal likelihood \(e^{-\log(d\mu/d u)}\) agrees \(\mu\)-almost everywhere with the real reverse Radon-Nikodym derivative \((d u/d\mu)^{\mathrm{real}}\). This derivative is integrable under \(\mu\), even when \( u\) has a singular component relative to \(\mu\). Thus the negative exponential of the log likelihood is always integrable; finite KL has not been assumed at this stage.

steps.title: integrable llr of integrable upper bound
steps.body: Suppose the log likelihood \(\ell=\log(d\mu/d\nu)\) has an integrable upper bound \(b\). Where \(\ell\ge0\), \(|\ell|\le b\le|b|\). Where \(\ell<0\), the elementary exponential bound gives \(|\ell|=-\ell\le e^{-\ell}\). Hence globally \(|\ell|\le|b|+e^{-\ell}\). The first term is integrable by hypothesis, and the second by reciprocal-likelihood integrability. Measurable domination proves \(\ell\in L^1(\mu)\), controlling its negative tail without a lower density bound.

steps.title: klDiv finite and le of reference density bound
steps.body:
Assume finite \(H(\mu\mid ho)\), \( ho\ll u\), and \(d ho/d u\le e^b\), with \(b\in L^1(\mu)\). Finite KL gives \(\mu\ll ho\), hence \(\mu\ll u\). The density bound transfers to \(\mu\)-almost every point, where positivity of the intermediate density permits logarithms. Thus \(\log(d ho/d u)\le b\).

The log-likelihood chain rule gives \(\log(d\mu/d u)\le\log(d\mu/d ho)+b\). Its right side is integrable. The preceding one-sided integrability theorem therefore proves the new log likelihood integrable and hence \(H(\mu\mid u)<\infty\). Only after proving finiteness do we integrate the inequality, yielding \(H(\mu\mid u)\le H(\mu\mid ho)+\mathbb E_\mu b\). Finite entropy against the new reference is a conclusion, rather than an additional premise.

steps.title: interpolationLaw klDiv le
steps.body: The interpolation is the measurable image of the initial law times standard Gaussian noise under \((x,z)\mapsto x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\). Apply KL data processing to this same map for both initial laws. The independent-noise product identity removes the common Gaussian factor, giving \(H( ho_t^\mu\mid ho_t^ u)\le H(\mu\mid u)\). This argument compares two evolved laws and does not assert that either law is invariant under the discrete step.

steps.title: interpolationLaw gradient moment
steps.body:
Write \( abla U(Y_t)=[ abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)]+ abla U(X)\). The initial gradient is \(L^2\), and the frozen-error energy theorem makes the bracketed discrepancy \(L^2\) on the independent initial/noise space. Their sum is \(L^2\); the map-measure equivalence transfers this to the actual interpolation law.

Pointwise, the squared norm of the sum is at most twice each squared norm. Integrate and insert \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). The initial-coordinate marginal gives the remaining \(G_0\), so \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\). This proves both integrability and the quantitative estimate without a position moment.

steps.title: interpolationLaw entropy bound of density bound
steps.body:
Let \( ho_t\) be the evolved input and \(\sigma_t\) the evolved Gibbs target. Data processing gives \(H( ho_t\mid\sigma_t)\le H_0<\infty\). Suppose the actual reference law satisfies \(d\sigma_t/d u\le\exp(b+c\| abla U\|^2)\), with its absolute continuity retained explicitly.

Finite initial KL first supplies finite \(G_0\) through the direct entropy/score estimate. The propagated gradient-moment theorem then proves \(G_t<\infty\). Consequently the logarithmic reference correction \(b+c\| abla U\|^2\) is integrable under \( ho_t\). Apply the finite-entropy change-of-reference theorem to obtain \(H( ho_t\mid u)<\infty\) and \(H( ho_t\mid u)\le H_0+b+cG_t\). The pointwise density comparison itself is established in the Gibbs interpolation module.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InitialEntropy.le.title: The initial entropy endpoint from an explicit upper envelope
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InitialEntropy.le.summary: The scalar entropy comparison needs an upper boundary at time zero, even if the initial density is irregular. This module constructs a continuous explicit function \(B(t)\) with \(B(0)=H_0\) and actual interpolation entropy \(H_t\le B(t)\) for sufficiently small positive \(t\). The proof uses the updated Gibbs density bound and data processing; no initial Fisher information, state second moment, or assumed entropy continuity is required.

steps.title: interpolationEntropyMajorant
steps.body: Put \(\delta(t)=1-4tL\) and \(G_0=\mathbb E_\mu\|\nabla U\|^2\). Define the explicit envelope \(B(t)=H_0-\frac d2\log\delta(t)+\frac{t}{4\delta(t)}[2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2]\). The logarithmic term is the normalizer correction from the updated Gibbs density; the final term uses the propagated gradient moment. The definition is a scalar function at all times, while its entropy interpretation below requires \(t>0\) and \(\delta(t)>0\).

steps.title: interpolationEntropyMajorant zero
steps.body: At \(t=0\), the logarithm has argument \(\delta(0)=1\), hence is zero. The coefficient \(t/(4\delta(t))\) is zero as well. Both correction terms vanish exactly, proving \(B(0)=H_0\). This is a direct algebraic evaluation of the constructed envelope, not an assumed limit of the actual entropy path.

steps.title: interpolationEntropyMajorant continuousAt zero
steps.body: The denominator \(\delta(t)\) has value one at zero, so it stays nonzero locally. The logarithm is continuous at that same positive value. All other terms in \(B\) are polynomial or constant scalar operations. Their continuity proves \(B(t)\to B(0)=H_0\) as \(t\to0\). The initial gradient integral is an already defined scalar; its genuine finiteness in the entropy application is established by the finite-KL moment theorem.

steps.title: interpolationLaw entropy le majorant
steps.body:
For positive \(t\) with \(\delta=1-4tL>0\), choose the comparison Gaussian time \(s=t/\delta\). The updated Gibbs law has an explicit relative density bounded by \((s/t)^{d/2}\exp(s\|\nabla U(y)\|^2/4)\). Since \(s/t=\delta^{-1}\), this is \(\exp[-(d/2)\log\delta+(s/4)\|\nabla U(y)\|^2]\).

The actual relative density identifies the Radon-Nikodym derivative and proves absolute continuity of the updated Gibbs reference law. The change-of-reference entropy estimate then gives finite \(H_t\) and \(H_t\le H_0-(d/2)\log\delta+(s/4)G_t\). The coefficient \(s/4\) is nonnegative, so inserting \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\) proves \(H_t\le B(t)\).

steps.title: interpolationLaw entropy eventually le majorant
steps.body: For all sufficiently small positive \(t\), specifically \(t<1/(8L)\), one has \(1-4tL>0\). The previous positive-time entropy bound therefore applies eventually in the right neighborhood of zero, giving \(H_t\le B(t)\). Combined with continuity of \(B\) and \(B(0)=H_0\), this supplies the upper initial boundary used in scalar comparison. It does not insert an assumption that \(H_t\) is differentiable or continuous at zero.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyChainRule..title: An integrated chain rule from spacetime integrability
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyChainRule..summary: To differentiate entropy, bounded approximations are first integrated in time. A pointwise time derivative together with joint spacetime \(L^1\) suffices for Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus; no common spatial majorant for every time derivative is assumed. The resulting spatial integral is absolutely continuous and has the integrated derivative almost everywhere. A dominated-limit theorem then passes truncated integral identities to the actual entropy identity.

steps.title: integral eq initial add integral of spacetime integrable
steps.body:
Assume \(f(a,\cdot)\in L^1( u)\), \(\dot f\in L^1((a,b] imes u)\), and \(\partial_t f(t,x)=\dot f(t,x)\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\) and almost every \(x\). Fubini gives \(\dot f(\cdot,x)\in L^1(a,b)\) for almost every \(x\). Apply the scalar fundamental theorem to these sections: \(f(b,x)=f(a,x)+\int_a^b\dot f(t,x)dt\).

The time-integrated derivative is integrable in \(x\) by spacetime integrability. The section identity therefore proves terminal integrability of \(f(b,\cdot)\), rather than requiring it separately. Integrate the identity and exchange time and space to obtain \(\int f(b)d u=\int f(a)d u+\int_a^b\int\dot f(t,x)d u(x)dt\).

steps.title: absolutelyContinuous integral of spacetime integrable
steps.body:
Apply the integrated fundamental theorem on every subinterval \([a,t]\subseteq[a,b]\). Restricting the spacetime measure preserves integrability, giving both integrability of \(f(t,\cdot)\) and \(F(t)=F(a)+\int_a^t q(u)du\), where \(F(t)=\int f(t,x)d\nu(x)\) and \(q(t)=\int\dot f(t,x)d\nu(x)\).

Fubini gives \(q\in L^1(a,b)\). An indefinite integral of an \(L^1\) function is absolutely continuous; adding the constant \(F(a)\) preserves this property. Equality on the interval transfers absolute continuity to \(F\). Thus regularity of the spatial integral is a conclusion of spacetime integrability and pointwise differentiation.

steps.title: integral hasDerivAt ae of spacetime integrable
steps.body: The subinterval argument gives \(F(t)=F(a)+\int_a^t q(u)du\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\), with \(q\in L^1(a,b)\). Lebesgue differentiation supplies derivative \(q(t)\) for the indefinite integral at almost every interior time. For each such \(t\), an open neighborhood stays inside \((a,b)\), where the displayed identity holds. The local equality transfers the derivative to \(F\), yielding \(F'(t)=\int\dot f(t,x)d\nu(x)\) almost everywhere. No pointwise derivative assertion at every time, or at the endpoints, is inferred.

steps.title: integral identity of dominated limits
steps.body:
Suppose truncated identities have the form \(B_n-A_n=\int q_n d u\). Assume the two endpoint sequences converge to their intended values, \(q_n o q\) almost everywhere, and \(|q_n|\le g\) with \(g\in L^1( u)\). Dominated convergence gives convergence of the right-hand integrals, while the endpoint limits give convergence of the left-hand differences. Their equality for every \(n\) and uniqueness of limits prove \(B-A=\int qd u\).

In the entropy application, the endpoints are truncated entropy integrals and \(q_n\) are bounded-test fluxes on a fixed time interval. Spatial energy estimates supply the pointwise flux limit and a time-integrable dominating bound. This lemma passes the integrated identities to the limit without assuming in advance that the full entropy has already been differentiated.

steps.title: regularity of integral identity
steps.body:
Assume only \(q\in L^1(a,b)\) and the exact identity \(H(t)=H(a)+\int_a^t q(u)du\) throughout \([a,b]\). The primitive of \(q\) is absolutely continuous; adding \(H(a)\) and using the identity proves that \(H\) is absolutely continuous.

Lebesgue differentiation gives derivative \(q(t)\) for the primitive at almost every interior time. The identity holds in an interior neighborhood of each such time, so the derivative transfers to \(H\). This gives precisely the final entropy comparison inputs: local absolute continuity and the actual flux as derivative almost everywhere.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEntropyId.title: The complete entropy chain rule for the actual Gaussian interpolation
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEntropyId.summary:
This module proves the entropy identity and positive-time absolute continuity for the actual frozen-drift Gaussian interpolation. The proof starts with bounded smooth log tests, applies the global Gaussian weak equation and a spacetime \(L^1\) time chain rule, then removes both spatial and time truncations by dominated convergence. All regularity and integrability needed in these steps are constructed from the original Gaussian update and the initial gradient energy.

Write \(\pi=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dx\), \(\rho_t=\operatorname{Law}(X-t\nabla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z_0)\), \(r_t=d\rho_t/d\pi\), and \(S_t=\nabla\log r_t\). Here \(Z_0\) is an independent standard Gaussian. The eventual conclusion is \(H(\rho_b\mid\pi)-H(\rho_a\mid\pi)=\int_a^b q(t)dt\), with the explicit raw Gaussian flux \(q\), for every \(0<a\le b\). This identity proves local absolute continuity and the a.e. derivative; they are not assumed.

steps.title: Removing bounded log weights by dominated convergence
steps.body:
Let \(w_m(z)=[1+(z/(m+1))^2]^{-1}\). For a measurable scalar field \(z\) and an integrable field \(f\),

\[\int w_m(z(x))f(x)\,d\nu(x)\longrightarrow\int f(x)\,d\nu(x).\]

The pointwise limit is \(w_m(z(x))\to1\), proved in boundedLogWeight_tendsto. Each weighted integrand is measurable, because the weight is obtained by division, squaring and inversion of measurable real functions. Furthermore \(0\le w_m\le1\), so \(|w_m(z)f|\le|f|\). The Lean proof invokes dominated convergence with the single integrable majorant hf.norm. This lemma later removes the truncation from the actual Gaussian flux, whose two factors are square integrable.

steps.title: Why the square-integrable flux pairing is integrable
steps.body:
If \(v,s\in L^2(\nu;E)\), then

\[|\langle v,s\rangle|\le\|v\|\|s\|,\qquad \|v\|\|s\|\in L^1(\nu).\]

The second assertion follows from Hölder's inequality with exponents \(2,2,1\). In Lean, hf.norm.mul hg.norm supplies membership of the norm product in \(L^1\); memLp_one_iff_integrable converts it to ordinary integrability without assuming that the ambient measure is finite. The measurable inner product is then dominated by this product using norm_inner_le_norm. This establishes actual integrability rather than relying on the default value of an undefined Bochner integral.

steps.title: The real Gibbs density and its normalization
steps.body:
Write \(Z=\int e^{-U(x)}\,dx\), and let \(\pi\) be the normalized Gibbs law. Define

\[J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}.\]

The existing probability-mass argument proves \(0<Z<\infty\); differentiability makes \(U\) measurable and gives strict positivity of the partition function. Consequently \(J(y)>0\) at every point. The measure identity is

\[\pi(dy)=J(y)\,dy.\]

The formal representation of \(\pi\) is initially an extended scalar multiple of volume.withDensity. withDensity_smul absorbs that scalar into the density. The conversion ENNReal.ofReal_toReal is justified by finite nonzero normalization, so the real formula agrees exactly with the original measure. These declarations introduce no strong-convexity assumption.

steps.title: The time derivative of the weighted entropy primitive
steps.body:
Let \(p_t\) be the actual Lebesgue density of the frozen Gaussian update, and let \(r_t=p_t/J\) be its relative density. For the bounded entropy primitive \(\Phi_m\), one has \(\Phi_m'(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\) for \(r>0\). At every positive time, the actual kernel differentiation theorem gives \(\partial_t p_t=\dot p_t\), hence

\[\partial_t r_t=Ze^{U}\dot p_t,\qquad \partial_t[J\Phi_m(r_t)]=\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t.\]

The Lean proof applies the time chain rule first to the constant multiple defining \(r_t\), then to boundedEntropy_hasDerivAt, then to multiplication by \(J\). The remaining coefficient cancels because \(J(y)Ze^{U(y)}=1\), using the inverse of the strictly positive real partition function and \(e^{-U}e^U=1\). This cancellation is what permits the spacetime estimate to use the Lebesgue \(L^1\) bound on \(\dot p_t\).

steps.title: Identifying finite entropy through the chosen density
steps.body:
Suppose \(\mu=r u\) is a probability measure, \(r\ge0\) is measurable, and \(H(\mu\mid u)<\infty\). Then

\[\mathrm{kl}(r)=r\log r+1-r\in L^1( u),\qquad \int\mathrm{kl}(r)\,d u=H(\mu\mid u).\]

Mathlib expresses KL using the Radon–Nikodym derivative. The equality Measure.rnDeriv_withDensity identifies that derivative almost everywhere with ENNReal.ofReal ∘ r. Nonnegativity of \(r\) makes its real part exactly \(r\). Finite KL yields integrability of the log-likelihood ratio, which the KL library converts to integrability of klFun of the derivative. An almost-everywhere change of representative gives both displayed conclusions for the chosen density itself.

steps.title: Integrability of every actual bounded entropy
steps.body:
At \(t>0\), the actual interpolation has a positive \(C^1\) relative density \(r_t\). Its Fisher information is finite from the initial score moment and Gaussian smoothing; LSI then gives finite actual KL. The bounded primitive satisfies

\[0\le\Phi_m(r_t(y))\le\mathrm{kl}(r_t(y)).\]

The preceding density lemma proves that the right-hand side is integrable. The left-hand side is measurable: continuity of \(r_t\) and the derivative of \(\Phi_m\) at positive arguments give continuity of their composition. The Lean mono' argument therefore derives integrability for each truncation from a verified KL majorant. Initial density differentiability, initial Fisher information and a second moment of the state are not required.

steps.title: Convergence of bounded entropy to actual KL
steps.body:
For every fixed positive time,

\[\int\Phi_m(r_t)\,d\pi\longrightarrow H(\rho_t\mid\pi).\]

Pointwise convergence \(\Phi_m(r)\to\mathrm{kl}(r)\) holds for \(r>0\). The domination \(0\le\Phi_m(r_t)\le\mathrm{kl}(r_t)\), together with integrability proved above, gives dominated convergence under the fixed Gibbs measure. Before taking the limit, Lean identifies the integral of klFun r_t with the actual KL through tiltedMeasure_interpolationRelativeDensity. Thus the limiting quantity is the KL of the actual Gaussian law, rather than an independently specified entropy path.

steps.title: The bounded entropy and its time flux
steps.body:
The two functions used in the time integration are

\[H_m(t)=\int\Phi_m(r_t(y))\,d\pi(y),\qquad q_m(t)=\int\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\dot p_t(y)\,dy.\]

interpolationBoundedEntropy uses the fixed Gibbs reference measure; interpolationBoundedEntropyFlux uses Lebesgue measure. Their different measures match the exact cancellation in the weighted chain rule. The definitions are explicit functions of the actual mixture density and its actual kernel time derivative.

steps.title: Admissibility of the actual bounded log test
steps.body:
The spatial weak test is \(\psi_m(y)=\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\). Positivity and \(C^1\) regularity of \(r_t\), combined with smoothness of \(\chi_m\), show that \(\psi_m\in C^1\). Its uniform bound is

\[|\psi_m(y)|\le(m+1)\pi/2.\]

The spatial chain rule gives

\[ abla\psi_m(y)=w_m(\log r_t(y)) abla\log r_t(y),\qquad \| abla\psi_m(y)\|\le\| abla\log r_t(y)\|.\]

The relative score is already in \(L^2( ho_t)\). Its norm domination therefore proves square integrability of the test gradient via MemLp.of_le. Lean explicitly constructs measurability of that gradient from its continuous Fréchet derivative. These are precisely the three hypotheses of the global Gaussian weak equation: a bounded \(C^1\) test and an \(L^2\) gradient.

steps.title: The bounded entropy flux is the actual spatial flux
steps.body:
Let \(K_t(x,y)\) be the Gaussian transition density, \(g=\nabla U\), and \(S_t=\nabla\log r_t\). The proved Gaussian weak equation, applied to the admissible test above, gives

\[q_m(t)=-\iint K_t(x,y)w_m(\log r_t(y))\left\langle g(x)-\frac{y-x+tg(x)}{2t},S_t(y)\right\rangle\,\mu(dx)\,dy.\]

The underlying flux is \(K_t[g(x)-(y-x+tg(x))/(2t)]\). Its divergence equals the actual kernel time derivative; global integration by parts is justified by the previously proved finite-gradient-energy estimates. The code substitutes the test-gradient chain rule and the equality between the explicit measurable score field and the actual relative score. The remaining rearrangement is bilinearity of the inner product and scalar multiplication.

steps.title: The bounded time chain rule without a spatial time-majorant
steps.body:
On any \(0<a\le b\), the weighted primitive has derivative \(\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t\). The kernel theorem proves \(\dot p\in L^1([a,b]\times E)\), while \(\chi_m\) is bounded by \((m+1)\pi/2\). Thus the derivative of the weighted primitive is jointly integrable.

Integrability at time \(a\) follows from the bounded-entropy lemma after rewriting Gibbs measure as \(J(y)dy\). The generic spacetime FTC/Fubini theorem then yields

\[H_m(b)-H_m(a)=\int_a^b q_m(t)\,dt.\]

Applying the same identity on every subinterval proves absolute continuity of \(H_m\); Lebesgue differentiation gives \(H_m'(t)=q_m(t)\) almost everywhere. In code, hdot is obtained by multiplying the actual spacetime \(L^1\) derivative by a bounded measurable function, hderiv supplies the pointwise chain rule, and hweight changes the integrated weighted primitive back to \(H_m\). No common bound on all time derivatives by a single spatial function is assumed.

steps.title: Expressing the flux on one independent probability space
steps.body:
Take \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Z\sim N(0,I)\) independently, and set \(Y_t=X-tg(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\). Define

\[V_t(X,Z)=g(X)-\frac{\sqrt{2t}}{2t}Z,\qquad \widehat S_t(X,Z)=S_t(Y_t),\qquad q(t)=-\mathbb E\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle.\]

The three Lean definitions give exactly these fields and the raw entropy flux. A fixed product probability space is used at every time, which makes joint measurability and time dominated convergence explicit. The field \(V_t\) is the frozen Gaussian spatial flux divided by its transition density after substituting the actual update.

steps.title: Square integrability of the two actual Gaussian factors
steps.body:
The initial gradient belongs to \(L^2(\mu)\), and the standard Gaussian noise belongs to \(L^2\). Pulling both to the independent product space and taking their scalar combination proves \(V_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma)\). The actual relative score belongs to \(L^2(\rho_t)\). Since \(\rho_t\) is the pushforward of \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) by \(Y_t\), the measurable-map characterization of \(L^2\) gives

\[\widehat S_t=S_t\circ Y_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma).\]

frozenGaussianVelocityField_memLp performs the product-space linear combination. interpolationScoreAlongUpdate_memLp first identifies the explicit score with the actual gradient of \(\log r_t\), then applies memLp_map_measure_iff. Consequently their inner product is integrable.

steps.title: The exact frozen velocity energy
steps.body:
Independence and the zero Gaussian mean cancel the drift-noise cross term:

\[\mathbb E\|V_t\|^2=\mathbb E\|g(X)\|^2+\frac{d}{2t},\qquad t>0.\]

The proof specializes the already verified affine-Gaussian moment formula with coefficients \(1\) and \(-\sqrt{2t}/(2t)\). The squared coefficient is \((2t)/(4t^2)=1/(2t)\), using \((\sqrt{2t})^2=2t\). This exact finite energy gives a compact-time bound that is uniform away from zero. No moment of \(X\) itself is used.

steps.title: Transporting the bounded flux to independent noise
steps.body:
The law of \((X,Y_t)\) has density \(K_t(x,y)\) with respect to \(\mu(dx)dy\). Therefore the joint flux identity becomes

\[q_m(t)=-\mathbb E\!\left[w_m(\log r_t(Y_t))\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle\right].\]

The code introduces the measurable map T sending \((x,z)\) to \((x,Y_t)\), the kernel K, and the weighted pairing F. frozenGaussianJointLaw_eq_density identifies the pushforward law. The integral under its real density becomes \(\iint K F\), and integral_map_of_stronglyMeasurable changes that integral back to the independent product space. Finally \(Y_t-(X-tg(X))=\sqrt{2t}Z\) reduces the residual to the declared velocity field. The change of variables concerns the actual Gaussian law and does not assume an invariant Euler step.

steps.title: Removing the truncation at fixed positive time
steps.body:
The raw pairing \(\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle\) is integrable by the two \(L^2\) estimates. The scalar map \((x,z)\mapsto\log r_t(Y_t)\) is measurable. Since \(0\le w_m\le1\) and \(w_m\to1\), dominated convergence on the independent probability space yields

\[q_m(t)\longrightarrow q(t),\qquad t>0.\]

The dominating function is \(|\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle|\). Crucially this limit is performed after spatial integration by parts; it does not ask for integrability of \(|\log r_t|\,|\dot p_t|\), which is not supplied by the original assumptions.

steps.title: A fixed-reference formula for the relative Fisher energy
steps.body:
Define

\[I(t)=\int r_t(y)\|S_t(y)\|^2\,d\pi(y).\]

The actual relative-density identity gives \(I(t)=\int\|S_t\|^2\,d\rho_t\). Applying the actual Gaussian pushforward once more yields

\[\mathbb E\|\widehat S_t\|^2=I(t).\]

The first definition fixes the reference measure for time measurability and spacetime integrability. The equality uses interpolationRelativeScoreField_weighted_energy and the measurable-map Bochner integral formula. The proof supplies strong measurability of the score norm square explicitly, fixing time in the joint measurable score field.

steps.title: A uniform bound for every truncated flux
steps.body:
For any vectors \(v,s\) and any \(0\le w\le1\),

\[|w\langle v,s\rangle|\le\|v\|\|s\|\le\tfrac12(\|v\|^2+\|s\|^2).\]

The second inequality is \((\|v\|-\|s\|)^2\ge0\). Integrate on the independent Gaussian space, use the norm inequality for Bochner integrals, and substitute the two exact energies:

\[|q_m(t)|\le\frac12\left(G_0+\frac d{2t}+I(t)\right),\qquad G_0=\int\|g\|^2\,d\mu.\]

In Lean, hi proves integrability of the bounded weighted pairing, hmajor proves integrability of the quadratic majorant, and hpoint is the pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz/Young estimate. Thus the bound is justified for every truncation without assuming convergence or integrability of the eventual entropy derivative.

steps.title: Joint measurability of both time fluxes
steps.body: The bounded flux is a parameter integral of \(\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\dot p_t(y)\). Both factors are jointly measurable in \((t,y)\), so parameter integration makes \(t\mapsto q_m(t)\) measurable. The raw flux uses the fixed independent space: the map \((t,x,z)\mapsto(t,Y_t)\) is measurable, the explicit relative-score field is jointly strongly measurable, and the velocity field is a measurable algebraic combination of \(g(X)\), \(t^{-1}\), \(\sqrt{2t}\), and \(Z\). Their inner product and its parameter integral are measurable. The definitions at nonpositive times serve only to make these globally specified measurable functions; all analytic conclusions are restricted to positive times.

steps.title: The integrable majorant for the time limit
steps.body:
Fix \(0<a\le b\). The actual Gaussian energy theorem proves \(I\in L^1([a,b])\). Set

\[D(t)=\tfrac12\left(G_0+\frac d{2a}+I(t)\right).\]

The interval has finite Lebesgue measure, so the constant term is integrable; hence \(D\in L^1([a,b])\). Since \(t\ge a>0\), \(d/(2t)\le d/(2a)\). The uniform flux estimate gives \(|q_m(t)|\le D(t)\) for every \(m\). The fixed-time limit \(q_m(t)\to q(t)\), followed by continuity of the absolute value, also gives \(|q(t)|\le D(t)\). The formal statement supplies the single majorant together with all three verified integrability/domination conclusions, ready for dominated convergence in time.

steps.title: The full actual entropy identity
steps.body:
Let \(H(t)=H(\rho_t\mid\pi)\), represented by the actual finite KL. For each truncation,

\[H_m(b)-H_m(a)=\int_a^b q_m(t)\,dt.\]

At both endpoints, the spatial dominated-convergence theorem gives \(H_m\to H\). In time, the common integrable majorant \(D\) and the pointwise convergence \(q_m\to q\) give \(\int_a^b q_m\to\int_a^b q\). Uniqueness of limits therefore yields

\[H(b)-H(a)=\int_a^b q(t)\,dt.\]

interpolationEntropy_integral_identity applies the general integral_identity_of_dominated_limits under Lebesgue measure restricted to \((a,b]\). Its endpoint convergence hypotheses are the already established actual-KL limits, and all time domination comes from the previous theorem. No entropy-path regularity is supplied as a hypothesis.

steps.title: Absolute continuity and the a.e. derivative of actual entropy
steps.body:
The raw flux is measurable and satisfies \(|q|\le D\), so it is integrable on every positive-time compact interval. Apply the full entropy identity with terminal time \(t\in[a,b]\):

\[H(t)=H(a)+\int_a^t q(u)\,du.\]

An indefinite integral of an \(L^1\) function is absolutely continuous, and the Lebesgue differentiation theorem identifies its derivative almost everywhere. Thus

\[H\in AC([a,b]),\qquad H'(t)=q(t)\quad\text{for almost every }t\in(a,b).\]

The Lean proof derives interval integrability from the actual raw-flux measurability and the verified majorant, then invokes regularity_of_integral_identity. This completes the analytic time-regularity bridge from the original potential, LSI and finite initial score-energy assumptions. A later score-pairing identity rewrites the raw Gaussian flux as negative Fisher energy plus the frozen gradient discrepancy, yielding the quantitative entropy-production estimate.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/UnconditionalTheo.title: The full Gaussian ULA entropy theorem
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/UnconditionalTheo.summary:
For a differentiable potential with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, its normalized Gibbs target satisfying LSI with constant \(\alpha>0\), and a finite-KL initial probability law, this module proves the actual ULA bound

\[\mathrm{KL}(\rho_k\mid\nu)\le e^{-\alpha hk}\mathrm{KL}(\rho_0\mid\nu)+8hdL^2/\alpha,\quad0The final conclusion includes finiteness of the actual divergence. All score moments, density calculus, weak equations, entropy endpoints, and numerical compatibility estimates are supplied by the preceding modules. The theorem applies also in dimension zero.

steps.title: Handle the singleton state space and a zero smoothness parameter
steps.body:
On a singleton state space every probability measure is equal: any measurable set either contains the unique point and is the whole space, or is empty. Measure extensionality and probability normalization therefore identify any two laws. In particular their KL divergence is zero.

Independently of dimension, a positive admissible step forces \(L>0\). If \(L=0\), Lean’s total-field convention gives \(\alpha/(4L^2)=0\), contradicting \(0

steps.title: Prove finiteness at every actual ULA iterate
steps.body:
Start from the supplied finite initial KL and induct on \(k\). If \(\rho_k\) has finite KL, the direct entropy/score estimate gives \(\nabla U\in L^2(\rho_k)\). For the actual positive-time Gaussian interpolation, the Lebesgue score energy is at most \(d/(2h)\), and the propagated gradient moment is finite. Thus relative Fisher information is finite. LSI with \(\alpha>0\) then gives finite KL of the output.

The endpoint identity identifies that output with \(\rho_{k+1}\). This induction uses no step restriction beyond positivity; it is a separate guard that prevents the extended value infinity from disappearing under toReal.

steps.title: Derive all scalar step restrictions
steps.body:
In positive dimension, the bounded sinusoidal tests in Compatibility give \(\alpha\le L\). Since \(\alpha>0\), also \(L>0\). Multiplying the original restriction by \(4L^2>0\) gives \(4hL^2\le\alpha\le L\), hence \(hL\le1/4\). Multiplying \(\alpha\le L\) by \(h>0\) also gives \(\alpha h\le1/4\).

The final theorem splits off the singleton case before invoking this positive-dimensional argument. No separate compatibility assumption is required.

steps.title: Apply LSI to the actual positive-time density
steps.body:
Finite initial KL supplies the initial gradient moment. The actual Gaussian mixture is positive C¹ relative to Gibbs, has finite KL, and has finite Fisher information at every \(t>0\). Apply the original extended-valued LSI to this density. Since both sides are finite, order is preserved on passing to their real values:

\[2\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}( ho_t\mid u)\le I_t.\]

The integral form identifies \(I_t\) with \(\int\|\mathcal S(t,y)\|^2d ho_t(y)\), using the proved equality between the measurable score field and \( abla\log r_t\), and the equality \(r_t u= ho_t\). The second version keeps the extended-Fisher notation for the entropy-production assembly.

steps.title: Supply the actual analytic inputs to scalar comparison
steps.body:
Fix any finite-KL probability law \(\mu\). The score-exponential argument gives the integrability of \(\| abla U\|^2\) and

\[G_0\le4L^2H_ u(\mu)/\alpha+2dL.\]

The bounded-log entropy identity proves local absolute continuity of the actual entropy \(H(t)\) on every \([s,h]\) with \(s>0\). The actual Gaussian weak equation and Young estimate give \(H^{\prime}\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\) almost everywhere. The preceding LSI estimate supplies \(2\alpha H\le I\).

The explicit initial majorant \(M\) is continuous at zero, satisfies \(M(0)=H_ u(\mu)\), and bounds \(H(t)\) for sufficiently small positive \(t\). These are exactly the premises of one_step_entropy_of_ae_interpolation, giving

\[H_ u(\mu P_h)\le e^{-\alpha h}H_ u(\mu)+6h^2dL^2.\]

The singleton case instead uses equality of probability laws and nonnegativity of the right side. No density path, weak equation, entropy derivative, or moment estimate is a theorem argument.

steps.title: Derive the actual discrete recurrence
steps.body:
The law \(\rho_k\) is a probability measure by the proved Gaussian Markov construction. Its KL is finite by the induction above. Apply the single-transition estimate with \(\mu=\rho_k\). The interpolation endpoint is precisely \(\rho_{k+1}\), yielding

\[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2dL^2.\]

ulaEntropy is the real value of the actual KL of ulaLaws. The recurrence is derived here; it is not supplied as a premise.

steps.title: Sum the recurrence and retain the finite-KL guard
steps.body:
Return the already-proved output finiteness as the first component of the conclusion. In positive dimension, the step estimates give \(\alpha h\le1/4\). The scalar geometric-sum theorem applied to the actual recurrence gives

\[H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+\frac{6h^2dL^2}{1-e^{-\alpha h}}\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+\frac{8hdL^2}{\alpha}.\]

The final inequality uses \(1-e^{-x}\ge3x/4\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\). In dimension zero, equality of probability measures makes the left side zero and the result follows by nonnegativity.

The complete binder list contains only differentiability, global gradient Lipschitzness, the original Gibbs LSI, positivity of \(\alpha\) and the step, the paper’s step restriction, and finite initial KL. The target probability normalization is included in the LSI definition. Lean’s kernel checks the entire chain, and Check.lean prints its axiom dependencies.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEntropy.l.title: Construct spatial smoothness, finite Fisher information and finite actual entropy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianEntropy.l.summary: For \(t>0\), the actual frozen Gaussian update \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}\,Z\) has the positive mixture density constructed in InterpolationDensity.lean. This module proves its spatial \(C^1\) regularity by differentiating the displayed Gaussian integral. Bayes' posterior formula and Jensen's inequality then give the universal Lebesgue Fisher bound \(\int\| abla\log p_t\|^2p_t\le d/(2t)\). If the initial gradient has finite energy, the relative score \( abla\log r_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t\) also has finite energy. The target LSI consequently proves finite actual KL at every positive time. No initial density or second moment of the state is assumed.

steps.title: Bound the quadratic Gaussian envelope uniformly
steps.body:
For \(a>0\), put \(u=a\|z\|^2\). The scalar inequality \(u e^{-u}\le e^{-1}\le1\) gives

\[\|z\|^2e^{-a\|z\|^2}\le a^{-1}.\]

Lean multiplies the desired inequality by the positive number \(a\), rewrites its left side as \(u e^{-u}\), and applies Real.mul_exp_neg_le_exp_neg_one. The final cancellation uses mul_inv_cancel₀ with the explicit nonzero witness from ha. This global bound later controls the conditional displacement variance even when the initial distribution has no moments.

steps.title: Bound the first Gaussian envelope without an initial moment
steps.body:
The elementary estimate \(r\le1+r^2\), together with \(e^{-ar^2}\le1\) and the quadratic envelope bound, gives

\[\|z\|e^{-a\|z\|^2}\le1+a^{-1}.\]

The proof records the exponential bound as hexp, the quadratic bound as hsq, and \(r\le1+r^2\) as hnorm. Multiplication by the nonnegative exponential and addition then yield the displayed result. The bound is intentionally simple rather than optimal: a finite constant independent of the proposed state and mixture component is what dominated differentiation requires.

steps.title: Specify the real Gaussian kernel and its derivative map
steps.body:
With precision \(a\), center \(c\), and the already normalized Gaussian constant \(N_a\), define

\[K_a(c,y)=N_a e^{-a\|y-c\|^2},\qquad D_yK_a(c,y)[v]=-2aK_a(c,y)\langle y-c,v\rangle.\]

realGaussianKernel is the ordinary real density. realGaussianKernelDeriv is its proposed Fréchet derivative as a continuous linear functional: the scalar realGaussianKernel a c y * (-2 * a) multiplies innerSL ℝ (y - c). The precision parameter keeps this helper reusable; the ULA specialization is \(a=1/(4t)\). The next theorem proves that this proposed derivative is the actual derivative.

steps.title: Differentiate the kernel by the squared-norm and exponential chain rules
steps.body:
The map \(y\mapsto y-c\) has derivative the identity. The squared-norm derivative is \(v\mapsto2\langle y-c,v\rangle\). Multiplication by \(-a\), exponentiation, and multiplication by \(N_a\) therefore produce exactly

\[D_yK_a(c,y)[v]=-2aK_a(c,y)\langle y-c,v\rangle.\]

The local Lean proof hd is this sequence of sub_const, norm_sq, const_mul, exp, and a final const_mul. The final extensionality argument compares the two continuous linear maps at an arbitrary vector v; elementary scalar algebra proves they agree. No regularity of the potential is involved in this fixed-center calculation.

steps.title: Find a common integrable bound for all component derivatives
steps.body:
The norm of the inner-product functional \(v\mapsto\langle y-c,v\rangle\) equals \(\|y-c\|\). Hence

\[\|D_yK_a(c,y)\|=2aN_a\|y-c\|e^{-a\|y-c\|^2}\le2aN_a(1+a^{-1}).\]

Lean uses norm_smul and innerSL_apply_norm, removes absolute values using positivity of \(N_a\) and the exponential, and applies the first Gaussian envelope bound. The resulting constant is independent of both \(y\) and \(c\). A probability mixture therefore integrates this bound without requiring any moment of its center map.

steps.title: Define the actual proposed mixture derivative
steps.body:
For \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\), define the continuous-linear-map-valued integral

\[P'_t(y)=\int D_yK_{1/(4t)}(c_t(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

This is interpolationLebesgueDensityDeriv. The symbol here denotes a spatial Fréchet derivative, not the time derivative of the density. The following domination lemmas establish its integrability, continuity, and equality with the actual spatial derivative of the explicit mixture. Keeping the definition as an integral of linear maps makes each directional evaluation correspond directly to the component kernel derivative.

steps.title: Integrate each Gaussian component over the mixing probability law
steps.body:
For a measurable center map \(c\), the function \(x\mapsto K_a(c(x),y)\) is measurable and satisfies \(0\le K_a(c(x),y)\le N_a\). Since \(\mu\) is a probability measure, the constant \(N_a\) is integrable, and so is the kernel.

Lean starts from integrable_const and uses Integrable.mono'. Its first obligation is measurability, assembled from the center's measurability by fun_prop. Its second obligation is the norm bound; positivity removes the absolute value, and Real.exp_le_one_iff supplies the Gaussian peak bound.

steps.title: Integrate the continuous-linear-map-valued component derivative
steps.body:
The common derivative bound is a finite constant \(2aN_a(1+a^{-1})\). Therefore

\[\int\|D_yK_a(c(x),y)\|\,d\mu(x)<\infty.\]

The Lean proof again applies Integrable.mono' to an integrable constant, now with values in the Banach space of continuous linear functionals. Measurability follows from the explicit derivative formula; the second obligation is exactly norm_realGaussianKernelDeriv_le. This supplies the Bochner-integrability premise needed to identify the derivative of the mixture.

steps.title: Differentiate the mixture under the integral sign
steps.body:
For each proposed state \(y\),

\[D_y\!\left(\int K_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x)\right)=\int D_yK_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

Lean applies hasFDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_of_fderiv_le with the whole spatial domain as the common neighborhood. Kernel integrability supplies the value at the base point, derivative-kernel integrability supplies derivative measurability, the uniform Gaussian bound supplies domination, and hasFDerivAt_realGaussianKernel supplies pointwise differentiation. All these premises were proved from the actual kernel. In particular, a derivative of the mixture is not among the hypotheses.

steps.title: Prove continuity of the mixture derivative with the same domination
steps.body:
For every fixed initial point \(x\), the derivative kernel \(y\mapsto D_yK_a(c(x),y)\) is continuous. Its operator norm is bounded by the same integrable constant for every \(y\). Dominated continuity therefore proves continuity of

\[y\longmapsto\int D_yK_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

The Lean theorem continuous_of_dominated requires measurability of every section, a common integrable bound, and almost-everywhere continuity of the component map. The preceding lemmas provide the first three facts, while the explicit formula and fun_prop prove continuity. This continuity is what strengthens mere differentiability to \(C^1\).

steps.title: Combine the derivative and its continuity into a C1 theorem
steps.body:
A function is \(C^1\) exactly when it has a continuous Fréchet derivative. Apply this criterion to the derivative field \(y\mapsto\int D_yK_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x)\).

contDiff_one_iff_hasFDerivAt reduces the Lean proof to the two preceding results: continuous_integral_realGaussianKernelDeriv gives continuity of this field, and hasFDerivAt_integral_realGaussianKernel identifies it as the derivative at every point. The conclusion applies to every probability mixing measure, including singular ones.

steps.title: Apply Gaussian smoothing to the actual frozen-drift law
steps.body:
The explicit real density of the update satisfies

\[p_t(y)=\int K_{1/(4t)}(x-t\nabla U(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

The proof first establishes this equality as heq, using the integral formula from InterpolationDensity.lean and the scalar identity \(-\|z\|^2/(4t)=-(1/(4t))\|z\|^2\). The center map is measurable because the gradient is Lipschitz. The general Gaussian-mixture \(C^1\) theorem then applies with positive precision \(1/(4t)\). Thus spatial regularity is a consequence of the actual transition law, not an assumption about a chosen interpolation density.

steps.title: Identify the exact spatial derivative of the actual density
steps.body:
The derivative field defined earlier is now certified:

\[D_yp_t(y)=P'_t(y)=\int D_yK_{1/(4t)}(x-t\nabla U(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

Lean applies the general dominated-differentiation theorem to the measurable frozen center and rewrites its mixture back to interpolationLebesgueDensity. The final rfl checks that the derivative integral is exactly interpolationLebesgueDensityDeriv. This identity is later used to define a jointly measurable score field while retaining its agreement with the actual spatial derivative.

steps.title: Recover C1 regularity of the potential from its Lipschitz gradient
steps.body:
The assumptions are differentiability of \(U\) and Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla U\). The Riesz isometry identifies

\[DU(x)=\operatorname{Riesz}(\nabla U(x)).\]

Since the Riesz map and the gradient are continuous, \(x\mapsto DU(x)\) is continuous. The criterion contDiff_one_iff_fderiv now yields \(U\in C^1\). Lean rewrites the derivative field by toDual_comp_gradient and composes the two continuous maps. No Hessian or twice-continuously-differentiable potential is assumed.

steps.title: Establish spatial admissibility of the actual Gibbs-relative density
steps.body:
The relative density is \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). The partition factor \(Z\) is constant in space, \(e^U\) is \(C^1\) because \(U\) is \(C^1\), and the actual Gaussian mixture \(p_t\) is \(C^1\). Therefore \(r_t\) is \(C^1\) at every positive time.

The Lean proof follows this product exactly using contDiff_const.mul, the potential theorem followed by exp, and interpolationLebesgueDensity_contDiff. Together with pointwise positivity and normalization from the density-construction module, this discharges the smooth test-class premises of IsLogSobolev.

steps.title: Apply the target LSI directly to the constructed interpolation law
steps.body:
Use the actual positive normalized \(C^1\) relative density as the LSI test. This gives

\[2\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\rho_t\mid\nu)\le I(\rho_t\mid\nu).\]

This theorem retains extended nonnegative values, so neither finiteness is silently assumed. Lean obtains the Gibbs probability instance from hLSI.1; hLSI.2 is applied with the already proved positivity, \(C^1\) regularity, and relative probability normalization. Finally tiltedMeasure_interpolationRelativeDensity replaces the induced tilted measure with the actual Gaussian interpolation law. The only functional-inequality hypothesis is the target's LSI.

steps.title: Record the square-norm Jensen inequality for probability measures
steps.body:
For a square-integrable random vector \(F\) under a probability measure, convexity of squared norm gives

\[\left\|\int F\,d\mu\right\|^2\le\int\|F\|^2\,d\mu.\]

Lean obtains convexity by applying ConvexOn.pow to convexity and nonnegativity of the norm, with exponent two. map_integral_le then applies Jensen on the whole vector space. MemLp supplies both integrability of \(F\) and of \(\|F\|^2\). This general lemma is used under the normalized Gaussian posterior at each proposed state.

steps.title: Define Bayes posterior on the initial mixture component
steps.body:
At a fixed proposed point \(y\), let \(p(y)=\int K_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x)\). The posterior law of the initial component is

\[\lambda_y(dx)=\frac{K_a(c(x),y)}{p(y)}\,\mu(dx).\]

gaussianPosterior constructs this measure with withDensity. The definition is total, while its intended probability interpretation uses \(a>0\), measurability of the center, and positivity of the mixing probability law. The following lemmas establish positivity of the denominator and normalization explicitly, before using Jensen.

steps.title: Prove the real mixture denominator is everywhere positive
steps.body:
Every component \(K_a(c(x),y)\) is positive because its normalizer and exponential are positive. Its support as a function of \(x\) is therefore the whole initial-state space, which has probability one.

The Lean proof uses integral_pos_iff_support_of_nonneg, with integrability from the common Gaussian peak bound. The local support equality hs converts the condition to positive mass of the whole space. Thus \(p(y)>0\) at every point, allowing Bayes normalization and the logarithmic score to be defined pointwise.

steps.title: Check posterior normalization by cancellation of the actual mixture integral
steps.body:
The total posterior mass equals

\[\int\frac{K_a(c(x),y)}{p(y)}\,d\mu(x)=\frac{p(y)}{p(y)}=1.\]

Lean first records positive denominator hp and integrable kernel hq. The definition of withDensity expresses mass as a nonnegative integral. ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal converts it to the ordinary integral, justified by integrability and nonnegativity of the normalized kernel. integral_div pulls out the denominator and div_self hp.ne' performs the normalization.

steps.title: Prove posterior displacement has finite conditional second moment
steps.body:
The posterior may arise from an initial law without moments. Nevertheless, at each fixed \(y\),

\[\int\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\lambda_y(x)=\frac{1}{p(y)}\int K_a(c(x),y)\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\mu(x)<\infty.\]

The quadratic Gaussian envelope bounds the numerator's integrand by \(N_a/a\). Lean's integrable_withDensity_iff_integrable_smul' changes posterior integrability into the displayed weighted integral under \(\mu\). The proof hsquare dominates it by the integrable constant \(N_a/(ap(y))\). Measurability follows from the measurable center and absolute continuity of the posterior. The standard \(L^2\) characterization then supplies MemLp for the displacement.

steps.title: Identify the mixture score as the posterior component-score mean
steps.body:
Dividing the mixture derivative by its positive value gives

\[\nabla\log p(y)=-2a\int(y-c(x))\,d\lambda_y(x).\]

Lean differentiates \(\log p\) using the actual mixture derivative and the nonzero denominator. The Riesz inverse commutes with the Bochner integral; hgrad identifies the inverse image of each component derivative with \(-2aK_a(c(x),y)(y-c(x))\). Expanding the posterior via integral_withDensity_eq_integral_toReal_smul gives the same integral divided by \(p(y)\). The final scalar cancellations establish the equality pointwise, rather than merely choosing an almost-everywhere score representative.

steps.title: Use posterior Jensen to bound the pointwise mixture score energy
steps.body:
Applying square-norm Jensen to the posterior score identity yields

\[p(y)\|\nabla\log p(y)\|^2\le4a^2\int K_a(c(x),y)\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\mu(x).\]

The posterior is a probability measure, and its displacement is square integrable by the preceding lemmas; these are the exact hypotheses needed for Jensen. Lean records that inequality as hj, scales it by \(4a^2p(y)\), expands the posterior integral, and cancels \(p(y)\) using positivity. This gives a usable unnormalized density inequality whose right side can be integrated over the proposed state by Fubini.

steps.title: Compute the exact Gaussian component displacement energy
steps.body:
